Allyl halides are organic compounds that include an allyl group, made up of a carbon atom joined to two other carbons via a double bond, having the formula (CH₂=CH-CH₂). This group is attached to a halogen atom, creating different kinds of allyl halides. The prevalent allyl halides consist of: - Allyl chloride (3-chloro-1-propene), having the chemical formula CH2=CH-CH2Cl. - Allyl bromide (3-bromo-1-propene), with the chemical formula CH2=CH-CH2Br. - Allyl iodide (3-iodo-1-propene), with the chemical formula CH2=CH-CH2I. - Allyl fluoride (3-fluoro-1-propene), with the chemical formula CH2=CH-CH2F. These compounds are widely used in organic synthesis and as intermediates in the production of various chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Allyl halides are noted for their reactivity, particularly in reactions such as nucleophilic substitution and addition across double bonds. For further exploration and research, you might look into sections that cover the allyl group and its various applications in chemical studies.

The paper provides a detailed examination of unitary representations for the $\mathfrak{su}(\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}|\mathsf{m})$ Lie superalgebra. The researchers conduct an in-depth study of the algebraic framework, emphasizing the isomorphisms and automorphisms that define the structure of the algebra. They also examine how these properties affect the classification of unitary representations, demonstrating that each must be categorized as either maximum or minimum weight depending on certain conditions. A key contribution of the paper is the introduction of a novel graphical method for analyzing the algebraic structure, using a two-dimensional lattice to represent the weight lattice and the grading functions. This method facilitates a clearer comprehension of the algebra and its representations, thereby streamlining the process of determining the circumstances in which unitary representations can occur. The authors also provide a proof that the $\mathfrak{su}(\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}|\mathsf{r},\mathsf{s})$ real form, with all parameters non-zero, only admits the trivial unitary representation. This result is significant as it sets a clear boundary on the types of unitary representations that can be associated with this algebra. Furthermore, the paper explores the impact of duality transformations on the classification of unitary representations. The authors show that while some transformations can lead to a loss of the highest-weight property, others, specifically those involving $p$-odd nodes, preserve this property. This insight is crucial for understanding the structure of the algebra and its representations. The paper presents its results in a clear and succinct way, using both mathematical proofs and visual aids to support its claims. The use of a weight lattice to represent the fundamental weights of the algebra is a particularly innovative aspect of the research, offering a new perspective on the classification of unitary representations. In conclusion, the paper makes a significant contribution to the understanding of unitary representations for the $\mathfrak{su}(\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}|\mathsf{m})$ Lie superalgebra. The authors' novel method for examining the algebraic structure and their thorough analysis of the circumstances in which unitary representations occur offer important perspectives for scholars working in this area. The clear presentation of the results and the use of graphical methods to illustrate key concepts make the paper accessible to a wide audience, enhancing its impact and relevance.

This section offers an in-depth examination of the cross sections and kinematic distributions associated with $W$-pair production in proton-proton ($pp$) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 14 TeV, with particular attention given to the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Tevatron. The analysis shows that one-loop corrections to the total cross sections are important, especially when the vector bosons have high transverse momenta or large invariant masses. The authors suggest a specific scale selection to address these corrections and examine the impact of varying the scale on the cross-sections, showing that the next-to-leading order (NLO) outcomes show less sensitivity to the scale, particularly when a jet veto is applied. The study introduces a novel approach to improve the robustness of the perturbative series by employing a jet veto, which suppresses one-loop contributions and reveals a consistent behavior across different scenarios. The researchers also examine the effect of extra constraints on the transverse momentum of charged leptons, discovering that these can markedly influence the scale dependence and the reliability of the leading-order results. The study's new contributions include a detailed examination of scale dependence and the introduction of a jet veto to improve the robustness of the perturbative expansion, both of which are crucial for understanding the dynamics of $W$-pair production at the LHC and the Tevatron. The findings yield important information about the theoretical uncertainties associated with scale dependence and present an improved characterization of $W$-pair production at these colliders. Furthermore, the study presents kinematic distributions for the processes $pp \to W^-W^+ \to \ell^- \bar u \ell^{\prime +} u^\prime$ and $p \bar{p} \to W^-W^+ \to \ell^- \bar u \ell^{\prime +} u^\prime$, focusing on eight observables defined in terms of momenta. The distributions at the Tevatron are shown at both leading order (LO) and NLO, revealing that NLO corrections are generally moderate, except for the missing transverse momentum distribution. The angular distributions exhibit more stable behavior compared to those resembling $p_T$, which frequently show significant NLO effects in their tail regions. Overall, this section provides an in-depth analysis of the cross-sections and kinematic distributions for $W$-pair production, emphasizing the importance of identifying and mitigating scale dependence, as well as the impact of additional cuts on the validity of the perturbative expansion. The findings contribute to the field by offering a deeper understanding of the behavior of $W$-pair production at high-energy colliders.

Pelvic wall cancer can result in discomfort in one of the iliac fossae. Patients who experience pain during ambulation, severe enough to require bed rest, might have cancer that has either attached to or spread into the iliacus muscle. Hypogastric pain, located between the navel and the pubic bone, is often associated with cancers of the uterus and bladder. It can also occur in colorectal cancer, particularly when the tumor extends into or becomes attached to the uterus or bladder. Visceral pain, which arises from the internal organs of the body, is often widespread and difficult to locate precisely. It is frequently referred to more distant and typically superficial areas. For example, sudden bleeding into a hepatocellular carcinoma may result in intense pain in the upper right abdomen, which can be life-threatening and require immediate surgical or other urgent treatments. A tumor can enlarge the liver significantly, leading to stretching of its capsule and causing aching pain in the right hypochondrium. Other causes of pain in an enlarged liver include: - Traction of the supporting ligaments when standing or walking - The liver pressing against the rib cage or pinching the abdominal wall - Straining the lumbar spine - In some postures, the liver may pinch the parietal peritoneum against the lower rib cage, resulting in sharp, transient pain that is relieved by changing position Additionally, a tumor may infiltrate the liver's capsule, causing dull or occasionally stabbing pain. In contrast, cancers of the kidney and spleen generally result in less discomfort compared to tumors in the liver. Kidney tumors typically cause pain only when the organ has been significantly affected. It is important to note that the information provided here is general and may not apply to every individual case. Diagnosis and treatment should always be based on a thorough medical evaluation by a qualified healthcare professional.

High Dynamic Range Imaging (HDRI) is a technique that enables the capture and display of a wider range of light intensities than conventional imaging methods. This technology proves especially beneficial in situations involving a large difference in brightness between the lightest and darkest parts, like in exterior photography or graphic design applications. The creation of HDRI in computer graphics has been strongly linked to progress in shader technology, which are compact programs responsible for controlling how images are displayed on a screen. The evolution of shader models has played a crucial role in enabling the rendering of high-dynamic-range images. The initial release of Shader Model 1.0 with DirectX 8 in the early 2000s introduced standard lighting, which illuminated 3D worlds. However, this method had limitations. The lighting precision was confined to 8-bit integers, which restricted the contrast ratio to 256:1. This showed that the maximum white could only be 255 levels brighter than the darkest tone above pure black. Additionally, lighting calculations were based on integers, which did not accurately represent the real world, where light intensities can vary infinitely. On December 24, 2002, Microsoft released DirectX 9.0, which included Shader Model 2.0. This release represented a significant step forward in enabling the production of high-dynamic-range images. Shader Model 2.0 allowed for lighting precision beyond the 8-bit limitation, with programmers having the option to use up to 24 bits for lighting precision. Although calculations were still primarily integer-based, this increased precision provided a more accurate representation of lighting in 3D scenes. One of the earliest graphics cards to offer native support for DirectX 9.0 was ATI's Radeon 9700. However, it took several years for game developers to fully utilize the capabilities of Shader Model 2.0 in their games. On August 23, 2003, Microsoft further updated DirectX to version 9.0b, which introduced the Pixel Shader 2.x. This update further enhanced the capabilities of shader technology, paving the way for more advanced rendering techniques and a more realistic representation of high-dynamic-range images in computer graphics.

We began our investigation by conducting a Grey Literature Review (GLR) to gain an initial insight into the approaches used by practitioners in handling flaky tests. This review is foundational for our subsequent mitigation analysis and informs the design of our interviews. Our GLR is exploratory and non-exhaustive, aiming to map the existing mitigation measures. We adhered to established guidelines for conducting a systematic review, focusing on materials that detail practitioners' experiences and strategies in addressing flakiness, such as technical reports, presentations, and blogs. Our search method yielded 276,000 results, which were narrowed down to 100 articles through the use of an optimized Google search query. We meticulously selected 56 articles written by practitioners that provided practical insights into flakiness mitigation, excluding theoretical discussions and research articles. In our analysis, we applied a quality assessment checklist to ensure the relevance and reliability of the selected articles. We determined three key exclusion factors: objectivity, methodological sufficiency, and subject matter appropriateness, which enabled us to narrow down our selection to 38 articles. Using a consensus-based approach, we developed a classification of the mitigation strategies outlined by practitioners, as presented in Table~\ref{table:strategies} and elaborated upon in Section~\ref{sec:results}. Our GLR identified a notable gap in the literature concerning the reasoning behind the selection of mitigation measures and their outcomes, which our interviews were designed to tackle. Furthermore, the implications of our study point to future efforts in utilizing monitoring and log analysis, creating testing standards, and building tools for identifying root causes and reproducing flaky tests. These insights open avenues for research that could assist practitioners in managing flakiness more effectively. Our introduction underscores the critical importance of software testing in modern development practices, while also addressing the challenges posed by flaky tests, which can reduce developers' trust in test frameworks and impact the overall software quality. We highlight the prevalence and significant cost associated with flaky tests in large-scale software systems, citing Google's scenario where over 50 million test cases are executed daily, along with the considerable efforts required to manage these unreliable tests. Our study builds on previous empirical research by examining the industrial context of flakiness and conducting qualitative analyses based on 14 practitioner interviews. By employing this approach, we aim to identify the typical tactics used by practitioners and explore how research-informed methods could enhance these practices. Our research centers on investigating the localization of flakiness, how practitioners perceive its impact, and the techniques they employ to deal with it.

This section introduces a novel approach for variable selection in high-dimensional data, leveraging the harmonic mean p-value and a refined tuning parameter selection strategy. The proposed method transcends the limitations of traditional approaches, such as Fisher’s method, because it does not depend on the assumption that p-values are independent of each other. We use p-values to construct an estimator, $\hat{\pi}$, that represents the proportion of non-zero coefficients, a crucial element in enhancing the selection of the tuning parameter, $\lambda$, in penalized regression methods. Specifically, we introduce a data-driven approach to determine a tighter and more efficient range for $\lambda$, based on the estimated proportion of non-zero variables, $\hat{\pi}p$. This strategy is exemplified through a Lasso solution path and cross-validation curve, demonstrating a significant reduction in the search space for \(\lambda\) and leading to a more accurate model selection. The innovative contributions of this research are manifold: 1. The proposal of a harmonic mean p-value reduces the necessity for p-values to be independent, thus expanding the scope in which the method can be applied. 2. The development of a novel estimator, \(\hat{\pi}\), that provides a more nuanced understanding of the underlying variable structure in high-dimensional data. 3. Proposing an enhanced range for $\lambda$ that is both data-driven and grounded in theory, resulting in improved selection of models within penalized regression techniques. Our findings are substantiated through rigorous simulation studies that compare the performance of Lasso, adaptive Lasso, SCAD, and MCP under varying signal strengths and block dependence structures. The results illustrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of true positive rate, false positive rate, and overall model accuracy, as evaluated by diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) and F1 score. The simulation experiments not only validate the theoretical gains but also provide empirical evidence for the efficacy of our method in variable selection processes.

We establish a novel framework for analyzing the structure of vector spaces and algebras over a quotient field, with a focus on the properties of matrices and their transformations within this context. Our approach relies on the concept of a vector space $ V $ defined over the quotient field $ \tilde{K} $ of a ring $ K $, together with the dimension $ n $ of $ V_{\tilde{K}} $. By leveraging the non-zero element \( P_{11} \), we construct a basis \( B_{1} \) for \( V_{\tilde{K}} \) and demonstrate that the matrices \( f_{1}(P_{ij}) \) have rank 1 over \( K \). This insight allows us to decompose these matrices into products of matrices \( A \) and \( B \), leading to the key result \( BA = I \), which simplifies the analysis of the matrix transformations. Our work presents a technique for expressing elements $ P_{ij} $ as elementary matrices within a particular basis $ B_{3} $ of the module $ V $ over $ K $. This representation is pivotal in understanding the underlying algebraic structure and its implications for the study of algebraic varieties and their automorphisms. In the realm of homogeneous varieties of algebras, we delve into the properties of the T-ideal and its implications for the structure of the variety. We demonstrate that multiple varieties, such as associative, nilpotent, Lie, alternative, and Jordan algebras, are homogeneous, and we explore the manner in which free algebras decompose within these classes. A key result is the lemma that any endomorphism \( \varphi \) of \( F \) maps \( F' \) into itself, which is instrumental in our subsequent analysis. Our main assertion is that for a homogeneous variety $ \Theta $ of linear algebras over an R$_{1}$MF-domain $ K $, whenever $ \Theta $ is included in either the variety defined by $ x_{1}^{2} = 0 $ or the class of nilpotent algebras of index at most $ m $, each automorphism of the semigroup $ End\,F $ is quasi-inner. The proof necessitates a detailed examination of the matrices representing the endomorphisms together with their properties, leading finally to the conclusion that these automorphisms can be represented as conjugations by elementary matrices. We further demonstrate the practical implications of our results via an example that incorporates a range of linear algebras defined over a Dedekind domain, in which we build a non-quasi-inner automorphism of the endomorphism semigroup, thereby emphasizing the limitations set forth by our main theorem. Our study advances the field by offering a more profound insight into algebraic structures over quotient fields and their automorphisms, suggesting possible directions for future research on algebraic varieties and related applications.

Cheesemakers have traditionally employed coloring agents to improve the look of their cheeses. In times past, farmers would sometimes produce milk of lesser quality, which would result in a whiter cheese. To enhance the cheese's appeal to consumers, they started incorporating colorants to resemble the deeper tones of superior-quality summer cheeses. Initially, these colorants were derived from natural sources such as saffron, marigold, and carrot juice. However, during the 17th century, the Dutch introduced an innovative colorant called annatto. The Dutch had established colonies in Guyana and traded food, including annatto, with the indigenous communities. Zeeland traders, under the authority of the West India Company, purchased annatto from the coastal regions of Guyana and Suriname and sold it in the Netherlands as "verw," which translates to "paint." The first recorded use of annatto in cheese dates back to 1743, as mentioned in the Dutch work "Huishoudelyk Woordboek" (Household Dictionary), per Paul Kindstedt, an American academic at the University of Vermont. Other historical documents from the same period confirm that the use of annatto, also referred to as "orleaan" or "orleans," to color cheese was already in practice by the mid-18th century. England is another country with a history of using annatto to color its cheeses. As far back as the 16th century, dyes were used in Gloucester cheese to disguise lower quality as that of the higher-grade Double Gloucester type. Annatto was later adopted for this purpose as well. In summary, the use of colorants in cheese production has been a common practice for centuries, with annatto emerging as a popular choice due to its vibrant orange-red hue. This method enabled cheesemakers to enhance the appearance of their cheeses and, in certain instances, misled consumers into thinking they were buying a premium product.

This study investigates the impact of environmental factors on the behavior of star-forming galaxies over different epochs in cosmic history, focusing on the relationship between stellar mass ($M_*$), star formation rate (SFR), and departure from the main sequence. Our findings indicate no significant environmental differences among the three analyzed time periods, suggesting that star-forming processes in cluster and field galaxies follow similar evolutionary paths. Notably, at redshift $z=2.2$, there appears to be a subtle indication that cluster galaxies might possess greater stellar masses and SFRs, aligning with prior research emphasizing faster galaxy development in proto-cluster settings during the initial stages of cluster formation. The specific star formation rate (SSFR) of H$\alpha$-selected galaxies in both cluster and field environments declines significantly with redshift, following a trend of approximately $(1+z)^3$ since $z\sim 2$. This decline aligns well with the broader understanding of the cosmic star formation history. Our study reinforces the idea that star-forming galaxies within clusters have evolved in a manner comparable to those in the field, at least as indicated by SFRs measured through H$\alpha$ emissions. Our results contribute to the ongoing debate on the environmental dependence of galaxy star formation in the distant Universe. While certain research indicates an elevated SFR in dense regions, other studies point to a weak or nonexistent link between SSFR and environmental density. Our study contributes to the growing body of evidence indicating that the relationship between star formation rate and stellar mass for star-forming galaxies does not show a strong environmental dependence since $z\sim 2$. However, the potential influence of AGNs on our findings warrants further investigation. While most of our H$\alpha$-selected galaxies are likely powered by star formation, there remains a possibility that AGN contributions could vary with redshift, mass, and environmental conditions, potentially influencing our results. Future in-depth investigations, such as spectroscopic analyses, are needed to better understand the impact of AGNs on the observed star formation processes. In summary, this research provides a robust analysis of star-forming galaxies across cluster and field environments, showing consistent evolution over cosmic time. Our results highlight the importance of continued study on the impact of AGNs and the complex effects of environmental factors on star formation.

\section*{Keywords} Stochastic dynamical systems, Neuronal network modeling, Asymptotic analysis, WKB approximation, Eikonal equations, Attractor escape. \section*{AMS classification} 37A50, 60G40, 92B25, 41A60 \section{Introduction} In this study, we delve into the intricate dynamics of stochastic dynamical systems, particularly focusing on the role of small noise perturbations. These perturbations may notably change system paths, allowing departure from stable attractor regions and causing effects like stochastic resonance and shifts in bifurcations \cite{dykman1994observable, dykman1994large, maier1993, lindner2004, schimanskyGeier1985, arnold1979, arnold1990, Wihstutz_book2003}. Our work holds particular significance in the study of biological neuronal networks, where noise plays a key role in generating coordinated rhythms and achieving synchronization \cite{Tsodyks1997, BrunelHakim1999, Hansel2001, Holcman_Tsodyks2006, Barak2007, daoduc2015}. We introduce a reduced stochastic dynamical system based on synaptic depression-facilitation, a model that captures the essence of neuronal network bursting activity \cite{Tsodyks1997, daoduc2015}. Our approach involves analyzing the distribution of interburst intervals, which correspond to escapes from an attractor. We reveal that the escape rate and the distribution of exit points can be determined using the WKB approximation, a method that provides insights into the small noise limit \cite{Matkowsky1977exit, Schuss:Book, Schuss1980, BobrovskySchuss1982}. Our research contributes to the understanding of escape dynamics in periodically-driven systems, where the escape rate is influenced by field intensity \cite{smelyanskiy1999time, dykman2005}. We highlight the distinction between exiting and escaping, a clarification that is crucial for our analysis. The manuscript is structured to first present our reduced stochastic model, followed by an exploration of a generic two-dimensional dynamical system containing an attractor and a saddle-point. We demonstrate that the maximum of the probability density function of trajectories before escape is shifted, depending on the noise amplitude $\sigma$. Our analysis culminates in an examination of the escape from the basin of attraction, where trajectories can reenter the basin multiple times before final escape, a phenomenon that has implications for the large tail distribution of interburst intervals observed in experimental data \cite{Rouach_CxKO}. \section{Modeling the Interburst Durations in Neuronal Networks} \subsection{Noisy Depression-Facilitation Model} Neuronal networks exhibit complex activity patterns, which can be modeled using mean-field models to represent the dynamics as stochastic differential equations. Bursting dynamics, characterized by transient periods of neuronal discharge, can be understood through the lens of short-term synaptic plasticity properties such as depression and facilitation \cite{Tsodyks1997, Barak2007, daoduc2015}. These characteristics play a key role in explaining the intervals between bursts, when the network exhibits reduced activity. We focus on a depression-facilitation short-term synaptic plasticity model that describes network neuronal bursting \cite{Tsodyks1997, daoduc2015frontiers, Holcman_Tsodyks2006}. This model is defined by three equations that represent the mean voltage $h$, the depression state $y$, and the facilitation state $x$. The model includes the recovery to baseline levels, the rise in the probability of vesicle release, and the reduction of available vesicle stores, all of which are crucial for interpreting the network's behavior. \subsection{Reduction to a Two-Dimensional System and Phase-Space Analysis} The system under consideration has three critical points: one attractor and two saddle-points. By reducing the system to a 2D-plane, we simplify the analysis while retaining the essential dynamics. The deterministic system, when reduced, has two attractors and one saddle-point. Our analysis reveals that the attractor's dynamics are anisotropic, with the eigenvalues indicating the stability and nature of the critical points. The escape dynamics from the attractor basin are characterized by trajectories that can reenter the basin multiple times before eventually escaping to infinity. This behavior is distinct from systems where escape ends upon the first encounter with the separatrix. Our study provides a novel explanation for the observed large tail distribution of interburst intervals in experimental time series, suggesting that each excursion outside and inside the basin of attraction contributes to an increased total escape time.

In this section, we present the Group-Sort-Fuse (GSF) method, a new penalized maximum likelihood technique designed to estimate both the order and the elements of a finite mixture model. Given a random sample from an unknown true mixing measure \( G_0 \) with at most \( K_0 \) components, we propose a method to address overfitting issues associated with the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) when an upper bound \( K \geq K_0 \) is known. The overfit MLE may exhibit slow convergence and include redundant components, leading to an inaccurate estimation of $ K_0 $. Our proposed GSF approach incorporates two distinct penalty terms to address these challenges: one aimed at suppressing near-zero mixing weights and the other designed to combine nearby estimated atoms. We begin by defining a preliminary penalized log-likelihood function incorporating a nonnegative penalty $ \varphi $, which ensures that the maximizer has mixing probabilities that remain bounded away from zero, resulting in a consistent estimator for the atoms of $ G_0 $. However, this preliminary estimator does not consistently estimate the order \( K_0 \) due to not addressing the second type of overfitting. To tackle this issue, we propose applying a sparsity-inducing penalty $ r_{\lambda_n} $ to the distances between selected atom pairs, specifically targeting their consecutive distances following a sorting process, instead of considering all possible pairwise distances, thereby decreasing dependence on the selection of $ K $. The GSF approach is based on the idea of cluster partitioning, in which atoms are organized into groups so that distances inside each group are less than those between different groups. The method aims to integrate the results from each cluster in a way that accurately represents the true atoms of $ G_0 $. To achieve this, we define a cluster ordering, a permutation of atoms that respects the cluster partition and is invariant to relabeling. The GSF method then fuses the ordered atoms within each cluster to produce a consistent estimator of both the order and components of the true mixing measure. The innovative aspects of our research include the introduction of a double penalized log-likelihood function that effectively addresses overfitting in mixture models, the development of a cluster partitioning strategy that enhances the estimation of the true atoms, and the use of cluster ordering to merge closely located atoms. Our approach marks a significant advancement in the field of mixture model estimation, providing a more accurate and dependable technique for revealing the actual structure of the data.

Reverse Reverb is a sound effect that has found application across multiple music genres and media productions. It employs the technique of reversed reverb, producing a distinctive and otherworldly auditory experience. This method has been utilized by many artists and musical groups throughout the years, helping to shape the unique character of their sound. One of the earliest known uses of reverse reverb can be traced back to the song "Whole Lotta Love" by Led Zeppelin, released in 1969. The effect was used in the bridge of the song, adding a haunting quality to the music. Another early instance can be heard in "Alucard" from Gentle Giant's self-titled album, which came out in 1970. During the 1970s, reverse reverb started gaining more widespread use, as evidenced by its inclusion in "Crying to the Sky" by Be-Bop Deluxe. In the realm of shoegaze music, reverse reverb is a popular technique, particularly among bands like My Bloody Valentine and Spacemen 3. The effect is often used to create a dreamy, atmospheric sound that is characteristic of the genre. Additionally, reverse reverb has found its way into hardstyle music, electronic dance music (EDM), and pop music, where it is commonly applied to the first word or syllable of a vocal passage. This technique serves as a lead-in to vocal sections, creating a build-up effect or an other-worldly sound. Notable examples of reverse reverb in popular music include Metallica's use of the effect on James Hetfield's vocals in the song "Fade To Black" from their 1984 album "Ride The Lightning." Similarly, Genesis utilized the effect, particularly on Phil Collins' snare drum, towards the conclusion of the track "Deep in the Motherload" from their 1978 album "And Then There Three." Beyond music, reverse reverb has also been used in other media, such as filmmaking and television production. It is often utilized to create an otherworldly effect on voices, particularly in horror movies, where it can add a sense of eeriness and suspense. Additionally, the effect has been used in the company logo for production company CBS Studios, demonstrating its versatility and impact in various forms of media. In summary, reverse reverb is a sound effect that has become popular with musicians and media producers, adding a unique and captivating aspect to their work. The use across various genres and formats demonstrates the creative potential of this technique and its enduring appeal in audio production.

Oral delivery consists of administering agents, such as pharmaceuticals, through the mouth, which are subsequently ingested and metabolized by the gastrointestinal tract. It is a widely used route for various drugs due to its ease of use and relatively painless nature compared to other methods like injections. However, the efficacy of oral medications may be affected by factors like adequate absorption in the digestive tract and possible degradation by digestive enzymes prior to entering the bloodstream. Additionally, some medications may cause gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea or vomiting. Oral administration is suitable for conscious patients who are able to swallow. The expression "per os," derived from Latin, signifies "by mouth" or "through the mouth" and is frequently used in medical language to describe oral medication administration. The abbreviation "P.O." is frequently seen on medical prescriptions as a sign that the medication should be taken by mouth. Enteral administration, a subset of oral administration, encompasses several methods: 1. Buccal: The medication is dissolved inside the cheek. 2. Sublabial: The medication is dissolved under the lip. 3. Sublingual administration (SL): The medication is dissolved under the tongue. Due to rapid absorption, some consider SL a parenteral route. 4. Oral (PO): The medication is given in the form of a pill, capsule, or liquid that is taken by mouth. Enteral medications come in multiple formats, such as oral solid dosage (OSD) forms, which include tablets that can be swallowed, chewed, dissolved in water, or held under the tongue. It is important to adhere strictly to the directions given with each medication in order to achieve maximum efficacy and reduce the risk of adverse reactions.

Universal quantification and existential quantification are key concepts in first-order logic, a foundational system for mathematical reasoning. These concepts were notably discussed by Thoralf Skolem, who introduced the notion of a "definite property." According to van Heijenoort, a property is considered definite in Skolem's framework if it can be expressed as a well-formed formula in the first-order simple predicate calculus, using only the predicate constants epsilon (ε) and possibly equality (=). In modern set theory, axiomatizations are typically embedded within a logical calculus framework. The formulation of the axiom of separation, which is crucial for defining subsets, is largely influenced by the approaches of Hermann Weyl and Skolem. It is important to note a shift in terminology from "propositional function" to terms like "formula," "predicate calculus," "predicate," and "logical calculus." This development is further detailed in sections that examine the notion of "function" as it appears in contemporary set theory. The history of the "ordered pair" concept is somewhat unclear. Gottlob Frege introduced a notion of order in his 1879 definition of a two-place function Ψ(A, B) in an informal manner. Norbert Wiener, in his 1914 work, recognized that his approach was fundamentally similar to Ernst Schröder's method of treating a relation as a set of ordered pairs. Bertrand Russell, in 1903, considered defining a relation as a "class of couples" but later rejected this idea, asserting that it avoided the necessity for a deeper understanding of relations. In conclusion, the growth of set theory and the logical foundations of mathematical thought have been influenced by the work of many mathematicians and logicians. The evolution of terminology and the exploration of foundational concepts, such as ordered pairs and definite properties, have played a significant role in the advancement of these fields.

This section introduces the methodology for estimating the parameters of the HIV transmission model using Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC). The average of the target distribution is approximated through the Nadaraya-Watson regression method, while other measures like medians, modes, and confidence intervals are also determined. The Cuban HIV-AIDS dataset, spanning from 1986 to 2007, is used for analysis, with summary statistics derived from the detection times and methods of detection. A comparison of ABC and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approaches is conducted for a conventional SIR model, showing that ABC can achieve results similar to those based on likelihood under suitable circumstances. The impact of tolerance rate on the posterior distribution is discussed, highlighting the tendency of ABC to produce larger tails compared to MCMC. The paper also addresses the challenge of the "curse of dimensionality" in ABC, where the bias may increase with the number of summary statistics. Regression-based approaches are suggested to alleviate this problem, such as local linear regression and nonlinear conditional heteroscedastic regression, with the goal of establishing a connection between the distributions and reducing the parameter estimates toward an approximate sample from the target distribution. The innovative aspects of this research include the application of ABC to the HIV transmission model, the comparison with MCMC methods, and the introduction of regression adjustments to address the curse of dimensionality. The findings contribute to the understanding of parameter estimation in complex models where direct likelihood-based inference is challenging.

This section delves into the competitive dynamics that characterize Wikipedia's collaborative content creation process, where contributors often vie for ownership of the content they produce. We utilize psychological ownership theory and territoriality theory to account for why contributors might feel a sense of ownership towards Wikipedia articles or parts of them, resulting in rivalry and possible disputes regarding the content and direction of such articles. Wikipedia's governance model, which is based on community-developed norms and policies, plays a critical role in mitigating these competitive tendencies. The Neutral Point of View (NPOV) principle is central to this model, promoting objectivity and preventing any single viewpoint from dominating an article. However, achieving NPOV can be challenging due to the complexity of issues, difficulty in verifying information, and intentional attempts by contributors to influence readers' perspectives. Our research aims to investigate the relationship between competitive elements and socio-technical governance frameworks in the context of Wikipedia's collaborative content development. Our focus is on two research questions: First, how do participants evaluate the trade-offs involved in peer production, and what is the relationship between their editing efforts and partial ownership of articles? Second, what impact do governance mechanisms, especially the enforcement of NPOV, have on competitive interactions and the link between contributors' editing activities and content ownership? We propose a game-theoretic model to analyze competition and governance in Wikipedia's co-production process. This model seeks to capture the essential features of the system, considering both cooperative and competitive behaviors, and provides insight into the complex interactions between participants and the community's structural governance. Our study's innovative aspects lie in examining the competitive dynamics within Wikipedia's collaborative environment and understanding how these dynamics are influenced by the community's governance efforts, particularly in relation to the NPOV principle. By achieving this, we seek to add value to the existing body of research on peer production and the socio-technical frameworks that support it.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian spatio-temporal approach for analyzing respiratory prescription data across General Practitioner (GP) surgeries in Scotland from 2015 to 2016. Respiratory prescriptions account for 13% of the costs of all prescriptions in Scotland, underscoring the significance of understanding the factors influencing their distribution and the spatial disparities in prescription rates. The data's distinctive feature of being at the point level yet having fixed positions, where forecasts for locations that have not been measured are impossible, presented a difficulty. To address this problem, we proposed a finite-dimensional process-convolution model that does not presuppose a globally observable underlying spatial process. Our methodology advances existing process-convolution models by incorporating an adaptive or localized spatial structure through a tapered random weighting scheme. We offer open-source software to guarantee that the research can be replicated. The adaptive model shows significantly improved performance compared to a simpler global smoothing model, leading to two important conclusions. First, the findings suggest a positive correlation between the rates of respiratory prescriptions and the levels of air pollution, especially those related to PM2.5. An increase of 1.23 µg/m³ in PM2.5 is linked to a 2.2% rise in prescription rates. This finding is consistent with existing literature that associates air pollution with more severe health outcomes, such as hospitalization or death, and reinforces the evidence that air pollution significantly impacts respiratory health and associated healthcare costs, even at concentrations below legal limits. Second, the study reveals substantial health inequalities in respiratory prescription rates across Scottish health boards. Dumfries and Galloway, and Greater Glasgow and Clyde exhibit the highest rates, with increases of 27% and 19% respectively compared to the Scottish average. Conversely, Grampian and Orkney show the lowest rates, with decreases of 30% and 40% respectively. These disparities are evident both before and after adjusting for known covariates, indicating a significant residual health board effect on respiratory prescription rates. These findings are crucial for guiding public health policy and supporting decisions on resource distribution, especially in light of current discussions initiated by the Marmot review in England and recent analyses that emphasize enduring health inequities. The study also presents opportunities for further research, such as expanding the model into a multivariate version to examine connections among prescribing rates for various diseases and developing interactive software for visualizing data in order to more effectively convey health disparities to policymakers.

We introduce a novel method for approximating the value of $\psi(P)$, which relies on the behavior of the tail of a probability distribution $P$. Instead of modeling the distribution $P$ using a parametric approach, we propose an optimization framework that imposes a geometric constraint on the tail of $P$, particularly for values of $x$ that are greater than or equal to a sufficiently large threshold $a$. This method ensures consistent extrapolation from the non-tail region and incorporates auxiliary constraints to provide additional information about \(P\). The optimization problem is designed to generate an upper confidence bound for $\psi(P)$, supported by a statistical guarantee that if the constraints are met by the true distribution $P_{\text{true}}$ with probability $1-\alpha$, then the optimal solution $Z^*$ acts as an upper confidence bound for the real value $Z_{\text{true}}$ with at least the same degree of certainty. Our method centers on $\psi(P)$, which captures either the expected value or a specific percentile of the random variable $X$. We impose geometric conditions such as monotonicity and convexity on the tail of \(P\), which are common to most parametric distributions. These conditions include specific distributional characteristics at the threshold $a$, functioning as boundary conditions to enable smooth extrapolation and to avoid the optimization process from being overly simplistic. The additional constraints, which take the form of moment conditions, are adjusted based on data and assist in decreasing the degree of conservatism in the extrapolation. The optimization problem can be expressed as: \[ \begin{aligned} \max_P \quad & \psi(P) \\ \text{subject to} \quad & P \in \mathscr{P}, \quad \mathbb{E}_P[\bm{g}(X)] \in \mathbb{S} \end{aligned} \] where \(\mathscr{P}\) represents the set of distributions satisfying the geometric shape conditions, and \(\mathbb{S}\) represents the set of permissible moment conditions. The set of viable solutions for this problem is represented by $\mathbb F(\mathfrak{P}(\mathscr{P},\bm{g},\mathbb{S}))$. Our method's innovation lies in its ability to provide statistical guarantees for the estimated quantity \(\psi(P)\), even when little is known about the tail of the distribution. By combining geometric shape assumptions with extra moment conditions, we offer a dependable framework for tackling estimation issues connected to distribution tails. This approach is particularly useful in scenarios where traditional parametric fitting may not be appropriate or when the tail behavior of the distribution is of primary interest.

In this paper, we explore the complex interactions of mean curvature flow, a key mechanism in geometric evolution, especially in the setting of symmetric spaces. We begin by introducing the concept of a mean curvature flow, which is a one-parameter family of immersions that evolves a manifold by its mean curvature vector. Our focus is on the study of submanifolds, especially equifocal and proper complex equifocal types, which act as generalizations of isoparametric submanifolds from Euclidean spaces to the more general setting of symmetric spaces. Our work builds upon earlier research by Liu-Terng and Terng-Thorbergsson, who investigated the behavior of mean curvature flows starting from isoparametric and equifocal submanifolds in Euclidean spaces and symmetric spaces of compact type, respectively. These studies uncovered fascinating characteristics, including the shrinking of submanifolds into focal submanifolds and the occurrence of singularities when specific conditions are met. Expanding on these concepts, we introduce the notion of a proper complex equifocal submanifold in a symmetric space of non-compact type, characterized by its complex focal structure and the action of a symmetric subgroup. We highlight the importance of curvature-adapted submanifolds, which are those that align with the curvature of the ambient space, and their role as principal orbits in Hermann type actions. Our primary contribution is the development and demonstration of a theorem that examines the behavior of mean curvature flows initiated by curvature-adapted proper complex equifocal submanifolds or their focal submanifolds in non-compact symmetric spaces, with the exception of hyperbolic spaces. This theorem extends the understanding of the geometric evolution of submanifolds under mean curvature flow and provides a deeper insight into the interplay between submanifold geometry and the ambient space's curvature. In summary, our paper presents a detailed study of the mean curvature flow for complex equifocal submanifolds in symmetric spaces, offering new perspectives on their geometric progression and the underlying forces that shape their evolution. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we contribute to the field by elucidating the complex dynamics at play and setting the stage for further research in this area.

Induction motors are known for their significant reactive component, which results in a low power factor. This low power factor leads to increased reactive current drawn from the power supply, causing additional losses in the power system. To mitigate this issue, synchronous motors can be employed in industrial plants to supply the necessary reactive power for induction motors. This method improves the plant's overall power factor and decreases the amount of reactive current taken from the grid. Synchronous condensers are a type of synchronous motor specifically designed for power factor correction. They offer seamless, automatic power factor correction and can generate up to 150% additional reactive power (vars). These units remain immune to electrical harmonics within the system and may in certain instances also absorb them. Synchronous condensers do not produce switching transients, excessive voltage levels, or electrical resonances. The rotating inertia of a synchronous condenser allows it to provide limited voltage support during brief power drops. First introduced in the 1930s and extensively utilized during the 1950s, synchronous condensers were later supplanted by static var compensators (SVCs) in newer setups because of their increased expenses. However, they still serve as a feasible alternative or complement to capacitors in power factor correction, particularly when harmonics lead to capacitor overheating and malfunction. Synchronous condensers may also help in keeping voltage levels consistent. The reactive power from a capacitor bank varies in direct proportion to the square of its terminal voltage. This relationship underscores the necessity of keeping voltage levels suitable for achieving maximum performance and efficiency in power systems.

This section introduces the formulation of Convolutional Kernel Networks (CKNs) and their connection to traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets). CKNs are infinite-dimensional analogues of ConvNets, utilizing kernel functions to capture spatial relationships in data. The key hyperparameter in CKNs is the selection of a kernel, which generally uses a normalized form derived from a dot product kernel defined on the sphere. This choice allows filters to be restricted to the spherical surface, necessitating an extra projection step during the optimization process. The representation at each layer in a CKN is constructed through a series of operations including patch extraction, normalization, projection, and pooling. After multiple layers, a final representation appropriate for classification purposes is achieved. The training of CKNs requires solving an optimization problem where the goal is to minimize a loss function while ensuring that the filters are constrained to lie on a product of Euclidean spheres. A key aspect of CKNs is their correspondence to ConvNet components, as detailed in Table~\ref{tab:correspondence}. This table demonstrates the link among different layers and operations within ConvNets, such as convolutional layers, partially connected layers, and pooling, along with their equivalent elements in CKNs. The proposition presented formalizes the connection between the pointwise nonlinearity in ConvNets and the approximation of a kernel on patches. The section continues by examining the specific ways in which various layer types within ConvNets, including convolutional, partially connected, and fully connected layers, correspond to CKNs through subspace mappings. It also explores the idea of pooling in ConvNets and how it aligns with the averaging of feature maps in CKNs. Moreover, the normalization methods commonly used in ConvNets, like local response normalization, are analyzed within the framework of CKNs. The innovative aspect of this research lies in the detailed exploration of the relationship between CKNs and ConvNets, providing insights into how the traditional finite-dimensional ConvNet operations can be generalized to the infinite-dimensional CKN framework. This knowledge may enable the development of more efficient and effective network architectures by utilizing the powerful representation capabilities of kernel methods.

This section offers a thorough mathematical examination of the large deviations principle (LDP) concerning empirical measures within the framework of mean-field games. We establish the LDP by leveraging the contraction principle, which allows us to transfer the LDP from empirical measures of initial states and noise variables to the state-action empirical measures. The main result is encapsulated in Theorem \ref{theorem3}, which characterizes the rate function for the LDP in terms of the game dynamics. Our approach begins by proving that the bounded function $h_f^{k+1}$ is continuous for all its arguments except noise variables, which is crucial for the induction argument. This continuity is subsequently leveraged to demonstrate the weak convergence of the empirical measures towards the actual measures for every $t\geq0$. The proof is completed by applying the contraction principle, which yields the LDP for the empirical measures. In Theorem \ref{theorem3}, we express the rate function $J$ in terms of the noise distributions $\Theta_w$ and $\Theta_v$. However, these distributions may not always be known. To address this, we derive an equivalent rate function that can be expressed solely in terms of the components of the game dynamics. This is achieved by using the chain rule for relative entropy and redefining the rate function $J$ in terms of the empirical measure $ u_{0,{\mathsf X}}$ and the relative entropy with respect to the product measure $ u_{0,{\mathsf X}}\times\Theta_w\times\Theta_v$. We then propose a simpler particle model in order to enable a more detailed examination of the rate function. This model decouples the agents and replaces the empirical measure of states with a fixed measure in the state dynamics. By applying Sanov's Theorem and the contraction principle, we establish the LDP for the empirical measures of this simplified model with a rate function $\tilde{J}$. The connection between the rate functions $J$ and $\tilde{J}$ is established through Lemma \ref{lemma3}, which shows that the sets of measures that map to a given empirical measure under $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{{\boldsymbol u}}$ are the same. This allows us to express $J$ as the sum of the relative entropy with respect to the initial measure and the rate function $\tilde{J}$. Finally, we provide a characterization of the rate function $\tilde{J}$ in terms of the game dynamics, which leads to the final expression for $J$ in Theorem \ref{theorem2}. This outcome is derived by examining the empirical distributions of the trajectories and employing Sanov's Theorem within the framework of weak convergence topology. In conclusion, this section presents a comprehensive analysis of the LDP for empirical measures in mean-field games, providing a deeper understanding of the behavior of these measures under the mean-field equilibrium policy. The results have potential applications in various fields, such as economics, finance, and social sciences, where understanding the dynamics of large populations is crucial. Future research directions could include studying concentration bounds for these empirical measures and exploring the implications of the LDP in different contexts.

This article delves into a $p$-adic study of a minimal degree differential algebraic equation that nullifies an arithmetic Gevrey series of order $-1$, specifically an $E$-function. We establish a conjecture by Yves Andr\'e (Conjecture 4.7 of [A2]). Initially, we set some notations. Let $K$ be a number field and $V_{0}$ the set of all finite places $v$ of $K$. For each $v \in V_{0}$ above a prime number $p = p(v)$, we normalize the $v$-adic absolute value such that $|p|_{v} = p^{-1}$ and denote $\pi_{v} = p^{\frac{-1}{p-1}}$. Let $K_{v}$ be the completion of $K$ for this absolute value, and fix an embedding $K \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. For any real number $r > 0$, the \emph{generic convergence radius} $R_{v}(\phi, r)$ of a differential operator $\displaystyle\phi \in K[x, d/dx]$ is defined as the convergence radius, upper bounded by $r$, of a solution base of $\phi$ near a generic $v$-adic point of absolute value $r$. A formal series $\sum_{n\ge 0}a_nx^n$ is termed an \emph{arithmetic Gevrey series} of order $s \in \mathbb{Q}$ if its coefficients $a_n$ are algebraic numbers and there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that the algebraic numbers $a_n/(n!)^s$ have conjugates with absolute value less than $C^n$, and for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the common denominator $d_n$ of the numbers $a_0/(0!)^s, \ldots, a_n/(n!)^s$ is less than $C^n$. This category encompasses generalized convergent or divergent hypergeometric series that feature rational parameters. The set of such series is denoted by $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\{x\}_s$. A formal series having algebraic coefficients is referred to as holonomic when it satisfies a linear differential equation whose coefficients lie in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x)$. The $G$-functions (resp. $E$-functions) are defined as the holonomic elements of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\{x\}_0$ (resp. $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\{x\}_{-1}$). The field of $G$-functions has experienced significant development over the past few decades, mainly as a result of the research conducted by Chudnovsky, Bombieri, and Andr\'e. Their contributions have highlighted certain connections with transcendence and arithmetic geometry. In particular, Chudnovsky proved that the differential operator $\phi$ of $K[x, d/dx]$ of minimal order in $d/dx$ annihilating a $G$-function satisfies the so-called Galochkin condition (cf. [CC], [A1, VI]). A differential operator in $K[x, d/dx]$ that meets this criterion is referred to as a \emph{$G$-operator}. Andr\'e later established the equivalence between this condition and that of Bombieri, that is, a differential operator $\phi$ of $K[x, d/dx]$ is a $G$-operator if and only if it satisfies $\prod_{v\in V_0}R_{v}(\phi,1) e 0$ [A1, IV 5.2]. Thanks to Katz's theorem [Ka, 13.0], we verify that $G$-operators have only regular singularities with rational exponents. Moreover, all formal series involved in their solutions, at any finite or infinite point, are $G$-functions [A1, V]. The investigation into non-vanishing order holonomic arithmetic Gevrey series has recently been advanced by Y. Andr\'e in [A2]. In particular, he introduced a novel category of differential operators referred to as $E$-operators. By definition, an $E$-operator is the Fourier-Laplace transform of a $G$-operator. This designation is justified by the fact that the differential operator of minimal degree in $x$ of $K[x, d/dx]$ nullifying an $E$-function is the Fourier-Laplace transform of a $G$-operator [A2, 4.2].

Context-Adaptive Variable-Length Coding (CAVLC) is an entropy coding technique employed in H.264/MPEG-4 AVC video encoding. As a lossless compression technique, it exhibits this trait common to many entropy coders. CAVLC is utilized to encode residual, zig-zag ordered blocks of transform coefficients, specifically for 4x4 (and 2x2) blocks. It serves as an alternative to Context-Based Adaptive Binary Arithmetic Coding (CABAC), requiring less processing power for decoding, although it may not achieve the same level of compression efficiency. One of the key advantages of CAVLC is its universal support across all H.264 profiles, unlike CABAC, which is not supported in the Baseline and Extended profiles. CAVLC proves especially efficient because of its architecture that takes advantage of specific features within quantized 4x4 blocks. After the processes of prediction, transformation, and quantization, these blocks tend to be sparse, predominantly containing zeros. The largest non-zero coefficients that appear after a zig-zag traversal are typically made up of +1 or -1 values, which are efficiently encoded by CAVLC. CAVLC also benefits from the correlation in the number of non-zero coefficients found in neighboring blocks. The encoding of the number of coefficients is facilitated through the use of a look-up table, with the selection of the table being dependent on the non-zero coefficients present in adjacent blocks. Moreover, the number of non-zero coefficients, referred to as the level, generally increases as one approaches the beginning of the reordered array, which is near the DC coefficient, and tends to decrease as one moves toward higher frequency components. In conclusion, CAVLC serves as an effective method in video coding due to its efficiency and ability to work across different H.264 profile standards, providing a favorable trade-off between decoding complexity and compression effectiveness.

The paper offers a detailed examination of the error structure within sparse linear models, with particular attention to how variance underestimation affects the process of enforcing sparsity. The authors demonstrate that while large coefficients are accurately approximated, smaller ones are damped more strongly, leading to a selective variance underestimation effect. This effect, however, is found to be benign or even beneficial in sparse linear models. The paper extends its analysis to group potentials, showing that the algorithms can be easily generalized to models with potentials of the form \( t_i(\|\vs{i}\|) \), where \( \vs{i} \) is a subvector of \( \vs{} \). The authors additionally present the open-source 'glm-ie' toolbox, which realizes the algorithms and methods presented in the paper. The toolbox is designed to be generic and can be applied to a range of problems, with many super-Gaussian potentials included and the ability for users to add more. The authors then contrast sparse Bayesian inference with point estimation for sparse linear models, highlighting the distinct goals and algorithmic characteristics of each. Sparse Bayesian inference aims to quantify uncertainty in decisions and dependencies between components, while sparse estimation seeks to eliminate unnecessary variables for efficient computation. The paper emphasizes a key difference between these methods, showing that precise sparsity in $ \vgamma{} $ is not attained through inference, while sparse estimation involves setting many $ \gamma_i $ values to zero. The paper further examines the circumstances in which sparsity emerges within maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation and automatic relevance determination (ARD), a sparse reconstruction method that played a significant role in shaping the algorithms presented in the paper. The authors show that local minima of SLM MAP estimation are largely exactly sparse, exhibiting consistent sparsity structures between $ \vs{*} $ and $ \vgamma{*} $. The paper ends by exploring the different contributions of Gaussian functions within the framework of sparse estimation relative to sparse inference. In sparse estimation, Gaussian functions are normalized, encouraging \( \gamma_i \to 0 \), while in variational inference, Gaussian functions lower bound \( t_i(s_i) \), with their mass vanishing as \( \gamma_i \to 0 \), providing no incentive to eliminate \( \gamma_i \). The authors suggest that type A bounding should be preferred for variational inference, while type B bounding is best suited for sparse estimation. The research introduces several novel contributions, including an in-depth examination of the error structure within sparse linear models, the generalization to group potentials, and the creation of the 'glm-ie' toolbox. The paper also provides a clear contrast between sparse Bayesian inference and point estimation, highlighting the importance of understanding the distinct goals and characteristics of each approach. The findings and results are presented in a concise and clear language, making it easier for reviewers to understand the paper.

We demonstrate that the satisfiability problem for symbolic automatic relations is undecidable by showing that if a two-counter machine $ P $ halts after executing a sequence of instructions $ \mathbf{Code}(i_0), \mathbf{Code}(i_1), \ldots, \mathbf{Code}(i_n) $ with $ i_0 = 0 $ and $ \mathbf{Code}(i_n) = \mathbf{halt} $, then an accepting computation can be obtained from the execution trace. Let $ w_r $ and $ w'_r $ denote the values held in registers $ r_0 $ and $ r_1 $ throughout the entire execution, where $ r $ is either 0 or 1. We show that \( \conv(w_0, w_1, w'_0, w'_1) \) constitutes an accepting run. For each step $ 0 \le m \le l-1 $, if $ \mathbf{Code}(i_m) $ does not denote a stop instruction, then there exist transitions inside the machine's state diagram, as defined by $ \Delta $. Specifically, \( q_{i_m} \trans{(j_{0m},j_{1m},j_{0(m+1)},j_{1(m+1)})}_{M_P} q_{i_{m+1}} \). When $ m = l $, which corresponds to the halt command, a move to the accepting state is possible: $ q_{i_m} \trans{(j_{0m}, j_{1m} \pad, \pad)} q_{\mathrm{accept}} $. This approach utilizes the established undecidability of the halting problem for two-counter machines, thus proving the undecidability of the satisfiability problem for symbolic automatic relations.

In this study, we performed a thorough analysis of the impact of five key factors on the imaging resolution of a lens-free on-chip digital holographic microscopy (LFOCDHM) system. These factors encompass the distance between the sample and the sensor, the spatial and temporal coherence of the light source, the limited size of the sensor pixels, and the restricted area of the image sub-field of view (sub-FOV) utilized for reconstruction. Our analysis and experiments revealed that the sensor pixel size is the most significant factor limiting the imaging resolution of LFOCDHM systems. The side effects from other experimental factors are relatively manageable. For instance, using a laser as an ideal temporally coherent light source and increasing the source-to-sample distance can approximate an ideal spatially coherent source. Employing pixel super-resolution (SR) algorithms can reduce the effective size of the imaging sensor. However, even with these efforts, using a sensor with a smaller pixel size can further enhance the quality of the SR reconstruction outcomes. Specifically, if the desired resolution is around $1 \mu m$, the up-sampling factor $w$ will vary for different pixel sizes. When the pixel size approaches the desired resolution, the up-sampling factor $w$ becomes smaller, necessitating less data for accurate reconstruction. Conversely, a higher up-sampling factor $w$ (for larger pixel sizes) can lead to more criss-crossed frequency gaps that cannot be recovered, even with pixel SR reconstruction algorithms. Therefore, for LFOCDHM techniques, a smaller pixel size is crucial for achieving higher resolution and requires less information to reach the expected super-resolved resolution. Furthermore, employing an LED as the light source can result in a more compact, portable, and economical system. However, the coherence length of the LED will also affect the reconstructed resolution. According to our equations, increasing ${z_1}$ and decreasing ${z_2}$ can effectively improve the coherence of light sources and enhance the imaging resolution. Furthermore, reducing ${z_2}$ may lead to a smaller reconstructed region once the required resolution is fixed. Our analysis of these parameters based on transfer functions has provided a quantitative resolution limit determined by the minimum first cut-off frequency of these transfer functions. This quantitative relationship allows for preliminary estimates of the ultimate resolution after employing SR methods. Thus, the derived theoretical models can offer valuable guidance in selecting appropriate system parameters to achieve higher imaging resolution. To verify the theoretical models, we applied the variable-controlling approach, altering just one or two parameters in each experimental run. The resolution criterion was used to assess the imaging resolution, and the resulting data confirmed the validity of our theoretical models. It is crucial to recognize that although this study illustrates the potential of our theoretical models to enhance imaging resolution by refining the optical configuration of a LFOCDHM system, there might also be an opportunity to mitigate the impact of these system imperfections via computational methods. Based on the transfer functions we have derived, we can establish the forward image formation model (from object to image) for a given LFOCDHM system. Then, specific mathematical algorithms can be used to extract the required object information from the acquired data, thereby solving the corresponding inverse problem. In subsequent research, our emphasis will be placed on tackling the resolution loss caused by these factors and mitigating their negative effects via post-processing techniques. Over the last ten years, the use of data science, especially predictive modeling, has significantly increased in numerous areas. A key area of emphasis in learning analytics research has centered on predicting student success through modeling techniques. The advent and proliferation of digital learning platforms, such as Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), have facilitated the collection, management, and analysis of learner data. Concurrently, advancements in open-source statistical software have expanded the range of modeling techniques available to researchers. However, a critical aspect of predictive modeling research that has not kept pace is the methodology of model evaluation and selection. This paper highlights a major deficiency in the approaches used for evaluating and selecting models within the learning analytics and educational data mining communities, and suggests a survey of methods aimed at tackling this problem. We start by examining existing practices in the field, creating a "state of the practice" by analyzing 87 peer-reviewed experiments in MOOCs published in leading journals and conferences. This review reveals a strong consensus on the use of certain techniques for predictive model evaluation, many of which are statistically problematic. We delve into the specifics of model evaluation methods, the prevalent use of cross-validation, and the lack of statistical testing in the context of model performance comparison. Our analysis also points to a troubling pattern in hyperparameter tuning, where the choice and adjustment of model parameters are frequently not documented or carried out without a proper approach. This oversight can significantly impact the robustness and reliability of the models developed. In response to these findings, we present a case study applying three distinct evaluation methods to a large sample of MOOCs. This case study not only demonstrates the varying conclusions that different evaluation methods can yield but also provides empirical insights relevant to future modeling research in MOOCs. Our innovative contribution lies in highlighting the methodological gap in model evaluation and selection, offering a comprehensive survey of techniques to improve current practices, and providing empirical evidence through a case study that underscores the importance of robust model evaluation methods. We conclude by suggesting ways to improve model evaluation practices in learning analytics, with the goal of increasing the scientific rigor in predictive modeling research.

The triode is a type of vacuum tube that played a crucial role in the development of electronic devices, particularly in the field of radio communication. It consists of three primary components: the filament, functioning as the cathode, the grid, and the plate, commonly referred to as the anode. The operation of the triode is based on the principle of controlling the flow of electrons from the cathode to the plate through the grid. The concept of the triode was first patented by Lee de Forest in 1908 (U.S. patent 879,532), who initially called it the Audion. De Forest's original device utilized conventional vacuum technology, which left a small amount of residual gas inside the tube. This residual gas would cause a blue glow, visible as ionization, when the plate voltage was high (above about 60 volts). The operation of the device was not fully understood at the time, but it was clear that a change in the voltage applied to the grid could lead to a significant change in the plate current, resulting in voltage and power amplification. In 1912, de Forest and John Stone Stone demonstrated the Audion to AT&T's engineering department. Dr. Harold D. Arnold at AT&T noticed that the blue light was caused by ionized gas. He recommended that AT&T purchase the patent, which they did. Arnold then developed high-vacuum tubes, which were tested in the summer of 1913 on AT&T's long-distance network. These high-vacuum tubes could operate at high plate voltages without the blue glow, significantly improving their performance. Finnish inventor Eric Tigerstedt introduced major enhancements to the initial triode configuration in 1914 as he developed his sound-on-film system. The triode's ability to amplify electronic signals made it an essential component in various electronic devices, including radio receivers, early televisions, and the first computers. The triode's influence on the development of electronics is undeniable, and its legacy can still be seen in modern vacuum tube-based devices.

Plasmas represent the fourth state of matter, distinct from solids, liquids, and gases. They are composed of a mixture of ions, electrons, and neutral particles, and are characterized by their unique properties such as high electrical conductivity and the presence of electric and magnetic fields. The plasma's behavior can be influenced by various factors, including how it interacts with surrounding gases. Under specific circumstances, preserving the integrity of the plasma-gas boundary for several tens of seconds may result in a process referred to as viscous heating. This secondary mode of heating can significantly alter the kinetics of reactions within the plasma, potentially leading to the formation of complex nanomaterials. The study of plasma physics is a multidisciplinary field that encompasses areas such as physics, chemistry, and engineering. It has numerous applications in various industries, including energy production, materials science, and space research. For individuals looking to enhance their knowledge of plasma physics, there are multiple resources at their disposal. These include academic courses, such as the graduate-level course offered by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (M.I.T.), which is taught by Richard Fitzpatrick. Additionally, introductory materials on plasma physics can be found in books and online resources, such as the work by I.H. Hutchinson. In a lighter display of plasma behavior, a well-known experiment creates a glowing plasma sphere in a microwave by using a grape. This experiment illustrates key principles behind plasma formation and its interaction with electromagnetic fields. A video of this experiment can be found online, providing a visual representation of the process. For those wishing to examine plasma dynamics from a more technical perspective, simulation tools such as OpenPIC3D offer a 3D hybrid Particle-In-Cell approach to modeling plasma behavior. This type of software can be invaluable for researchers and students looking to gain a deeper understanding of plasma physics. In summary, plasmas are a fascinating state of matter with a wide range of applications and areas of study. From classroom learning to practical experimentation and sophisticated simulation techniques, there are many avenues for investigating and comprehending the intricate nature of plasma physics.

The FeaturePak is a modular electronic interface standard designed to enhance input/output (I/O) signal isolation within the primary I/O group. It achieves this by leaving alternate pins on the MXM connector interface unused. FeaturePak cards operate at 3.3V and utilize standard 3.3V logic levels. Additionally, the socket provides a 5V input option for cards that require extra voltage to power auxiliary functions. The standard supports 34 isolated signal pairs, with no specified assignment for the signals in the primary and secondary I/O groups. This adaptability enables FeaturePak cards to be tailored for different application requirements. FeaturePak cards possess defined horizontal measurements of 1.75 x 2.55 inches (43 x 65 mm). There are two choices for the thickness of components on the top side: "tall" FeaturePak modules, which allow components up to 0.4 inches (10 mm) in thickness, and "standard" modules, restricted to a maximum of 0.19 inches (4.8 mm) for top-side component thickness. The FeaturePak standard was introduced by the FeaturePak Initiative at Embedded World 2010, held in Nuremberg, Germany, in March 2010. The Initiative was led by Diamond Systems, the originator of FeaturePak, and included charter members Arbor Technology, Cogent Computer Systems, congatec, Connect Tech, Douglas Electronics, Hectronic, and IXXAT Automation. Later, the FeaturePak Initiative was taken over by a California-based nonprofit organization, the FeaturePak Trade Association, which still supports and promotes the standard.

We introduce an algorithm that allows for the insertion of a set $ S_0 \subset [n] $ into a semistandard set-valued tableau $ T $, referred to as the Forward Insertion Algorithm. This algorithm iteratively inserts elements into rows of \( T \), maintaining the semistandard property. The output, denoted \( T' = S \hookrightarrow T \), is proven to be a semistandard set-valued tableau with specific shape properties related to \( T \) and \( S \). We then construct an inverse algorithm, demonstrating that the forward and backward algorithms are genuine inverses of each other, thus establishing a bijection. Our research introduces the factorial Grothendieck polynomials, defined over an arbitrary field with an indeterminate \( \beta \) and a sequence of variables \( a \). These polynomials are expressed as a sum over all semistandard set-valued tableaux of a given shape, incorporating a novel binary operation \( \oplus \) and its inverse \( \ominus \). We prove that these polynomials are symmetric in their variables and explore their properties, including their relationship to ordinary Grothendieck polynomials and Schur functions. A key innovation of our research is the introduction of the binary operation \( \oplus \) and its inverse \( \ominus \), which allows for a new perspective on the structure of Grothendieck polynomials. We also demonstrate a correspondence between pairs of subsets and tableaux, resulting in a fresh proof of a theorem by Lenart, which plays a crucial role in our investigation. Furthermore, we delve into the properties of the factorial Grothendieck polynomials, demonstrating their symmetry and exploring their implications for the study of semistandard tableaux. Our results encompass known special cases and extend them within a unified framework, providing a comprehensive understanding of these polynomials and their applications in algebraic combinatorics. In conclusion, our work adds value to the field through the introduction of factorial Grothendieck polynomials, demonstrating their symmetry, and setting up a bijection that supports their characteristics. These findings not only enrich the theory of Grothendieck polynomials but also open new avenues for further exploration and application in related areas of mathematics.
