The Ljungström air preheater is a type of air preheater designed by the Swedish engineer Fredrik Ljungström (1875-1964). Ljungström obtained the patent for this invention in 1930. This innovative technology is widely used in modern utility boilers, contributing up to 20 percent of the total heat transfer in the boiler process, while representing only about two percent of the investment. In the 1920s, Ljungström's factory, workshop, and laboratory operations, together with his research facilities, were situated in Lidingö and employed approximately 70 staff members. In the 1930s, the site was transformed into a film studio. Eventually, the facilities were demolished in the 1970s to make way for new industrial premises. The Ljungström air preheater has made a major contribution to improving the efficiency of power plants around the world. It is estimated that this technology has saved approximately 4,960,000,000 tons of oil, making it one of the most successful fuel-saving inventions in history. The American Society of Mechanical Engineers recognized the Ljungström air preheater as the 44th International Historic Mechanical Engineering Landmark in 1995. Today, the Ljungström air preheater continues to be an integral component in numerous modern power stations across the globe, enhancing their operational efficiency and reducing fuel consumption. The technology's enduring legacy is a testament to the ingenuity of its inventor, Fredrik Ljungström, and his contribution to the field of mechanical engineering.

In this section, we delve into the construction of the quantum trace map, a pivotal component of our research, and its implications for the study of ideal triangulations of punctured surfaces. We begin by introducing the coordinate change map, which transitions between different ideal triangulations while preserving the integrity of the associated quantum traces. This map plays a vital role in our analysis of how the quantum trace remains unchanged when the triangulation is modified. Our method is based on the research of Bonahon and Wong, who developed the idea of a split ideal triangulation and set criteria for a link to be properly positioned with respect to this framework. This favorable positioning is crucial for defining the quantum trace on biangle parts and extending it across the whole surface. We define the quantum trace for a stated skein in a biangle, leveraging the state sum method and skein relations to generalize this definition to arbitrary stated skeins. This procedure enables us to associate a quantum trace with every framed link that is in a favorable position relative to a split ideal triangulation. Our study presents the quantum canonical map, a new feature that links a particular quantum trace to any lamination on a punctured surface. This map is first defined for particular laminations and later generalized to all cases by means of multiplicativity. We demonstrate that this map is well-behaved under changes of triangulation, a property that is vital for its applicability in various mathematical contexts. Furthermore, we examine the link between the quantum trace and Chebyshev polynomials, uncovering a connection between matrix traces and these polynomials that plays a crucial role in calculating the quantum trace for higher-weight laminations. The primary contributions of this research lie in the detailed construction of the quantum trace map and the quantum canonical map, which build upon existing mathematical tools and offer new approaches for analyzing quantum surfaces and their properties. Our findings enhance understanding of the interaction between quantum algebraic structures and geometric topological characteristics, paving the way for novel research directions in the area of quantum topology.

In the realm of information technology, various design patterns facilitate the exchange and management of data. These include one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many, and many-to-one relationships. Technological progress has brought forth tools like blogs, wikis, Really Simple Syndication (RSS), tagging, and chat to facilitate these interactions. An example of a one-to-one exchange model implemented by the United States government is the National Information Exchange Model (NIEM). However, it is important to note that one-to-one models alone may not fully support the complex requirements of data exploitation technology. Advanced information-sharing platforms are built to meet these demands through the use of structured terminology, data alignment, and established policies and guidelines for data management. These platforms also adhere to standards for uniform data concerning privacy, security, and data quality. The term "information sharing" gained prominence following the 9/11 Commission Hearings and the subsequent report on the United States government's response to information about the planned terrorist attack on the New York City World Trade Center. The report highlighted the need for improved information sharing across government agencies. In response, President Bush signed multiple executive orders requiring agencies to adopt policies that encourage the exchange of information between different departments. The 2004 Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act also highlighted the significance of promoting information exchange among various entities. An Information Sharing Environment Program Manager (PM-ISE) was appointed to oversee the implementation of the provisions outlined in the Act. The goal was to create a more integrated and effective approach for exchanging information, enhancing national security and intelligence operations. In summary, the evolution of information sharing design patterns and technologies has been driven by the need for improved communication and collaboration among various entities. The United States government has taken significant steps to address these challenges, implementing policies and programs aimed at enhancing information sharing and data exploitation capabilities.

Water conditioners are specially formulated products designed to be added to tap water before its use in an aquarium. They help enhance water quality, creating a safer and more pleasant environment for aquatic organisms. In situations where tap water has been treated with chlorine, a water conditioner with a dechlorinating agent is usually employed. These products commonly include sodium thiosulfate, which aids in converting chlorine into chloride, a substance that poses less risk to aquatic life. Nevertheless, it is important to note that chloramine has gained widespread use in water disinfection processes. Simple dechlorinators are not effective against chloramine and may even release free ammonia, which can be very harmful to fish. To tackle this problem, advanced water conditioners have been created. These products incorporate sulfonates, which are capable of neutralizing both chlorine and ammonia. This creates a more secure habitat for fish and other aquatic life forms. The most advanced water conditioners go a step further by including chelators, such as ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA). These chelators bind and remove heavy metals from the water, further enhancing the water quality in an aquarium. Additionally, some water conditioners contain slime coat protectors, such as polyvinylpyrrolidones or aloe vera extracts. These substances help to protect the natural slime coat on fish, reducing stress behavior and promoting overall well-being. In conclusion, water conditioners are essential for creating and sustaining a safe and healthy habitat for aquatic organisms in an aquarium. They tackle multiple water quality problems such as chlorine, chloramine, ammonia, and heavy metals, and also help reduce stress in fish.

In molecular mechanics, the potential energy function plays a key role in representing the energy of a system based on the positions of its atoms. One method of representing potential energy involves a quadratic expression involving generalized displacement forces, which are connected to the negative gradient of the potential energy function. This method proves especially valuable in the formation of chemical bonds and in assessing the stability of molecular frameworks. The potential energy, represented by V, can be written as a quadratic expression that includes the generalized displacement forces (Gq) and a matrix C, referred to as the compliance matrix. The relationship is given by the following equation: \[ V = \frac{1}{2} G_q^T C G_q \quad \text{(eq. 5)} \] Here, Gq represents the first derivative of the potential energy with respect to the displacement coordinates. It can be expressed as: \[ G_q = H_q Q \quad \text{(eq. 6)} \] In this equation, Hq is a matrix that relates the displacement forces to the displacement coordinates, and Q is a vector representing the displacement coordinates. By substituting the expression for Gq from equation 6 into equation 5, we obtain an alternative formulation of the potential energy: \[ V = \frac{1}{2} Q^T H_q^T C H_q Q \quad \text{(eq. 7)} \] This formulation is advantageous because it is independent of the choice of coordinate system and avoids issues with redundant Hessian matrices, which can complicate the calculation of force constants in traditional methods. The compliance matrix C must be positive definite for the potential energy to be well-defined. This implies that C is the inverse of the matrix Hq: \[ C = H_q^{-1} \quad \text{(eq. 8)} \] This relationship ensures that the potential energy is minimized when the system is in its equilibrium state, which corresponds to the lowest energy configuration. The calculation of compliance constants can be applied regardless of the redundancy of the coordinates, making it a versatile tool for analyzing molecular structures. As an example, the force constants of a molecule like cyclobutane can be calculated using this method, providing insights into the stability and bonding characteristics of the molecule. In conclusion, representing potential energy through a quadratic form involving generalized displacement forces and the compliance matrix provides a robust approach for analyzing the energy aspects of molecular structures. This method is especially effective for modeling chemical bonds and assessing the stability of molecular structures, due to its independence from specific coordinate systems and its ability to handle issues related to redundant Hessian matrices.

The Extended Hubbard Model (EHM) has played a key role in explaining phenomena like metal-insulator transitions, antiferromagnetism, and high-temperature superconductivity. Although it is relatively simple, the EHM captures the essential features of strongly correlated electron systems. However, many aspects of the model remain unresolved. In our previous work, we applied the Self-Consistent Random Phase Approximation (SCRPA) to the one-dimensional EHM, demonstrating its effectiveness in treating electron correlations rigorously. Our findings revealed that repulsive off-site interactions enhance conductivity, as evidenced by the vanishing SCRPA energy gap under strong on-site and intermediate off-site repulsions. However, the one-dimensional character of the model prevents the emergence of ferromagnetism, restricting its use to conventional conductors. Motivated by the discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprate planes, the two-dimensional EHM has garnered significant attention. Solving the model in a general setting, however, remains challenging. While an exact solution has not been achieved, various approximations have been proposed. Recently, E. Kovacs et al. presented an exact solution for a small 4x4 cluster of the conventional Hubbard Model, highlighting the dynamics of electrons described by hopping energy and on-site repulsion. In this paper, we build upon this method by applying it to the EHM, including off-site interactions characterized by the interaction energy V. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 describes the model and the computational technique employed to construct an 85x85 Hamiltonian matrix. Section 3 presents our results for ground and gap energies, discussing the impact of off-site interactions on system dynamics. Finally, Section 4 concludes the paper. The two-dimensional EHM on a square lattice is defined by the Hamiltonian: \[ H = -\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle, \sigma} t_{ij} c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger} c_{j,\sigma} + U\sum_{i} n_{i,\uparrow} n_{i,\downarrow} + V\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle, \sigma, \sigma'} n_{i,\sigma} n_{j,\sigma'} \] This Hamiltonian captures the hopping term \( t \), local repulsion \( U \), and nearest-neighbor repulsion \( V \). For a finite system, the model yields exact solutions for ground state energy, energy gap, and occupation numbers. We examine a 4x4 square lattice at one-eighth filling under periodic boundary conditions, resulting in three distinct particle arrangements along with their associated states. By defining a linear operator \( T \) and leveraging the symmetry properties of the 4x4 cluster, we consolidate the 28800 possible electron distributions into 85 orthogonal cluster states. The Hamiltonian, when applied to the basis vector, results in a non-diagonal r-space basis, necessitating the definition of an 85x85 energy matrix \( E_{nm} \). Computational methods for finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors enable the analysis of localized characteristics within the lattice structure. Our results, presented in Figures 2 and 3, reveal that the ground state energy exhibits a smooth dependence on the on-site interaction \( U \) and a linear dependence on the off-site interaction \( V \). This trend underscores the significant role that off-site interactions play in shaping the electronic properties of the system.

Ophthalmology services have played a major role in Cuba's global medical diplomacy, especially via the Operación Milagro program. This effort has centered on offering eye procedures to Cuban, Venezuelan, and Latin American individuals, both inside Cuba and in other countries. As of August 2007, Cuba had performed over 750,000 eye surgeries free of charge, including 113,000 surgeries for its own citizens. The initiative has continued to grow, with 69 Operación Milagro clinics set up in 15 nations by 2017. By 2019, the initiative had delivered complimentary surgical treatments to more than 4 million individuals in 34 different countries. However, some claims have been made about the program's procedures. In 2017, The Miami Herald reported that people who exited the program claimed that due to daily patient quotas, Cuban medical workers often felt pressured to modify records and throw away drugs. This reportedly stemmed from regular inventory checks that compelled them to match the number of patients they had treated. Those who failed to meet their quotas faced threats of pay cuts or being sent back to Cuba. Other than the Operación Milagro initiative, Cuba has participated in additional medical assistance programs. Since 1990, the country has provided long-term care for 24,000 victims of the Chernobyl disaster, offering treatment for hair loss, skin disorders, cancer, leukemia, and other illnesses attributed to radioactivity, all free of charge. Cuba has also sent its medical teams to nations such as Bolivia and South Africa. Particularly after the 2005 election of Evo Morales, Cuban medical assistance became more prominent in Bolivia. In South Africa, a 1995 cooperation agreement has enabled hundreds of Cuban doctors to work in the country. Concurrently, South Africa has been sending medical professionals to Cuba, fostering a mutually beneficial exchange of medical expertise and services.

In this section, we examine the effectiveness of our suggested approach by means of several examples, highlighting its novel features and key contributions. We analyze different subpopulations within the overall population, distributing expected results to ensure a consistent range that encompasses the predicted outcomes of the subpopulation under examination. Utilizing reliability diagrams, we distinguish between the full population (gray points and lines) and the specific subpopulation (black points and lines). Our initial example examines a combination of subpopulations exhibiting a wide variation in predicted outcomes, with the exception of a small range centered around particular scores. We select a subpopulation with the highest expected outcomes for each score, using a scoring system that concentrates scores near zero. The second example looks at a subpopulation where expected outcomes vary continuously across the full range of minimum and maximum values observed in all subpopulations. The third example analyzes a subpopulation with discrete oscillations in expected outcomes, using a scoring system that is less concentrated near zero. In the fourth example, we introduce weighted sampling, constructing the full population as a mixture of subpopulations with oscillating probabilities of success. We select a subpopulation with a uniform probability of success and introduce three outliers to study their impact on the analysis. Remarkably, we observe that heavily weighted observations can lead to misleading results in reliability diagrams, akin to Simpson's Paradox. However, our method of comparing subpopulations via cumulative differences effectively mitigates this issue by subtracting baseline rates, similar to de-trending. Our findings show that although reliability diagrams and scalar summary statistics reflect certain features of subpopulation discrepancies, they have difficulty in identifying high-frequency variations and the influence of strongly weighted data points. In contrast, our cumulative deviation plots provide a more accurate representation of the subpopulation's expected outcomes, despite the presence of some random fluctuations. Furthermore, we examine the standard training dataset "ImageNet-1000," treating each of the thousand labeled classes as a distinct natural subpopulation. This analysis further validates the robustness and applicability of our method in real-world scenarios. Our innovative approach offers a more thorough understanding of differences among subpopulations, offering substantial advantages to both researchers and practitioners in the field.

We are currently adapting our routines for the parallel PLUTO code to enhance computational efficiency. Our study presents multiple novel features, such as taking into account radiation emitted by the central accretion disk and stars, which influences both the heating of dust and gas and the behavior of AGN dust tori. Our comprehensive radiative transfer analysis shows that infrared radiation pressure plays a significant role only in the inner areas near the midplane, consistent with the results reported by Krolik (2007). However, radiation pressure has a limited impact on large-scale filaments overall, except in regions that are directly exposed, where it could potentially generate outflows along the torus axis. Future studies will concentrate on performing detailed radiative transfer calculations inside hydrodynamic models to gain a clearer understanding of these phenomena. Our study also investigates the impact of weak magnetic fields, which, when combined with shear due to differential rotation, might trigger magneto-rotational instability, facilitating the accumulation of material towards the core. Strong magnetic fields in specific areas could also result in hydromagnetic outflows, possibly increasing the torus opening angle. However, self-gravity and star formation are not yet included in our current models, even though we recognize that certain portions of the inner turbulent disk and filamentary structures are Jeans unstable and could give rise to stars, in line with the findings of Nayakshin (2006) and Paumard (2006). Future studies will include self-gravity in order to better model the accretion process and the impacts of supernova events. In addition to the central accretion disk, we consider the contribution of radiation from stars in the post-starburst phase. Observations of Seyfert galaxies indicate that the light emitted by stars during this phase contributes only minimally to the overall luminosity of the central accretion disk, prompting us to disregard its effect on motion and thermal processes at present. However, we acknowledge the significance of additional mass coming from the galaxy, such as dusty mini-spirals, which may play a role in feeding the AGN. Our approach to simulating the observational properties of dust tori involves hydrodynamic simulations using the TRAMP code, followed by postprocessing to convert gas density into dust density. We employ a constant gas-to-dust ratio and account for different grain species and sublimation temperatures. The resulting dust density distributions are subsequently input into the 3D radiative transfer code MC3D to determine temperature distributions and generate observable quantities such as spectral energy distributions (SEDs) or images across multiple wavelength ranges. Our standard model, shown in Figure \ref{fig:mc3d_hydro}, demonstrates the dust re-emission and central radiation at different inclination angles, providing a basis for comparison with observational data. Our method allows for a detailed comparison with mid-infrared interferometric data and provides understanding that guides our simulations of nuclear star clusters and the supply of material to the central active region. In summary, our study provides a holistic framework for modeling the dynamics and observed characteristics of AGN dust tori, integrating factors such as radiation, magnetic fields, and additional mass contributions. Our findings contribute to the understanding of AGN structure and evolution, with the potential for further refinement through the inclusion of self-gravity and detailed radiative transfer calculations in future work.

The creation of polio vaccines represents a major achievement in the field of medicine. In the initial phase, efforts were undertaken to develop a vaccine by employing spinal cords from monkeys that had been infected with the polio virus, which were subsequently exposed to formaldehyde. One such effort was carried out by Dr. Brodie, who first tested the vaccine on himself and his assistants before administering it to three thousand children. Although some children experienced allergic reactions, the vaccine did not confer immunity against polio. A significant advancement in polio vaccine development took place in the late 1940s and early 1950s, when a team led by John Enders at Boston Children's Hospital successfully grew the poliovirus in human tissue. This achievement laid the foundation for the creation of effective polio vaccines. Enders, along with his colleagues Thomas H. Weller and Frederick C. Robbins, were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1954 for their groundbreaking work. Two kinds of polio vaccines are in use around the globe to fight the disease. The first, developed by Jonas Salk, was tested in 1952 using the HeLa cell line and announced to the public on April 12, 1955. Known as the inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV), it is made up of an injected dose of inactivated poliovirus. In 1954, the vaccine went through large-scale field trials, which at that time were the biggest medical studies ever conducted. It was subsequently adopted for use in the United States in 1955. Following mass immunization campaigns promoted by the March of Dimes, the annual number of polio cases in the country dropped dramatically, from nearly 58,000 cases at its peak to just 5,600 cases by 1957. Eight years after Salk's achievement, Dr. Albert Sabin developed an alternative polio vaccine known as the oral polio vaccine (OPV). This vaccine employs live, attenuated strains of the poliovirus, which can be taken by mouth. The development of these vaccines has played a crucial role in the global effort to eradicate polio.

Uptake assays serve as an important means of identifying essential kinetic parameters like Km, Ki, and Vmax, which play a vital role in elucidating the early alterations in cellular ion levels. One method of measuring these changes involves the use of the radioactive isotope 28Mg. This isotope decays through the emission of high-energy beta or gamma particles, detectable using a scintillation counter. However, the half-life of 28Mg is a mere 21 hours, significantly limiting its use in experimental settings. Since 1990, no facility has been known to routinely produce 28Mg, and the cost of this isotope has escalated, with the price per millicurie (mCi) estimated to be around US$30,000. This high cost and limited availability make it a less practical option for many researchers. The chemical properties of Mg2+ ions are unique, and finding suitable substitutes can be challenging. However, certain cations, such as Co2+, Mn2+, and Ni2+, have been found to mimic the properties of Mg2+ in some enzyme reactions. Radioactive forms of these elements have been successfully employed in cation transport studies. It is important to note, though, that the relationship between enzyme activities with the replacement ion compared to the original can be difficult to determine, which may complicate the interpretation of results. Alternative methods, such as fluorescent indicators, provide a means to examine the dynamics of divalent cations. Several chelators of these cations exhibit different fluorescence spectra in their bound and unbound states. For Ca2+, chelators with high affinity and low interference from other ions are well established. However, Mg²⁺ chelators have not achieved the same degree of advancement, and the primary fluorescent dye used for Mg²⁺, Mag-Fura 2, shows a higher preference for Ca²⁺. This characteristic may limit the applicability of this dye to specific cell types, as it might not accurately reflect Mg²⁺ behavior in all cellular environments.

The concept of vaccine overload has been deemed biologically implausible due to several reasons. Firstly, both vaccinated and unvaccinated children exhibit similar immune responses to infections unrelated to vaccines. Secondly, autism does not fall under the category of immune-related illnesses. Consequently, the notion that vaccines could trigger autism by overwhelming the immune system contradicts the current understanding of autism's pathogenesis. As a result, the hypothesis that vaccines cause autism has been largely discredited by the preponderance of scientific evidence. Regarding prenatal infections, research has established a correlation between schizophrenia and exposure to certain infections during pregnancy, such as rubella, influenza, and toxoplasmosis. For example, a study found that mothers who contracted influenza in their first trimester were seven times more likely to have children who later developed schizophrenia. This finding has significant public health implications, as preventative measures against infections include vaccination, maintaining good hygiene, and, in the case of toxoplasmosis, the use of antibiotics. In animal models, theoretical concerns have been raised about a potential link between schizophrenia and the maternal immune response triggered by viral antigens. A 2009 review concluded that there was inadequate evidence to endorse the routine use of the trivalent influenza vaccine during the first trimester of pregnancy. However, the vaccine is still recommended for use outside the first trimester and in specific situations, such as during pandemics or for women with certain health conditions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists have provided guidelines on vaccination during pregnancy to ensure the health and safety of both the mother and the developing fetus. It is crucial to follow these recommendations to minimize the risk of prenatal infections and their potential consequences.

In this study, we explore the use of supplementary inputs to address the challenges brought about by partial observability in reinforcement learning (RL). Our main contributions consist of introducing new auxiliary inputs along with an extensive experimental evaluation that highlights their efficacy. Specifically, we advocate for utilizing future forecasts, generalized value functions, and predictive state representations to boost learning in partially observable settings. We also suggest combining different forms of auxiliary inputs to capture both past and future information, as well as using them to improve exploration strategies. Our experimental setup involves the Lobster Fishing environment, a partially observable Markov decision process (MDP) where an agent must collect rewards while dealing with stochastic transitions and reward regeneration. We detail the observation vector, sources of stochasticity, and the MDP structure in Figure~\ref{fig:lobster_mdp}. Our experiments employ the Sarsa(0) learning algorithm combined with linear function approximation and the Adam optimizer, testing multiple hyperparameter settings to find the most effective configurations. We compare the performance of agents using auxiliary inputs against two baselines: an observations-only agent and an optimal agent with full knowledge of the environment's dynamics. The observations-only agent serves as a benchmark for assessing the impact of auxiliary inputs, while the optimal agent signifies the peak level of performance that can be achieved. We introduce two main types of auxiliary inputs for the Lobster environment: exponential decaying traces and particle filtering. The decaying traces capture the history of reward collection, while particle filtering provides an approximate belief state based on particle weights. Both approaches are incorporated into the agent's state representation, enabling the agent to develop a policy that takes into account extra contextual information beyond the current observation. Our findings, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:lobster_pf_likelihood_3d}, indicate that agents using auxiliary inputs can reach performance levels closer to the optimal agent than those relying solely on observations. This demonstrates the potential of auxiliary inputs to mitigate the challenges of partial observability in RL. In conclusion, our work highlights the importance of considering auxiliary inputs in RL, particularly in complex, partially observable environments. By integrating additional information into the learning process, agents can develop more robust policies that account for uncertainties and improve overall performance. Future research directions include exploring more sophisticated auxiliary inputs and investigating their impact on exploration and generalization in RL.

Inrush current is a phenomenon that occurs when electrical devices, such as incandescent lamps, are powered on. The initial surge of current can be as much as 14 times the steady-state current, and it may last for a few milliseconds in smaller lamps or several seconds in lamps of 500 watts or more. This can be problematic for control circuits and power supplies. Carbon-filament lamps, which are seldom employed nowadays, possess a negative temperature coefficient, implying that their current draw increases as they heat up. However, these lamps do not experience a surge in current. To prevent an inrush current, a resistor can be inserted into the circuit in series, thereby restricting the amount of current that charges the capacitors. While this method is effective, it is not very efficient, especially in high-power devices, as the resistor will have a voltage drop and dissipate some power. Another approach to mitigating the effects of inrush current involves the use of inrush current limiters. Negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) thermistors are widely utilized in various applications including switching power supplies, motor controllers, and audio systems to avoid damage from inrush current. A thermistor is a thermally-sensitive resistor whose resistance changes significantly and predictably with temperature changes. The resistance of an NTC thermistor decreases as its temperature increases. When an inrush current limiter is employed, it generates heat as current starts to flow through it, causing it to become warmer. This results in decreased resistance, allowing a lower current to charge the input capacitors. Once the capacitors in the power supply are charged, the self-heated inrush current limiter offers little resistance in the circuit, resulting in a low voltage drop. This makes NTC thermistors an effective and efficient way to manage inrush current and protect sensitive electronic components.

In the fields of telecommunications, computer networking, and programming, the term "timeout" or "time-out" encompasses a variety of concepts. It generally refers to a network parameter that initiates an event after a set period of time has elapsed. The timeout mechanism is intended to enhance resource efficiency through more effective use of limited resources and prevent extended delays in receiving specific actions or responses. A timeout refers to a set period during which a system waits for a particular event to happen. If the event does not take place within the allotted time, the system will proceed with a predefined action. Importantly, a timeout condition may be revoked if a suitable timeout cancellation signal is detected. Timeouts are crucial in various scenarios where a system needs to wait for an action or response. By setting a timeout, the system avoids indefinite waiting, which can be inefficient and wasteful of resources. Instead, the system takes a predefined action once the timeout period elapses, based on the assumption that further waiting is futile and a different course of action is necessary. Several examples illustrate the application of timeouts in different contexts: 1. In the Microsoft Windows and ReactOS command-line interfaces, the "timeout" command is used to pause the command processor for a specified number of seconds. This allows for a temporary halt in the execution of subsequent commands. 2. In Post Office Protocol (POP) connections, the server typically closes the connection if it remains idle for a certain period. This timeout mechanism ensures that resources are not wasted on inactive connections and are instead made available for other users or tasks. Timeouts play a vital role in optimizing system performance and resource allocation. By establishing appropriate timeouts, systems are able to effectively control their resources and react suitably to different scenarios, thus improving overall performance and user satisfaction.

In this section, we delve into the UAV-to-Ground (UAV-G) communication channel, a critical aspect of the segregated airspace system. We imagine a simple configuration that includes a UAV and a Ground Control Station (GCS), utilizing separate frequency bands for the UAV-GCS downlink and uplink transmissions. Given the usual operational distance of UAVs, we differentiate between line-of-sight (LoS) and beyond-line-of-sight (BLoS) communication situations, with particular attention given to LoS connections because of the expected prevalence of Small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (SUAVs) and Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) UAVs, which typically operate within a restricted range. The UAV-G communication channel is pivotal for various data links, each with its unique requirements. The Air-to-Ground (ATG) payload connection, commonly utilized for video streaming, requires significant data transfer capacity. For surveillance and acquisition (S&A) video links, both latency and throughput are crucial, as these links must be relayed to the GCS or Air Traffic Control (ATC) for decision-making. Command and Control (C2) links, which are vital for ensuring UAV operational capability, focus on reliability and minimal delay, even though they have less stringent throughput requirements. Given these diverse requirements, a flexible wideband communication system is deemed appropriate. Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is seen as a viable option because of its high spectral efficiency, adjustable data rates, and capability to use different spectrum quantities depending on availability and need. Our research specifically examines wideband channel models for ATG links in order to determine the best parameters for the OFDM signal. SUAVs and MALE UAVs generally operate at altitudes below 3,000 meters, with commercial applications often occurring in urban environments. Building on our previous work, we conducted an extensive literature review on ATG channels \cite{Jaber}. From the existing wideband measurement studies, we found that the results presented in \cite{Newhall} best capture the fading behavior for SUAV and MALE channels during the en-route stage. However, these findings are limited in that they lack Doppler spread data and rely on a 2.05 GHz frequency, which is not commonly used in future SUAV and MALE systems. We extracted a power-delay-profile (PDP) prototype characterized by a delay vector $\tau=[0\; 33\; 70\; 115\; 175\; 262\; 405\; 682]$ ns and a normalized power vector $P_{dB}=[0\; -8.7\; -9.6\; -11.3\; -13.4\; -15.2\; -17.0\; -20.2]$. The derived Root Mean Square (RMS) delay spread is $\sigma_{t}=87.5$ ns. Our PDP prototype aligns closely with the 3GPP's rural area channel model, which, for default velocities of $v=\{120,180\}$ km/h and a classical Jakes Doppler Spectrum, suggests an RMS delay spread of $\sigma_{t}=100$ ns. Additionally, a maximum excess delay spread of $\tau_{\max}\approx 1.5$ $\mu$s was observed in \cite{Newhall}. Our innovative contribution lies in the detailed analysis and adaptation of existing channel models to suit the specific needs of UAV-G communications, providing a solid foundation for the development of efficient and reliable OFDM-based communication systems for UAV operations.

This section presents a new method for building a Pickands function that can be easily adapted to fit the data. Our approach provides a highly parameterized approximation that conforms to the requirements of a Pickands function while maintaining computational efficiency. The paper is organized as follows: it begins with a review of prior Extreme Value Copula (EVC) modeling methods, followed by a detailed description of our approach, covering both theoretical and applied components. Subsequent sections include a simulation study and real data application, culminating in a discussion of the method's performance and potential future work. In the related work section, we discuss the categorization of EVC modeling methods into non-parametric and parametric estimation. Non-parametric approaches provide increased adaptability, especially when dealing with skewed data, although they tend to exhibit greater variability. Parametric models show good performance in higher dimensions with slight asymmetry, particularly when applying Khoudraji's asymmetric extension. We highlight the limitations of existing methods and propose a semiparametric approach using splines, inspired by recent advancements in the field. Our method involves a geometric transformation that simplifies the modeling of a Pickands function by converting it into a 2-monotone function. This transformation is achieved through an affine transformation, which maps the support lines of the Pickands function onto a new coordinate system. The resulting 2-monotone function is easier to model and can be derived from the Pickands function using a one-to-one correspondence. This approach allows for a more flexible and accurate representation of the Pickands function, overcoming the limitations of existing methods. The innovative aspects of our research include the development of a new semiparametric EVC model, the use of splines for Pickands function approximation, and the application of the Williamson transform to model an Archimedean generator. Our work seeks to offer a more robust and broadly applicable framework for constructing the bivariate EVC family, especially with regard to handling asymmetry.

In electric motors, a short circuit occurring between the commutator and brushes can lead to several issues. When the power output is several hundred watts, such a short can cause severe commutator overheating, brush damage, and in the case of metallic brushes, potential welding of the brushes to the commutator. It is important to keep in mind that carbon brushes, which are commonly used, would not lead to welding. This type of short circuit is highly inefficient as it rapidly drains the battery and necessitates power supply components to meet much higher standards than required for the motor to operate without the shorting. To address this issue, one possible remedy is to create a space between the commutator plates that is greater than the length of the brush ends. This approach not only eliminates the shorting issue but also increases the zero-torque range of angular positions. When a motor featuring this adjustment is set into motion by an outside force, it will keep rotating continuously. It can also be efficiently deactivated by locking it in a position within the zero-torque angle range, where the commutator does not touch the brushes. This setup is sometimes used in home-made hobby motors, such as those created for science fair projects, and is featured in various published science project materials. However, there is a clear disadvantage to this simple method. The motor now glides along a significant portion of its rotational path twice during each cycle, with the torque fluctuating in pulses. While this may be suitable for applications like electric fans or maintaining the spin of a flywheel, it is not adequate for many other uses. For example, it would be inappropriate for operating the capstan in a tape transport system or any comparable scenario that demands constant, non-stop torque.

The Tsunami UDP Protocol is a high-speed file transfer protocol designed to operate over network paths characterized by a high bandwidth-delay product. It was specifically crafted to overcome the shortcomings of the conventional TCP protocol, which typically faces challenges in performance under those network circumstances. The Tsunami protocol was developed by the Advanced Network Management Laboratory at Indiana University. The protocol enables file transfers by breaking the file into a sequence of numbered parts, with each part being roughly 32 kilobytes in size. This method allows for efficient data transmission by optimizing the use of the available bandwidth. Data transfer takes place between the client and server over a low-bandwidth TCP connection, enabling efficient management of the data flow process. In contrast, the actual data is sent through UDP, taking advantage of its capacity to efficiently manage large amounts of data at high speeds. The use of TCP for control tasks and UDP for data transmission enables the Tsunami UDP Protocol to function as a flexible option for quick file transfers in difficult network conditions. It proves especially valuable in situations where the bandwidth-delay product plays a major role, like in extended distance or satellite-dependent networks. For more information and resources related to the Tsunami UDP Protocol, interested readers can refer to the project's page on SourceForge, which provides additional details, documentation, and community support.

In this study, we investigate the newly developing area of Zero-Knowledge Zero-Shot Learning (ZK-ZSL), which marks a significant advancement compared to Generalized Zero-Shot Learning (GZSL) and Open-Set Recognition (OSR). The ZK-ZSL framework is intended to recognize classes from the original data set and also detect novel, previously unknown classes, without relying on existing information, while at the same time recovering their semantic features. This study tackles two major issues in ZK-ZSL: accurately classifying new entities without existing labels, and the lack of semantic information for these new categories, which may result in biased predictions. Our approach innovatively recovers clustering configurations for both known and unknown classes in the target dataset, leveraging source labels to guide the positioning of observed categories. We introduce a new structural alignment loss that enhances the semantic understanding of unseen classes by making use of their recovered clustering patterns. Through extensive testing across four benchmark datasets, our approach achieves better results in classification accuracy and semantic reconstruction, confirming the efficacy of our new contributions. To further validate our approach, we conducted a hyperparameter analysis on the AWA2 dataset, examining the impact of varying the prediction loss and structural alignment loss parameters, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. We determined that maximum classification and semantic recovery accuracy is reached when both parameters are assigned a value of 1.0, highlighting the reliability of our default settings. The analysis revealed an inverse U-shaped relationship between the parameters and performance metrics, indicating a fragile balance that our method successfully manages. In summary, our work presents a novel technique in the field of visual recognition, pushing the boundaries of what is possible in zero-shot learning scenarios. The innovative aspects of our research, including the structural alignment loss and the method's adaptability to unseen categories, contribute significantly to the advancement of knowledge in this domain.

This section outlines different approaches to estimating multivariate probability density functions, which play a key role in enabling effective Bayesian inference within high-dimensional settings. We begin by examining the estimation of Gaussian distributions, making use of a full covariance matrix for dimensions up to four, and applying a diagonal covariance matrix for higher dimensions, scaled by a factor based on the normal reference rule. For mixture modeling, we suggest employing Gaussian mixtures where the parameters are estimated via the expectation-maximization algorithm, and the number of components is selected using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). In scenarios where the prior distribution is bounded, we introduce truncated Gaussian mixtures that incorporate known bounds within the mixture components. We also investigate the application of vine copulas to break down multivariate distributions into individual marginal distributions and a copula function that models the dependency structures. The optimal copula function is chosen by minimizing the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and the vine structure is determined using a maximum spanning tree with Kendall's tau edge weights. For the marginal distributions, empirical distribution functions are used, combined with Pareto tails to enhance accuracy in the tails, and parametric mixtures that are applicable to both unbounded and bounded variables. The parameters for these distributions are estimated using expectation maximization, with the number of components selected to minimize the BIC value. For regression-based density estimation, we utilize Gaussian process regression, which is flexible and naturally handles multivariate regressors. The Gaussian process is normalized to sum to one by computing its integral and applying a normalization factor. We experiment with two covariance functions, the squared exponential and the Matérn kernel with ν=3/2, optimizing the length scale parameter through cross-validation. Lastly, we discuss the use of importance reweighting, which leverages the initial Monte Carlo samples for direct reweighting, serving as a reference for the approximation methods presented. This method highlights the distinctive features of our work, offering a wide array of approaches for estimating multivariate probability density functions within Bayesian inference frameworks.

Fiber optic communication has transformed the telecommunications industry, enabling fast data transfer with very little signal degradation. The technology initially showcased its capabilities in Long Beach, California, where fiber optic traffic reached a throughput of 6 Mbit/s. This breakthrough paved the way for the widespread adoption of fiber optics in telecommunications networks. One of the earliest wide area network fiber optic cable systems was installed by Rediffusion in Hastings, East Sussex, UK, in 1978. The system utilized cables placed in ducting throughout the town, serving over 1000 subscribers. At the time, the primary purpose of these cables was to transmit television channels that were not available due to local reception problems. The initial transatlantic telephone cable utilizing optical fiber was TAT-8, incorporating Desurvire's refined laser amplification technique. This pioneering cable became operational in 1988, thereby reinforcing the significance of fiber optics in worldwide communication networks. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, industry advocates and research firms like KMI and RHK anticipated a significant rise in demand for communications bandwidth. This increase is due to the increasing prevalence of Internet usage combined with the introduction of consumer products that require substantial bandwidth, such as video on demand services. The rapid expansion of Internet Protocol (IP) data traffic exceeded progress in integrated circuit complexity, as outlined by Moore's Law. Grasping the fundamental components of a telecommunication system is essential for fully comprehending the significance of fiber optics. A transmitter, which is also referred to as an information source, plays a role in transforming information into a signal that can be transmitted. In the fields of electronics and telecommunications, a transmitter, often referred to as a radio transmitter, functions as an electronic device that employs an antenna to produce radio waves. These radio waves are essential for broadcasting and are a vital component of many electronic devices that communicate wirelessly. The use of fiber optics in telecom networks has significantly enhanced data transmission rates, enabling faster and more reliable communication across extended distances. As technology continues to advance, the role of fiber optics in telecommunications is expected to grow, further shaping the way we connect and share information in the digital age.

The act of consuming the placenta, referred to as placentophagy, could be influenced by spiritual beliefs as well as practical considerations. In certain cultures, like Saudi Arabia, customary traditions for honoring the placenta might involve burial instead of eating it. These rituals typically entail delaying the cutting of the umbilical cord until its pulsations cease, thereby reducing blood loss and the risk of infection, and keeping the placenta connected until following childbirth and the initiation of breastfeeding. While placentophagy is rare among contemporary human societies, it gained some recognition in 2012 when American actress January Jones claimed that eating her placenta helped her return to work faster after giving birth. Instances of placentophagy have been documented in certain modern societies. For example, in the 1960s, a Czechoslovakian health authority reported that Vietnamese nurses and midwives of Chinese and Thai descent consumed placentas from young, healthy patients for unclear reasons. The placentas were first stripped of their outer membranes and then cooked with onions before consumption. A cross-cultural ethnographic study conducted by researchers at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, surveyed 179 contemporary human societies and identified instances of placentophagy. This study emphasizes the diversity of cultural approaches to childbirth and the varied customs surrounding the care and respect given to the placenta in different societies. It is important to note that while some individuals may choose to consume the placenta for personal or cultural reasons, the scientific evidence supporting the health benefits of placentophagy remains limited and inconclusive.

In this paper, we examine the perturbative approach to defining scattering amplitudes, which have historically been based on quantum field theory and defined through Feynman vertices and diagrams. We investigate a different framework in which amplitudes are primary, and the $S$-matrix is built from a core set of information and guidelines, referred to as a "diagrammar." Our approach hinges on defining the $S$-matrix through its singularities, a concept that has remained a vibrant and productive area of research. Our central contribution is the construction of an $S$-matrix for a theory of Einstein gravity, augmented by $R^3$ terms, using the singularity structure of three-point amplitudes. We work within the framework of massless theories, utilizing twistor variables to represent amplitudes with a clearly defined "spinor weight." We begin our theory with the standard three-point amplitudes of Einstein gravity and expand it by adding further three-point amplitudes involving higher powers of momenta. These extensions are non-trivial and must exclusively depend on either $\spa{i}.j$ or $\spb{i}.j$. The core of our approach lies in requiring amplitudes to display the appropriate symmetries and singularities. We demonstrate that the entire $S$-matrix can be determined from these vertices if we enforce the amplitudes to factorize on simple poles. This factorization is facilitated by two key shifts: the original Britto-Cachazo-Feng-Witten (BCFW) shift and the Risager shift. Both shifts convert the momenta into functions of a complex variable $z$, maintaining null conditions and guaranteeing the conservation of total momentum. We focus on the leading $\alpha$ contribution to the $S$-matrix, examining both four-point and five-point amplitudes. For the four-point amplitudes, we reveal that the all-plus amplitudes are non-zero and exhibit the correct symmetries when using the appropriate shift. Conversely, the single minus amplitude necessitates the BCFW shift. For the five-point amplitudes, we achieve an all-plus amplitude that maintains full crossing symmetry and is independent of an arbitrary spinor. Our findings not only agree with earlier calculations based on field theory techniques but also match the UV divergent components of gravity across different dimensions. This work underscores the power of on-shell recursive methods in determining scattering amplitudes and provides a fresh perspective on the construction of the $S$-matrix from a minimal set of amplitudes.

Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae. It mainly targets the skin, peripheral nerves, upper respiratory tract, and mucous membranes of the respiratory system. Early diagnosis and treatment with multidrug therapy (MDT) are crucial to prevent complications such as nerve damage and disability. In Indonesia, the prevalence rate of leprosy in the 21st century is slightly under one new case per 10,000 people, with approximately 20,000 new cases detected each year. However, the rate is much higher in specific areas, especially South Sulawesi, which has over three new cases per 10,000 population, and North Maluku, which reports more than five new cases per 10,000 population. The Indonesian government provides MDT free of charge to patients who require it. Several hospitals in major population centers are specifically designed to address the medical needs of those affected by the disease. Although early detection and treatment have improved, approximately 10% of patients in Indonesia have already experienced significant nerve or other damage before being diagnosed and treated. This is often due to a lack of awareness and the pervasive stigma associated with leprosy, which discourages those with the disease from seeking treatment. To combat this stigma and eliminate discrimination against people with leprosy, PERMATA (Perhimpunan Mandiri Kusta) Indonesia was established in 2007. The organization was started by a group of people who had each received treatment for leprosy. They worked to establish connections with key figures among those with the disease in communities in South Sulawesi, East Java, and NTT—three provinces with some of the highest incidence rates of leprosy in the country. Efforts focused on raising awareness, educating the public, and supporting people affected by leprosy are essential for reducing the impact of this disease in Indonesia. By addressing the social and medical challenges associated with leprosy, the country can work towards a future where no one suffers from the consequences of this ancient and curable disease.

High power radio frequency devices play a crucial role in various applications, including industrial radio frequency heating, particle accelerators, and broadcast transmitters. This is especially significant at microwave frequencies, where devices like klystrons and traveling-wave tubes are used for amplification at power levels that are currently unattainable using semiconductor devices. The household microwave oven is a common example of a device that efficiently generates microwave power, utilizing a magnetron tube to produce hundreds of watts. Although solid-state devices made from materials like gallium nitride show promise as potential replacements, they are still in the early stages of development and are quite expensive. In military use, high-power vacuum tubes are capable of producing signals ranging from 10 to 100 megawatts, which may pose a threat to an unprotected receiver's front end. These devices are classified as non-nuclear electromagnetic weapons and were first introduced in the late 1990s by both the United States and Russia. In the music industry, tube amplifiers continue to be commercially viable in specific niches. They are highly valued for their warm sound, performance when overdriven, and their ability to replicate the characteristics of tube-based recordings from previous eras. This makes them popular in audiophile equipment, musical instrument amplifiers, and devices used in recording studios. Many guitarists favor valve amps over solid-state ones because of their distinctive distortion characteristics when pushed to their limits. It is important to note that any amplifier can only accurately amplify a signal up to a certain volume. Once this threshold is exceeded, the amplifier starts to introduce distortion into the signal. Different circuits will cause varying degrees and types of distortion, which can be a desirable feature for some musicians.

Organoastatine chemistry is the study of organoastatine compounds, which are chemical compounds that contain a carbon-to-astatine bond. Astatine, a highly radioactive element, has the longest-lived isotope, 210At, with a half-life of only 8.1 hours. Because of its radioactivity, studying organoastatine chemistry requires the use of tracer methods with extremely small amounts. The challenges resulting from radiation damage, together with issues related to separation and detection, are greater in organic astatine compounds compared to inorganic ones. The majority of research in organoastatine chemistry is centered on 211At, an isotope with a half-life of 7.21 hours. This isotope holds special significance in nuclear medicine due to its superior ability to target and eliminate abnormal thyroid tissue compared to 131I. Astatine-based iodine compounds have been used to create different organoastatine molecules, such as RAt, RAtCl2, R2AtCl, and RAtO2, with R being either phenyl or p-tolyl groups. Alkyl and aryl astatides are relatively stable and have been analyzed at high temperatures (up to 120 °C) using radio gas chromatography. Demercuration reactions have also been employed to produce trace quantities of 211At-containing aromatic amino acids, steroids, and imidazoles, among other compounds. Astatine exhibits properties akin to halogens alongside metallic features, suggesting that analogies with iodine might be useful in certain situations, although they do not apply in all cases. Incorporation of astatine into organic molecules can be achieved through various methods, such as halogen exchange, halodediazotation (replacing a diazonium group), halodeprotonation, or halodemetallation. Despite the challenges associated with the radioactivity of astatine, organoastatine chemistry continues to be an important area of research, with potential applications in nuclear medicine and the development of new radiopharmaceuticals.

The golden ratio, often denoted by the Greek letter φ (phi), is a mathematical constant that has intrigued mathematicians and artists for centuries. It is defined as the ratio of two quantities where the sum of the quantities and the larger quantity are equal, expressed as φ = a/b. This ratio is approximately equal to 1.618033988749895. The golden angle, a concept closely related to the golden ratio, is the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc that is a fraction of the circle's circumference. This fraction is calculated by taking the reciprocal of the golden ratio, which can be written as f = b/(a+b) = 1/(1+φ). Since 1 + φ equals φ squared (φ^2), the fraction f simplifies to 1/φ^2. This implies that φ^2 golden angles can fit within a full circle. The golden angle's numerical value can be estimated by multiplying the fraction f with the total angle of a circle, equivalent to 360 degrees or 2π radians. Thus, the golden angle g can be calculated as follows: - In degrees: g ≈ 360 times 0.381966, giving approximately 137.50778° - In radians: g ≈ 2π times 0.381966, producing around 2.39996 radians. The golden angle exhibits a remarkable occurrence in nature, especially in the area of phyllotaxis, which refers to the organization of leaves on a stem. One well-known example is the pattern of florets on a sunflower, where the angle between adjacent florets is closely related to the golden angle. This configuration is thought to enhance the efficiency of floret packing, ensuring an optimal allocation of sunlight and nutrients. The significance of the golden angle in the natural world has been the subject of mathematical modeling, which suggests that the pattern observed in sunflowers and other plants may arise spontaneously from the solution of a nonlinear partial differential equation on a plane. This emphasizes the strong link between mathematics and the natural world, illustrating the golden angle as a crucial component in the complex patterns seen in nature.

Our methodology hinges on the concept of a 'factorized form', which allows us to express every element $f$ in $F^{\ast}$ as a product of simpler components, each associated with a pair of points on the curve. We consider three distinct types of these theories, each corresponding to a different algebraic structure: the Heisenberg Lie algebra, the lattice Lie algebra, and a central extension of the multiplicative group by the tame symbol. The Heisenberg Lie algebra, a central extension of the geometric loop algebra, is a cornerstone of our local quantum field theories. We define this algebra and its associated modules, which are key to understanding the algebraic structure of our fields. Our definitions are grounded in the continuous bilinear form, which is a fundamental aspect of the algebraic structure of the field. In summary, our research offers a novel perspective on the algebraic structure of fields associated with algebraic curves, introducing new concepts and methodologies that have the potential to enrich our understanding of these mathematical constructs. Our work is characterized by a blend of abstract algebraic theory and concrete examples, providing a comprehensive exploration of the topic.

Acupuncture, a traditional Chinese medical technique, has a lengthy history rooted in various belief systems that highlight the impact of cosmic and earthly forces. These systems held the view that particular elements aligned during specific times, affecting the efficacy of acupuncture treatments. As described by Needham and Lu, acupuncturists of the era used complex charts and specialized terminology to depict these "arbitrary predictions" (Needham and Lu, 140–41). During this period, acupuncture needles were significantly thicker than their modern counterparts, often leading to infections. Contrary to the contemporary understanding of sterilization, it was commonly believed that infections were caused by using the wrong needle, needling at the wrong location, or at an inopportune time (Needham and Lu, 102–03). To tackle this issue, needles were sometimes dipped in boiling water or held over flames, and at other times used while still hot to create a sealing effect at the site of insertion (Needham and Lu, 104). The Great Compendium of Acupuncture and Moxibustion, published in 1601, recommended the use of nine needles. This number may have been influenced by the ancient Chinese belief that nine held magical properties (Needham and Lu, 102–03). Some other belief systems proposed that the human body operated through a cycle, and acupuncture was most effective when used at the appropriate time within that cycle (Needham and Lu, 140–41). Imbalances between Yin and Yang were also viewed as a possible cause of illness in certain belief systems (Needham and Lu, 140–41). The early first century AD marked a significant turning point in the development of acupuncture, featuring early written accounts and the emergence of recognized authorities in the discipline. One of these early works was the *Zhen Jiu Jia Yi Jing*, which appeared in the middle of the 3rd century AD.

Digital twins, as virtual replicas of physical entities, are revolutionizing various sectors by offering real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and optimization. This paper explores the application of digital twins in education, smart cities, transportation, energy, and other industries, highlighting their potential to transform traditional practices. In education, digital twins can offer personalized learning experiences by leveraging AI-driven bots and adaptive learning frameworks. They can help bridge the gap between industry needs and academic curricula, fostering targeted talent development. For instance, Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) can benefit from AI-powered personalization, enhancing the effectiveness of teaching and learning. In the context of smart cities, digital twins can engage citizens in city planning, optimize energy consumption, and improve transportation systems. They can also enable real-time monitoring and control of urban infrastructure, enhancing sustainability and efficiency. Smart grids, for example, can leverage digital twins for dynamic power usage management and predictive maintenance. Our research introduces a new approach for generating digital twins, highlighting five key technologies that support this endeavor: physics-based modeling, data-driven modeling, big data cybernetics, infrastructure and platforms, and human-machine interfaces. Physics-based modeling, though limited in scope, continues to play a fundamental role in digital twin creation, providing essential insights into physical processes. Our approach combines experimental and numerical modeling techniques to create accurate and reliable digital twins. Data-driven modeling, on the other hand, leverages machine learning and AI algorithms to analyze large datasets, enabling predictive analytics and decision-making. This approach complements physics-based modeling, providing insights into complex systems that are difficult to model using traditional methods. Big data cybernetics is another critical component of our approach, addressing the challenges of data security, management, and quality. By harnessing the power of big data, we can develop more accurate and robust digital twins that can adapt to changing conditions and environments. Infrastructure and platforms are essential for supporting the development and deployment of digital twins. Our study investigates the application of cloud computing, IoT, and various other technologies to build scalable and adaptable digital twin platforms capable of addressing a wide range of application requirements. Finally, human-machine interfaces play a crucial role in ensuring the usability and accessibility of digital twins. Our approach focuses on developing intuitive and interactive interfaces that facilitate seamless interaction between users and digital twins, thus enhancing the overall experience and promoting more effective decision-making. In conclusion, our research presents a comprehensive and innovative approach to digital twin development, addressing the common challenges and leveraging enabling technologies to create impactful solutions across various sectors. By combining physics-based modeling, data-driven methods, big data cybernetics, infrastructure systems, and human-machine interfaces, we possess the ability to fully harness the potential of digital twins and drive rapid digital transformation throughout multiple industries.

Taste is a complex sensory experience that is influenced by various factors. The taste of a food item is determined not just by the natural scents in the ingredients and added flavors, but also by other components like flavor enhancers, sweeteners, acidulants, and salt substitutes. Polyols such as sorbitol and maltitol function as carriers in flavoring systems and also impart a sweet taste to the product. Interestingly, the hue of food can greatly influence how its taste is perceived. A research study discovered that enhancing the red hue of a beverage led to an increased perception of sweetness, with deeper colored versions receiving ratings 2-10% higher than lighter shades, even though they contained less sucrose. Food manufacturers often exploit this phenomenon, as seen in the varying colors of products like Froot Loops cereal and Gummy Bears, which often use the same flavorings. Flavor enhancers, commonly referred to as taste enhancers, are umami or "savory" substances that boost the flavor of food without acting as flavorings themselves. They mainly consist of amino acids and nucleotides and are usually applied in the form of sodium or calcium salts. The European Union acknowledges and accepts specific umami flavorings. In Europe, under EU law, substances that exclusively produce sweet, sour, or salty sensations are not considered flavorings (Article 2, Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008). Additionally, flavor enhancers are classified as additives rather than flavorings under EU legislation (Point 14 of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008). This distinction is important for the regulation and labeling of food products in the European market.

\subsection{Experiments on Synthetic Data} Our experiments with synthetic data are designed to assess the effectiveness of our proposed \textsc{Memorize} method in a controlled environment, employing evaluation measures and comparison benchmarks that are not present in actual datasets. We evaluate \textsc{Memorize} using two key metrics: recall probability at a future time point and forgetting rate. These metrics allow us to assess both long-term and short-term retention by adjusting the value of $\tau$. We compare \textsc{Memorize} with three baselines: uniform, last-minute, and threshold-based reviewing schedules. Our results, depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:synthetic_one_card}, demonstrate that \textsc{Memorize} consistently outperforms the baselines in terms of both quality metrics. It also exhibits increased stability across different runs and decreases the required review effort over time as recall likelihood increases. Additionally, we examine the effect of the learning effort parameter $q$, which determines the quantity of review sessions needed. Reduced $q$ values result in faster memorization, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:learning-effort}. Furthermore, we explore the effects of learner aptitude and item difficulty, represented by parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Higher values of $\alpha$ and lower values of $\beta$ indicate quicker memorization. Figure~\ref{fig:aptitude-learner} demonstrates the impact of these parameters on the time required to achieve a particular level of forgetting. \subsection{Experiments on Real Data} In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness of different reviewing schedules using real data from Duolingo, a popular language-learning platform. Our objective is to determine how effectively each schedule distributes review intervals. As we don't have access to real-world data, we depend on likelihood comparisons to evaluate the effectiveness of a specific reviewing schedule for a given (user, item) pair. We utilize a dataset containing roughly 12 million study sessions with approximately 5.3 million distinct (user, word) pairs. After preprocessing, our dataset consists of approximately 5.2 million unique pairs. We estimate model parameters using half-life regression and maximum likelihood estimation. We subsequently compute the likelihood of encountering events for every (user, item) combination under different reviewing timelines. Our methodology allows us to determine how closely a (user, item) pair follows a particular reviewing schedule, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:sample_trace}. Since future recall probability measurements are not available, we focus on alternative quality metrics that do not depend on the choice of memory model.

Food contamination occurs when food products are adulterated with foreign substances, which can happen at various stages of the food production chain, including production, transportation, packaging, storage, sales, and cooking. Contamination may present itself in various ways, such as through physical, chemical, or biological means. Physical contamination occurs when foreign substances are present and may consist of items such as hair, plant fibers, fragments of plastic, or metal. When such an object enters food, it is considered a physical contaminant. If these foreign substances are contaminated with bacteria, it leads to both physical and biological contamination. Common sources of physical contamination include hair, glass, metal, pests, jewelry, dirt, and fingernails. Physical contamination of food poses a significant risk, potentially resulting in harmful effects. It is a natural, albeit accidental, event that happens when food is contaminated with dangerous objects found in kitchens or production facilities during preparation. Unsanitary conditions in these areas increase the likelihood of physical contamination. Consuming food with physical contaminants can pose several risks to individuals, including choking, tooth damage, and internal injuries. Children and the elderly are especially at risk from the negative impacts of food contamination because of their less robust immune systems and delicate physical condition. One of the main causes of physical contamination occurs when food is left exposed and without covers, making it susceptible to possible contaminants. To avoid this type of contamination and ensure consumer safety, it is essential to uphold good hygiene and sanitation practices in food handling areas, particularly in restaurants and other food service facilities.

Interoperability is a critical concept that refers to the ability of different systems, units, or organizations to work together seamlessly. This concept is not limited to physical components but also involves the interactions among organizations and systems, particularly in the areas of communication and computing technologies. At the technological level, interoperability plays a key role in enabling systems to have the required technical features that allow them to function effectively together. This is particularly important in the context of mission compatibility, where the seamless integration of systems and data is essential for the success of coalition partners. One of the key benefits of technological interoperability is its impact on operational and tactical levels. It enhances flexibility by allowing for more efficient communication and coordination between different entities. This is especially important in situations where rapid response and decision-making are necessary. Public safety is another area where interoperability plays a vital role. First responders, such as law enforcement, firefighting, emergency medical services, and other public health and safety departments, need to be able to communicate effectively during wide-scale emergencies. Poor interoperability may impede the sharing of vital information, resulting in slower response times and possibly endangering public safety. Over the past 12 years, significant investments and research have been made in the field of interoperability, particularly in the public safety sector. However, the issue of disparate and incompatible hardware has posed challenges in achieving seamless communication between different agencies. Information systems, including computer-aided dispatch and records management systems, frequently function independently, resulting in the formation of isolated data systems referred to as "information islands." In an attempt to bridge these gaps, agencies have employed inefficient and temporary solutions. Larger agencies have also begun to implement limited interoperable systems, but these approaches have proven to be insufficient. The importance of interoperability in public safety was underscored during the 9/11 attacks on the Pentagon and World Trade Center, where the lack of interoperability was a significant issue. This highlighted the need for improved communication and coordination between various agencies and systems. Further evidence of the challenges posed by a lack of interoperability has emerged in various incidents, emphasizing the need for continued efforts to improve the integration and compatibility of systems across different organizations and sectors. As technology keeps advancing, the necessity of enabling systems to function together smoothly will become even more vital, positioning interoperability as a key component of contemporary communication and collaboration.
