In 1901, it was discovered that high doses of radiation could cause injury in humans. The French physicist Henri Becquerel conducted an experiment where he carried a sample of radium in his pocket. This resulted in a highly localized dose of radiation, causing a radiation burn. This event prompted additional research on the biological effects of radiation, ultimately leading to advancements in medical therapies. Ernest Rutherford, working in Canada and England, made significant contributions to the understanding of radioactive decay. He developed a straightforward equation, commonly referred to as first-order kinetics, to illustrate the process. This equation demonstrated that a specific radioactive substance has a unique "half-life," which is the time it takes for the radioactivity in a sample to decrease to half its original value. Rutherford also introduced the terms alpha, beta, and gamma rays to categorize different types of radiation. He famously converted nitrogen into oxygen through a series of experiments. Most notably, he oversaw the students who carried out the Geiger-Marsden experiment, commonly referred to as the gold foil experiment. This experiment disproved the "plum pudding model" of the atom, which was proposed by J.J. Thomson in 1904. The plum pudding model proposed that an atom is made up of electrons encircled by a positive charge distribution, which counteracts the negative charge of the electrons. However, the gold foil experiment showed that the positive charge is concentrated within a tiny nucleus. This discovery led to the development of the Rutherford model of the atom, which was later refined by the Bohr model. In the Bohr model, the positive nucleus is surrounded by negatively charged electrons. In 1934, Marie Curie's daughter, Irène Joliot-Curie, and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie, continued the work in the field of radioactivity. They人工合成了放射性同位素 and conducted further research that expanded the understanding of nuclear reactions and the properties of radioactive elements.

Johann Bürgi, a pioneering figure in the field of mathematics, sought to revolutionize the way trigonometric functions were understood and applied. In his own words, Bürgi expressed his belief that the traditional methods used by his ancestors were cumbersome and laborious, and he aimed to develop a more efficient and accurate approach. Bürgi's original ideas focused on the method of splitting a right angle into several segments, enabling the computation of sines without relying on intricate polygonal notations. This breakthrough had the potential to simplify the process of finding trigonometric values and make it more accessible to a wider audience. His work culminated in the creation of his seminal tables, which were published in his book "Fundamentum Astronomiæ" around 1586-1587. These tables represented a significant advancement in the field of trigonometry and laid the foundation for future developments in mathematics. It is essential to acknowledge that Bürgi's achievements did not occur in isolation. His ideas were influenced by the works of other prominent mathematicians and astronomers, such as Ptolemy in his "Almagest" and the mysterious Plimpton 322, an ancient Babylonian clay tablet that contains a trigonometric table. In conclusion, Johann Bürgi's contributions to the field of trigonometry were groundbreaking and have had a lasting impact on the way we understand and apply mathematical concepts today. His innovative approach to dividing a right angle and his development of trigonometric tables have made a significant and lasting contribution to the field of mathematics.

In this study, we conducted an extensive analysis of the GLIMPSE catalog, identifying several OH/IR stars together with their corresponding positions. Notably, OH0.3$-$0.2 was identified because of its unique reddish color and luminosity in the TIR, matching its SIMBAD entry as OH0.335$-$0.180. Discrepancies were observed in the reported NIR spectrum of OH$0.335-0.180$, which we attribute to a different object, 2MASS J17470734$-$2844282. Our method involved verifying the SIMBAD data by comparing it with other resources, such as the OH maser list from \citet{1997A&AS..122...79S}, to find and confirm the locations of OH/IR stars. For instance, OH1.5$-$0.0 was identified based on its position and characteristics, matching SSTGLMC G001.4837$-$00.0612, which exhibited a notably red color in the NIR. We also identified OH11.5+0.1, OH15.7+0.8, and OH17.7$-$2.0 through a combination of their positions in the SIMBAD database, their brightness in the 2MASS and IRAC images, and their distinctive red coloration. In certain instances, like OH18.3+0.4, the lack of detection in 2MASS images, combined with its visibility in IRAC images, suggested a highly red feature common to OH/IR stars. For OH359.4$-$1.3, we discovered a bright TIR source in the IRAC band 4 image, which coincided with the OH maser source listed in the catalog by \citet{1997A&AS..122...79S}. The UKIDSS K-band image provided additional support for this identification, revealing two barely resolved sources, prompting us to regard the dimmer of the two as the TIR/OH maser source. In our subsequent analysis of archived data, we studied the long-term variation in brightness of non-variable OH/IR stars using data from the 2MASS PSC, the UKIRT Infrared Deep Sky Survey (UKIDSS), and the Wide Field Camera at the Okayama Astrophysical Observatory. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the characteristics and positions of OH/IR stars, providing a valuable resource for upcoming astronomical research.

In this research, we present new measures—$T_c$, $W$, and $S$—to distinguish among populations and species according to the overall count of individuals. These metrics allow us to detect spontaneous symmetry breaking in biological systems. Specifically, $S$ measures the degree of orderliness based on dominance. Our approach not only identifies the critical point $T_c$ and the Weiss field $W$ but also distinguishes between various ordering states, such as random distribution, dominance of a particular species or population, and their potential phase transitions, including adaptations where $T_s \approx W$. This scenario mirrors the biological application of Bose-Einstein condensation in population dynamics, a concept that has previously been explored but with a different twist, as illustrated in Figure 3. Our model reveals that the phase separation is contingent upon the levels of biological hierarchies, such as populations and species. It allows us to evaluate the adaptive traits that develop throughout evolutionary processes at various points in time. For instance, during a period in which a population holds dominance, that specific population may dominate the community, yet during a time when a species is dominant, the whole species, rather than merely one population, could become the primary driving force. The transition through different phases reflects the development of novel dominant structures, where the results of the chaotic phase remain fundamentally uncertain. The model also indicates that some highly adapted species exhibit greater stability than others. Intriguingly, the zero points of the Riemann zeta function correspond to both adaptive species and prime numbers. The entropy $\ln k$, as presented in this paper, can be roughly estimated by $\pi(k)/k \approx 1/\ln k$, with $\pi(k)$ representing the prime counting function. The interplay between the diminishing prime number density and the increasing entropy suggests that the trend is disrupted only by the presence of higher-order hierarchies. For these organisms, higher-order hierarchies may act as catalysts in the development of adaptive ordered structures. The novel contributions of our work stem from creating these metrics, which offer an alternative framework for examining and interpreting biological systems. By integrating ideas from physics, such as Bose-Einstein condensation, into biological research, we introduce a novel method for studying population dynamics and species interactions. Our findings contribute to the broader understanding of how biological systems evolve and adapt, with potential implications for ecology and conservation efforts.

In literature, the technique of contrast is frequently employed by authors to highlight the differences between two or more entities. The Oxford Dictionary describes contrast as the process of comparing two entities in order to underscore their differences. This technique is widely used in numerous literary pieces. A prime example of contrast can be observed in John Steinbeck's "The Pearl," where a stark distinction is made between the lower and upper classes within the society depicted in the novel. The less privileged members of society, embodied by the protagonist Kino and fellow fishermen, live in simple huts constructed from thatch and mainly rely on fishing as their main means of earning a living. They are depicted as sociable individuals, forming close-knit communities. Conversely, the upper-class residents reside in more luxurious plastered structures and engage in esteemed economic endeavors, like medicine. These individuals are portrayed as being more focused on their economic pursuits rather than social interactions, thus creating a clear contrast between the two social strata. Another instance of contrast can be found in the opening lines of William Shakespeare's Sonnet 130. Here, Shakespeare juxtaposes a mistress with the sun, coral, snow, and wire, drawing attention to the differences between the subject and these natural elements. Contrast is the antonym of simile, another literary device used to create comparisons. In poetic works, poets frequently employ contrast or detailed similes to strengthen their arguments. The metaphysical poets, including John Donne, are known for their use of the conceit, a literary device that involves an elaborate, improbable, and surprising analogy. During the Renaissance era, contrast was commonly employed as a poetic argument, particularly in sonnets. These poems often argue that two seemingly similar or identical items are, in fact, quite distinct, thereby emphasizing the differences between them. This use of contrast serves to enrich the literary work and provide a deeper understanding of the themes and characters presented.

Cultural heritage conservation is a specialized field that requires a deep understanding of various aspects related to the preservation and protection of historically and culturally significant materials. Experts in this field must devise comprehensive plans, strategies, and treatments to ensure the longevity and integrity of these artifacts. A key component of cultural heritage conservation is the knowledge of the materials used in the original fabrication of an object, as well as those used in subsequent treatments and preservation efforts. This includes understanding the chemical and physical properties of a wide range of materials, their long-term behavior, and how they have evolved over time through various craft or manufacturing techniques and processes. Conservators must also be aware of the social and cultural context in which these artifacts are used, as this context can be critically important for understanding their condition, formulating appropriate treatment plans, and recommending future care. This demands knowledge of how culturally significant materials are accessed and used by society, as well as the potential difficulties that arise from these interactions. Safety in the workplace is another crucial aspect of cultural heritage conservation. Professionals working in this area are required to follow federal, state, and local rules and perform their tasks in a way that guarantees the safety of both themselves and the objects they are handling. In addition to hands-on expertise, conservators need a solid understanding of scientific concepts relevant to their field. This includes the ability to access and use scientific literature, assess the validity of published research in conservation and related fields, and apply this knowledge to their work. Recognizing the transformations that take place within cultural heritage across time is equally important. Conservators need to identify and differentiate the origins of these alterations, which may result from natural, chemical, physical, biological, or human factors. This requires a deep understanding of the many factors that can influence the condition of cultural artifacts, such as light, relative humidity, temperature, and pollutants. In summary, cultural heritage conservation is a multifaceted field that requires expertise in materials science, social and cultural context, workplace safety, scientific principles, and an understanding of the factors that influence the condition and preservation of historically and culturally significant artifacts.

Christianity posits that it is possible to discern the existence of God, while atheism asserts the opposite, claiming that there is no God. Agnosticism, on the other hand, maintains a neutral stance, arguing that there is insufficient evidence to definitively confirm or deny the existence of a higher power. In a philosophical essay, Bertrand Russell posits that unusual personal experiences, like hearing a voice from the sky that accurately forecasts particular occurrences, might lead someone to consider the possibility of a superior intelligence. Leslie Weatherhead, a Christian theologian (1893–1976), introduced a nuanced perspective on agnosticism in his 1965 publication, "The Christian Agnostic." He claimed that numerous people who label themselves as agnostics could truly have a more profound understanding of God than certain regular churchgoers who might hold misguided beliefs about the divine. Although Weatherhead's views were considered radical and unpalatable by traditional theologians, his form of agnosticism is less extreme than that of Thomas Huxley, often referred to as "Darwin's Bulldog." Weatherhead believed that the human soul naturally has the capacity to either reject or accept God, because of the inherent nature of free will, but he was confident that ultimately, no person would choose to distance themselves from the divine. In the United States, Robert G. Ingersoll (1833–1899), an Illinois lawyer, politician, and renowned orator of the 19th century, earned the moniker "The Great Agnostic." Ingersoll's skepticism and critical examination of religious dogma, particularly in an 1896 lecture, contributed to his reputation as a prominent figure in the agnostic movement.

Sentimentalism, as a literary mode, has been a significant and recurring aspect of world literature, emphasizing emotions and feelings as the foundation of a person's actions and reactions, rather than reason. This literary movement encompasses various forms, including sentimental poetry, novels, and the German Empfindsamkeit music movement. European literary sentimentalism arose in the Age of Enlightenment, in part as a reaction to philosophical sentimentalism. In the 18th century, England witnessed the rise of the sentimental novel as a major literary genre. This development took place between 1730 and 1780, during the height of the Enlightenment, and subsequently spread to other European literatures. The philosophical underpinnings of sentimentalism primarily originated from Anthony Ashley Cooper, the 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury, who was a student of John Locke. Sentimentalism in both philosophy and literature may at times be difficult to distinguish, since they frequently shape and reflect one another. As philosophical thought developed, literature aimed to mirror these concepts by integrating them into stories and character growth. Consequently, it is common to observe the coexistence of both philosophical and literary movements. Philosophically, sentimentalism was frequently placed alongside rationalism. While 18th-century rationalism focused on the development of the analytic mind as the basis for acquiring truth, sentimentalism emphasized the intrinsic human capacity for empathy, emotion, and moral sensibility. This literary mode sought to explore the depths of human emotions and the complexities of interpersonal relationships, providing a counterbalance to the rationalist approach of the time.

Gottlob Frege, a German philosopher, logician, and mathematician, significantly advanced the field of predicate logic through his publication "Begriffsschrift," titled Concept-script in English, from 1879. This pioneering work broadened the reach of logical analysis, enabling a greater variety of statements to be expressed in logical form, going beyond the constraints of traditional Aristotelian logic. During the late 19th century, German philosophy was largely influenced by Neo-Kantianism. Unlike the dominant psychologism of the era, Edmund Husserl's 1891 work "Philosophie der Arithmetik" argued that the idea of cardinal numbers stemmed from mental processes involving the grouping and counting of objects. Frege, on the other hand, offered an alternative viewpoint in his writings "The Foundations of Arithmetic" (1884) and "The Basic Laws of Arithmetic" (in German: "Grundgesetze der Arithmetik," 1893–1903). He maintained that mathematics and logic have their own public objects, separate from the personal beliefs or mental states of individual mathematicians and logicians, aligning with the ideas of Plato or Bernard Bolzano. Following Frege, the logicists began to advocate a form of mathematical platonism. Frege's influence extended beyond mathematics and logic, as he also played a pivotal role in the philosophy of language and the development of analytic philosophy's focus on meaning. Michael Dummett attributes the linguistic turn in analytic philosophy to Frege's "Foundations of Arithmetic" and his context principle. Frege's major work "On Sense and Reference" (1892) presented his paradoxes and laid the foundation for a theory of indirect reference, which continues to be a key element in the analysis of meaning in language. His 1918 essay "The Thought: A Logical Inquiry" further illustrated his opposition to idealism and psychological approaches, as well as his engagement with language, promoting a platonist view of propositions or thoughts. In summary, Gottlob Frege's work in predicate logic, philosophy of mathematics, and the philosophy of language has had a profound and lasting impact on various fields of study, shaping the course of modern philosophical and mathematical thought.

Phenomenology is a school of thought in philosophy that emphasizes the study of structures of consciousness from the first-person perspective. It focuses on how things appear to us in our experiences and how these perceptions shape our understanding of reality. The approach is primarily descriptive, rather than explanatory, and seeks to uncover the essential features of our experiences. In the early 21st century, phenomenology has experienced an increasing exchange with cognitive science and the philosophy of mind. This cross-disciplinary interaction has resulted in the creation of multiple techniques that seek to combine phenomenology with results from experimental studies. However, not all of these approaches are widely accepted as representing the core principles of phenomenology. Some of the more contentious models that seek to ground phenomenology in naturalistic terms involve neurophenomenology, embodied constructivism, and the cognitive neuroscience approach to phenomenology. These methods frequently bring consciousness down to the physical-neuronal dimension, marking a shift away from the conventional focus on subjective experience within phenomenology. There are other approaches that attempt to account for life-world experiences through sociological or anthropological frameworks. While these perspectives may offer valuable insights, they are not typically seen as central to phenomenology, which is primarily concerned with the individual's subjective experience. For a more thorough exploration of phenomenology, the following materials are available: - References and bibliographies to aid in detailed research. - External links for additional information and perspectives. - Media related to phenomenology at Wikimedia Commons. - Quotations related to phenomenology at Wikiquote. - The dictionary definition of phenomenology at Wiktionary. - Comprehensive articles on phenomenology at the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. These resources provide a wealth of information for those interested in understanding the rich history and diverse perspectives within the field of phenomenology.

William Kurelek, a renowned Canadian painter, is known for his vivid and often deeply personal artwork. One of his notable pieces is a series of panels that depict various scenes from his life and imagination. These panels, rich in symbolic imagery and narrative, offer a glimpse into the artist's personal experiences and the broader social context of that era. The initial panel depicts a scene involving bullying, which Kurelek refers to as a feeling of fear instead of a real recollection. In the scene, a boy is seen pointing and smiling, while a girl watches on. Kurelek reflects on the cruelty of schoolyard tormentors, particularly the girls who took pleasure in his suffering when he tried to stand up for himself. The second panel, referred to as the "fish panel," shows five fish stuck in a pool of water on the prairie, while two more are found in a dry area close by. Kurelek remembers shooting these fish with a slingshot together with his brother, believing there was no escape for them. This scene serves as a metaphor for the harsh realities of life in a closed society, such as a country schoolhouse, where individuals may feel trapped and helpless. In the "peasant panel," a father is shown pushing his son out of the house into a snowstorm. The image does not stem from a particular memory, but instead reflects Kurelek's anxieties regarding the possible severity of parental punishment. He suggests that this scene represents the cruelty of some mid-European parents, who believe they have total authority over their children simply because they were the ones who gave them life. The last panel, labeled "Social Pleasure (Middle Left)," features a carousel with dancing puppet pairs. Kurelek portrays these figures as ragged dolls with forced smiles stitched onto their faces, incapable of real joy because of their lack of personal identity. This panel critiques the superficiality of social connections and the challenge of finding true happiness in a society that often prioritizes appearance over authenticity. Kurelek's panels offer a thoughtful and perceptive look into human experiences, emotions, and societal expectations. Through his art, he encourages viewers to reflect on their own lives and the wider world, promoting a deeper understanding of what it means to be human.

Scholasticism is a method of learning and teaching that was prevalent during the medieval period, particularly from the 11th to the 15th centuries. It is characterized by a rigorous and systematic approach to the study of classical texts, with a focus on dialectical reasoning and logical argumentation. The term "scholasticism" is derived from the Latin word "scholasticus," which means "pertaining to schools." The origins of scholasticism can be traced back to the Carolingian Renaissance of the 8th and 9th centuries, when there was a revival of learning and education in Western Europe. However, it was during the High Middle Ages that scholasticism truly flourished, particularly in the universities of Paris, Oxford, and Bologna. Scholasticism was heavily influenced by the works of ancient Greek philosophers, such as Aristotle and Plato, as well as by Christian theology. The scholastics sought to reconcile the teachings of the Church with the insights of secular philosophy, often through the use of logical analysis and argumentation. This led to the development of a distinctive style of thought that combined elements of both faith and reason. One of the most famous scholastics was Thomas Aquinas, an Italian Dominican friar and theologian who lived in the 13th century. Aquinas is best known for his work "Summa Theologica," a comprehensive summary of Christian theology that draws heavily on the ideas of Aristotle. His approach to theology, which emphasized the importance of reason and logical argumentation, became a defining feature of scholasticism. Another prominent figure in the development of scholasticism was Peter Abelard, a French philosopher and theologian who lived in the 12th century. Abelard was known for his innovative teaching methods and his emphasis on the use of dialectical reasoning in the study of theology. His work "Sic et Non" is a classic example of scholastic dialectic, as it presents a series of arguments for and against various theological propositions. Scholasticism was not without its critics, however. Some, such as the English philosopher and theologian John Duns Scotus, argued that the scholastics placed too much emphasis on reason and logic, at the expense of faith and divine revelation. Others, like the English poet Geoffrey Chaucer, satirized the scholastic method in their works, suggesting that it was overly abstract and removed from the realities of everyday life. Despite these criticisms, scholasticism played a significant role in the intellectual life of the medieval period. It helped to lay the foundations for the development of modern Western philosophy and theology, and its influence can still be seen in many aspects of contemporary thought. Today, the examination of scholasticism continues to play a significant role in the history of ideas and the comprehension of the intellectual traditions that have influenced Western culture.

The Phra Say is a highly respected Buddhist figure in Thailand, along with two other notable images referred to as the Phra Seum and Phra Souk. These images are thought to have great religious and cultural significance throughout the nation. The Phra Seum is situated in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, whereas the Phra Souk resides in Lopburi, a province located north of Bangkok. In addition to these Thai masterpieces, the Phra Bang holds immense respect in Laos, made entirely of gold. The expertise required to produce the Phra Bang is often associated with Sinhalese origins rather than Lao, implying a major cultural exchange between the two regions. The Phra Bang is regarded as one of the most renowned sculptures in Laos, and it is thought to house relics of the Buddha, which adds to its religious importance. For those interested in learning more about the art and culture of Laos, the Ministry of Information and Culture, in collaboration with Visiting Arts, provides a comprehensive cultural profile. This overview provides important information about the nation's artistic legacy and traditional customs. External links and media related to the art of Laos can be found on platforms such as Wikimedia Commons, which houses a wealth of information and visual resources on the subject. References and further reading on the topic can be sought through various reliable sources, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the cultural and artistic landscape of Laos and its neighboring countries.

In 1989, artist Jeff Koons faced a lawsuit for copyright infringement brought by photographer Art Rogers. The disagreement focused on Koons' sculpture, "String of Puppies," which closely mirrored Rogers' black-and-white photo. This image had appeared on an airport souvenir card that Koons had bought. Koons claimed his work was a form of fair use and parody, yet the court decided in favor of the opposing side. The ruling took into account Koons' considerable artistic achievements and how he was portrayed in the media. The court also dismissed the parody claim, differentiating between parodies of contemporary society as a whole and those targeting a particular piece. The court concluded that parodying a specific, obscure work was not enough to justify a claim of fair use under the original. In a separate case in October 2006, Koons successfully defended his work by invoking "fair use." For a seven-piece painting commission at the Deutsche Guggenheim in Berlin, Koons utilized a portion of a photograph by Andrea Blanch entitled "Silk Sandals by Gucci," which appeared in the August 2000 edition of Allure magazine. The photograph depicted legs and diamond sandals, which Koons incorporated into his painting "Niagara." This artwork also featured three more sets of female legs, depicted in a dreamy style throughout a composition made up of pies and cakes. In his decision, Judge Louis L. Stanton of the U.S. District Court determined that "Niagara" was a "transformative use" of Blanch's photograph. He concluded that the painting's use did not "supersede" or duplicate the original photograph, thereby supporting Koons' claim of fair use. This case highlighted the difficulties in evaluating fair use in the art world, as the line between inspiration and imitation can blur.

Pragmatism, a philosophical movement that originated in the United States during the late 19th century, has faced various criticisms and interpretations over the years. Some initial criticisms of positivist views on scientific methods emphasize the importance of value judgments in factual statements, acknowledge the role of aesthetics in daily life, and place logical reasoning within the framework of political, cultural, and societal factors. Critics also argue that pragmatism links dominant discourses with domination, realigns theory with praxis, and resists the turn to epistemology in favor of emphasizing concrete experience. Feminist philosophers have identified Jane Addams as a founder of classical pragmatism. Mary Parker Follett, another important figure in feminist pragmatism, focused on organizational operations during the early 20th century. The ideas of John Dewey, George Herbert Mead, and William James are also consistent with many feminist principles. Addams, Dewey, and Mead developed their philosophies while interacting with each other and engaging in social activism, including their involvement in the Hull House and women's rights causes. In 1908, Arthur Oncken Lovejoy, in his essay "The Thirteen Pragmatisms," criticized the ambiguity in the concept of pragmatism. He argued that many pragmatists failed to recognize the distinction between the effects of the truth of a proposition and the effects of belief in a proposition. Lovejoy identified 13 separate philosophical viewpoints, all grouped under the heading of pragmatism, highlighting the diversity and complexity inherent in the movement. The Franciscan friar Celestine Bittle also presented multiple criticisms of pragmatism in his 1936 book, "Reality and the Mind." Bittle's analysis added to the continuing discussion about the nature and consequences of pragmatism as a philosophical method. Despite these critiques, pragmatism remains influential across multiple disciplines such as philosophy, psychology, and the social sciences, as it promotes a practical and flexible approach to addressing and solving complex problems.

The protagonist, having returned from a long absence, finds himself unknown to his family and friends, as no news of his return had reached them in the twelve months since his departure. After a brief period, he explains the reasons for his visit and, upon settling his affairs, contemplates a return to New York. His brother suggests a gathering of their siblings the following morning to explore alternative solutions. They advise him to stay in safety, believing that no one would trouble him if he were to remain at home, and recommend that he make his presence known in the neighborhood where he is well-known, while avoiding the towns. They predict that after a few days, he would no longer draw attention. Heeding their advice, he visits the King's Cove and is astonished to find that even those who knew him do not recognize him until they hear his voice. On the Sabbath, he attends a service at Trevean, where he experiences a profound spiritual awakening. The congregation, particularly the Methodists, are overjoyed to see him, having heard of his transformation. This unexpected return to his homeland fills him with awe and gratitude for God's mercy. As he participates in the preaching and meetings, he is initially reluctant to lead a hymn or pray aloud, having not done so before his return. However, after overcoming a period of intense inner turmoil, he embraces his new role with trepidation and begins to share his spiritual journey with others. His congregation grows rapidly, and prayer meetings spring up in various locations. Within eight or nine weeks, numerous individuals are converted, and their meetings are characterized by a mix of prayer, singing, crying, and praise. During a particularly memorable prayer meeting, he feels as if he is in the presence of the divine, much like his experiences in New York. Despite some initial resistance from older members, many others support his newfound calling. He emphasizes the importance of sharing one's thoughts with those who truly understand the ways of God, rather than those who may not comprehend the spiritual journey. As his spiritual journey progresses, he travels through the country, speaking to people in a clear and simple manner. He shares a story about being invited to speak at a chapel that is eight or nine miles away from his home, and when he arrives, he is confused for Captain Harry Carter. Despite his initial fear and uncertainty, he proceeds to address the packed chapel, drawing on his personal experiences rather than a specific biblical text. Despite the growing support for his ministry, he continues to grapple with self-doubt and the fear of being called to a task he may not be ready for. He acknowledges the immense burden of his calling and the physical and emotional toll it takes on him. However, he remains steadfast in his commitment to spreading the word of God. In February 1791, or just prior to that time, the enthusiasm of the Trevean society starts to decline, yet the gatherings continue to be spiritually uplifting. In late March or early April, he is summoned by a prominent individual from the neighborhood who expresses concern over potential trouble brewing against him. The man recounts a conversation he overheard in Helston, where a group of men were puzzled as to why he, being a Methodist preacher, was allowed to preach openly without encountering any legal repercussions. Fearing for his safety, the man advises him to return to America to avoid potential legal troubles and imprisonment. He offers to provide a letter of recommendation from a nobleman, which he believes could be beneficial for him. The fellow, who knows his family well, accompanies him for part of the way back, prompting him to ponder his next course of action.

"Gentlemen, I present to you a tall and splendid woman, noble in form, with a commanding nose that exudes majesty. She held a deep affection for me, and her lineage was equally impressive. Her uncle, a law stationer, suffered a financial setback of eight hundred pounds. This brings us to the three distinct types of this honorable profession. In my opinion, their respective ranks have not been accurately determined. Perker has consistently been held in high regard and esteem; Dodson and Fogg have encountered widespread disapproval; Mr. Pell, however, has remained largely unnoticed. Let us now assess the merits of these three gentlemen fairly. If Perker were alive today, he would likely face trial for his role in the Eatanswill election scandal. What is the real issue with Dodson and Fogg, aside from the Ramsey affair? That incident is merely a tale recounted by the clerk Wicks, whose credibility is questionable. What else did Dodson and Fogg do to warrant such public disdain? They initiated a lawsuit for breach of promise to marry, a move that some may argue should never be pursued. They also made a minor arrangement regarding costs, which, while unprofessional, does not justify the harsh criticism they have received. As for Mr. Pickwick, he had no complaints about their conduct, and it was quite inappropriate for him to use such language under the circumstances. However, there is nothing to be said against Mr. Pell, aside from a minor overstatement regarding his friendship with the Lord Chancellor, which is something we can all relate to. While I advocate for Mr. Pell to be recognized as the foremost in this matter, I regretfully assign Mr. Perker the third position. Now, let us move on to discuss the counsel mentioned in this remarkable work. Before delving into the more prominent figures, I would like to highlight a lesser-known member of the Bar, Mr. Prosee. Few of you may have heard of him, but he once dined with Mr. Perker at Montague Place, Russell Square. The gathering was rather dull, with attendees including two country agents, Mr. Snicks, the Life Office Secretary, Mr. Prosee, the eminent counsel, three solicitors, a Commissioner of Bankrupts, a special pleader from the Temple, a young man with keen insights on the law of demises, and several other distinguished individuals. I have always associated Mr. Prosee with the Equity Bar, perhaps due to the suggestive nature of his name. Now, let us turn our attention to the more renowned counsel, Serjeant Snubbin. "We've done everything necessary," Mr. Perker stated. "I have retained Serjeant Snubbin." "Is he a capable man?" Mr. Pickwick inquired. "Capable?" Perker replied. "My dear sir, Serjeant Snubbin is at the pinnacle of his profession. He receives triple the business of any other man in court and is involved in every case. However, I must mention that among our profession, we say that Serjeant Snubbin leads the court by the nose." "I would like to meet him," said Mr. Pickwick. "Meet Serjeant Snubbin?" Perker responded in disbelief. "My dear sir, that is impossible! To see Serjeant Snubbin, one must first pay a consultation fee and schedule a meeting. It cannot be done otherwise." Thus, Mr. Pickwick faced the challenge of meeting his own counsel. He could not comprehend why, after hiring a professional and paying for their services, there should be any obstacles preventing access to them. I will not discuss tonight whether or not the legal profession should be divided into two parts, but I do argue that any system that hinders litigants from having full personal communication with those they have paid to represent them is both anomalous and absurd. However, Mr. Pickwick was a determined individual, and he did manage to meet Serjeant Snubbin. He delivered a short address to the learned gentleman that was not only worthy of his attention but also of every member of the Bar, including your humble servant. "Gentlemen of your profession," Mr. Pickwick continued, "you witness the worst aspects of human nature. All its disputes, ill-will, and animosity are laid bare before you. Through your work with juries, you start to grasp just how significant the outcome is, and you might find yourself tempted to believe that others are motivated by a wish to deceive and place their own interests first—remarkably similar to the methods you use with complete honesty and genuine commitment to your clients. I believe this is the reason for the common, albeit vulgar, perception of lawyers as suspicious, distrustful, and overly cautious. Despite the potential disadvantage of making such a statement under these circumstances, I have come here to make it clear, as my friend Mr. Perker has said, that I am innocent of the charges against me.

The figure in the painting is colossal, her voluminous dress accentuating her presence. She simpers in profile, her elongated chin contrasting with her precariously slanted posture. The lamplight, emanating from below as if she stands on a grand platform, casts peculiar shadows across her expansive face. In the background, the figures of musicians, dressed in black with white shirts, stand out against the wall, their shadows blending with signs, guitars, and smeared fingerprints. This artwork captures a vivid sense of reality with remarkable breadth and boldness. However, its weakness stems from the disturbing impact it has on the viewer, which is regrettable because the image of a graceful and passionate dancer is not naturally unpleasant. "El Jaleo" errs on the side of ugliness, and beyond the dancer's cumbersome skirts, it lacks a sense of tranquility. This stands in sharp contrast to the attractive, dark-skinned figure in the Tangerine-themed painting featured at the 1880 Salon. This work, created during the artist's trip to the African coast while he was in Spain, portrays a woman standing on a carpet under a large white Moorish arch. Her hands raise her voluminous drapery, casting her head in shadow, with only her painted eyes and brows visible above her bandaged mouth. She gazes down at the fumes of a beautiful censer or chafing-dish on the carpet, her muffled contemplation and pearl-colored robes under the gleaming plastered arcade transporting and tormenting the viewer. The artwork is stunning, showcasing a brilliant blend of white hues, serving as a clear demonstration of the artist's ability to distinguish between closely related but separate shades. When dividing the accolades Mr. Sargent has garnered for his finest works, it is crucial to recognize the merit of his 1882 painting of four little girls, which was exhibited the following year to much acclaim. The artist has created a vivid, somber French setting, offering a complete portrayal of a family's playful environment, marked by an unusual approach that avoids the usual symmetrical placement of figures. The scene comes together as a unified whole, yet the children, wearing their white pinafores, are portrayed with remarkable intensity and poetic style, each showing a distinct sense of individuality. Two sisters stand hand in hand at the back, accompanied by a pair of towering, ornate jars that seem to share in the life of the painting. The porcelain and the children's aprons shine side by side, as a mirror in the background reflects the light. Another girl, with abundant hair and slim legs, stands to the left, and the youngest sits on the floor, playing with her doll. The genuine ambiance of the work, the charm of its overall impact, the gentle, realistic style, together with the understated symbolism, innate intuition, and perception, all contribute to positioning this artwork as a significant accomplishment for a young artist at the age of twenty-six. Mr. Sargent is sometimes criticized for a lack of "finish," but if finish signifies the ultimate expressiveness of touch, "The Hall with the Four Children" can serve as a permanent reference. If the Spanish dancer's portrait illustrates the potential pitfalls of Impressionist practice, this painting showcases the triumphs it can achieve. Just like the young lady holding the flower, this piece invites the viewer to reflect on what still lies ahead for the artist. It raises the question of whether it is advantageous for an artist to master their craft so early in life, potentially leading to a sense of irresponsibility or a lack of reverence. Such reflections belong to those who remain skeptical even in their most sincere praise, thinking perhaps it would be better for an artist to struggle with unresolved challenges. When this is not the case, the question of the artist's future becomes more focused. "What will he do with it?" we ask, referring to the artist's honed skills. It becomes a matter of responsibility, and we hold the artist to a higher standard. This is the case with Mr. Sargent; his extensive knowledge of painting may lead him to play with it or even waste it. Although he has focused on a limited range of subjects, primarily portraits, his willingness to experiment and take risks distinguishes him from those who stick strictly to the literal. Mr. Sargent's work has been predominantly represented by portraits, but there are a few subject-pictures that stand out. A small painting exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery, for instance, depicts a group of Venetian girls engaged in humble household tasks in the dim hall of an old palazzo. The light filtering through the shutters illuminates the scagliola pavement, and the vegetables they work with are painted with such enchanting detail that they appear as valuable as magnified pearls. The figures are remarkably natural and vivid, and the painter's touch is light and fine, evoking the small, familiar Venetian realities without succumbing to the clichés that often plague depictions of Italy. Noir fiction, a genre characterized by its dark, moody atmosphere and morally complex characters, has a rich history that spans several decades and continents. Pioneered by American writers including Elliott Chaze, Charles Williams, Gil Brewer, Harry Whittington, Peter Rabe, and Lionel White, alongside David Goodis and Jim Thompson, this style has continued to evolve and grow through the years. In the 1980s, Black Lizard, an American publisher, played a significant role in reviving interest in noir fiction by re-releasing many classic works. Today, Akashic Books continues to celebrate the genre with a diverse collection of noir short-story anthologies. The noir genre has also seen considerable growth in Europe, with notable authors such as Jean-Claude Izzo and Massimo Carlotto playing a key role in its evolution. According to Italian publisher Sandro Ferri, "Mediterranean noir" stands out for its exploration of the dual nature of Mediterranean life. These novels often depict Mediterranean cities as places that have been marred by crime, yet still possess a captivating charm. The genre is defined by a dual nature, juxtaposing the Mediterranean lifestyle, which emphasizes fine wine, good food, friendship, and lively social events, against the darker elements of violence, corruption, greed, and abuse of power. Among modern writers who combine aspects of hardboiled and noir fiction, James Ellroy stands out as especially significant. He describes noir as "the most intensely scrutinized aspect of the hard-boiled literary tradition," and highlights its appeal via the "excitement of moral compromise and the giving in to sensuality." Ellroy also recognizes the social relevance of noir, pointing out its exploration of important topics like race, class, gender, and institutional problems. Noir fiction's enduring popularity can be attributed to its ability to delve into the complexities of human nature and society, offering readers a compelling and thought-provoking experience.

The concept of having no opinion, known as [Greek: epochê], is a state that leads to a sense of tranquility called [Greek: ataraxia]. Pyrrho, a philosopher whose questions were posed in a manner reminiscent of Kant, sought not to develop a system of truth but to explore the nature of philosophy itself. His dedication to this pursuit is illustrated by an anecdote from Diogenes, in which Pyrrho was found talking to himself, contemplating how to become a virtuous person ([Greek: chrêstos]). This story reveals a depth of character distinct from the typical skepticism found in Sextus' works. The core of Pyrrho's philosophy and his way of living can primarily be traced back to his individual temperament. His indifference was inherent to his calm nature and was not solely a product of his philosophical beliefs. While this attitude could be aspired to, it could never be fully replicated. One of his disciples observed that in order to genuinely adopt Pyrrho's doctrines, an individual would need to have a comparable disposition. Diogenes records that Pyrrho was the first to propose the rudimentary principles of skepticism, although his ideas were not yet fully developed, as he left no written works. There is no evidence of Pyrrho formulating the Tropes, but it is likely that he recognized some contradictions in sensory experiences, possibly hinting at the Tropes in a nascent form. Among the many skeptical maxims, or [Greek: phônai], the three that are most closely associated with the origins of skepticism are the [Greek: antilogia], the [Greek: ouden horizô], and the [Greek: ou mallon]. Diogenes cites Protagoras as the source for the idea that there are always two opposing arguments for everything. The phrase "to determine nothing" is attributed to Timon's _Python_, and the other two maxims are also linked to him by Aristocles. The [Greek: ou mallon] has a direct connection with Democritus, although the interpretation of this phrase by Pyrrho was likely different, as indicated by Sextus. It is probable that Pyrrho employed all three of these sayings, as suggested by Diogenes. However, this led to accusations from the Dogmatics that the Skeptics were dogmatizing simply by possessing such sayings. Sextus refuted this by arguing that these maxims also encompass their own meaning, similar to how a purgative removes itself along with other harmful substances. In comparing the later Pyrrhonism with the teachings of Pyrrho, there is a stark contrast in the moral stance of the two. For Pyrrho, the equilibrium of the soul was a means to apply to his positive theory of life, whereas for the later Pyrrhoneans, it was the ultimate goal. However, the empirical tendency that characterized the history of Pyrrhonism can be traced back to Pyrrho as its originator. He was an empiricist thinker, and his impact in this area stood in sharp contrast to the dialectical approach of Academic Skepticism. The empiricism of the school is evident in its scientific knowledge, the fact that many Skeptics were physicians, and in the nature of the ten Tropes of [Greek: epochê]. It can be confidently stated that the core doctrines of Pyrrhonism trace back to Pyrrho and his innovative contributions, which served as the foundation for the school's development. However, the more elaborate arguments and the specifics of its maxims belong to later periods. Regarding the relationship between Pyrrhonism and the Academy, the connection is challenging to pinpoint with precision, especially between the time of Pyrrho and Aenesidemus. However, skepticism within the Academy was never entirely the same as Pyrrhonism, even though there were periods in the history of the Academy when the difference was minimal. Arcesilaus, who introduced doubt into the Academy, aimed to return to the dialectic of Socrates. He replaced lectures with discussions, which he believed to be a more Socratic method of teaching. Despite Sextus' assertion that Arcesilaus' skepticism was the closest to Pyrrhonism, his teachings were fundamentally rooted in the dialectical principle, which was in opposition to the empiricism of Pyrrho. The belief in the existence of absolute truth, as held by Socrates and Plato, never completely lost its influence over the Academy. This belief eventually led the Academy back to Dogmatism and paved the way for the Eclecticism that marked its departure from history. The histories of Pyrrhonism and Academic Skepticism were contemporaneous for some time. Timon, the immediate follower of Pyrrho and referred to by Sextus as the "prophet of Pyrrho," was a contemporary of Arcesilaus. His refusal to join the Academy and his writings indicate that he did not view the skepticism of the Academy as identical to Pyrrhonism.

Hans Melzian, a scholar, has contributed significantly to the understanding of the Bini language, which is predominantly spoken in Southern Nigeria. His work, "A Concise Dictionary of the Bini Language," is a valuable resource for those interested in this linguistic field. The dictionary is available for free download, lending, or streaming through the Internet Archive. In addition to Melzian's work, another important document related to the region is the autobiography of Jacob Egharevba, titled "ITAN ẸDAGBỌN MWEN." This autobiography is composed in the Edo tongue, which is yet another major language spoken in Nigeria. The Edo language is spoken by the Edo people, who mainly live in Edo State within Nigeria. Both works offer significant insight into the languages and cultures of Southern Nigeria, enabling readers to gain a greater appreciation of the region's linguistic diversity. The availability of these resources online allows for a wider audience to access and appreciate the rich linguistic heritage of Nigeria.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding the death of Seth Rich, a Democratic National Committee (DNC) staffer, and the subsequent media coverage. Rod Wheeler, a private investigator, was hired by Rodger Stone and a wealthy Trump supporter, Ed Butowsky, to investigate Rich's murder. There were assertions that Rich had disclosed DNC emails to WikiLeaks, but these accusations have mostly been refuted. In May 2017, Fox News published a story suggesting a link between Rich and the FBI, which was later retracted. The story was based on Wheeler's investigation, but he later claimed that quotes attributed to him were fabricated. Wheeler sued Fox News for defamation, alleging that the network had manipulated his claims. The lawsuit was dismissed in August 2018, with the judge ruling that there was no evidence of manipulation. Butowsky also faced a lawsuit from the Rich family, who accused him of exploiting their son's death for political purposes. The lawsuit was dismissed for similar reasons as Wheeler's, with the judge finding no evidence of wrongdoing on Butowsky's part. It is important to note that the claims of a connection between Rich, the DNC, and WikiLeaks have been widely discredited by multiple investigations, including those conducted by the U.S. intelligence community. The consensus among experts is that Russia was responsible for the hacking of the DNC's computer systems and the subsequent release of emails. In conclusion, the Seth Rich story has been a source of much controversy and misinformation. While some individuals have sought to use the incident to advance their political agendas, the evidence overwhelmingly points to Russia as the culprit behind the DNC hacking. It is crucial for the public to closely evaluate the information presented by the media and to rely on trustworthy sources for accurate reporting.

Suppose a President were elected on the promise of expanding military forces immediately following a European war. To consider the potential consequences further would be an insult to our intelligence. The creation of so-called "defensive" alliances, whether directed against or in support of us—should we even be able to convince others to participate—would result in increasing hostility, acts of provocation, and a recurrence of earlier historical disputes. However, if such a catastrophic conflict were to occur, it would not be a tragedy if we had brought it upon ourselves. The real tragedy would be if we lacked the intrinsic value that Germany possesses to justify our actions. The true sorrow would be that we were so preoccupied with the faults of others that we neglected to address our own shortcomings. I Am Woman Marguerite Swawite I am woman: as ancient as the Lebanon cedars and even older; as youthful as the newest green shoot that emerges through the snow in March. My face is turned toward the East, illuminated by the glow of my potential; my hands are restrained by the firm grasp of the lone woman who, driven by desire, sought merely a kiss on her neck and a child cradled in her arms. Today, I am a woman, a bit diminished yet somewhat grown; for I am discovering how to sing not his tune, nor someone else's, but my own, which has dwelled within my heart from the very first day. It will be a grand golden song, though not always gentle with sweet cadence, for I must labor to sing. I am learning to live with emptiness, yet still find peace; to warm my numb hands without flame; to press on without love or offspring, even as my mouth is red and my arms prepared. Yet, I know I will never cease until I have sung it all—every last note. Even in the far-off days ahead, as they call to me at the break of dawn, I shall remain a woman. My song will become sweetly familiar, and he who was once frightened will draw near, singing his separate song, always his own, yet blending its masculine tones with mine. Together, we shall weave a magnificent harmony that surrounds the world with our melodies, celebrating once again the joy of our unity. That day will come... But today, I am weary—the East is rosy with the promise of dawn. (The following is one of the poems in Edgar Lee Master’s “Spoon River Anthology” which has been featured in Reedy’s St. Louis Mirror and has garnered widespread attention. In our view, it ranks as one of the most outstanding works of poetry. Caroline Branson With our hearts like drifting suns, had we only walked as often before the April fields until starlight softened the darkness under the rock, our trysting place in the wood, where the brook turns! Had we only transitioned from courtship like notes of music that merge, into the inspired improvisation of love! But to leave behind the enchantment of the flesh, in which our souls swooned, descending into a realm where time, space, and our individual selves ceased to exist—annihilated in love! To abandon these experiences for a room with lamps; to stand with our secret mocking itself, hiding among flowers and mandolins, observed by all between salad and coffee. To witness his trembling and feel my own premonition, as if signing a bond—not ablaze with gifts and pledges heaped with rosy hands over his brow. And then, O night! Deliberate! Unlovely! With all of our courtship erased by the act of love in a chosen room at an hour known to all. The next day, he sat so listless, almost cold, so strangely changed, wondering why I wept, until a kind of sick despair and voluptuous madness seized us, leading us to make the pact of death. A stalk of the earth sphere, fragile as starlight, awaits being drawn once again into creation's stream. But next time, to be born under the gaze of Raphael and St. Francis, as they pass by. For I am their little brother, to be recognized clearly face to face in a cycle of rebirth in the future. You may know the seed and the soil; you may feel the cold rain fall. But only the earth-sphere and heaven know the secret of the seed in the nuptial chamber under the soil. Throw me into the stream again, give me another trial—Save me, Shelley! Music The Kneisel Quartet and Hofmannized Chopin Albert Spalding What more fortunate combination could be desired than this: Albert Spalding performing the Mendelssohn Violin Concerto with the Thomas Orchestra! On two separate occasions, four thousand people felt genuine enthusiasm; and during both the Friday and Saturday performances, the orchestra members (whose typical unemotional demeanor is their usual reaction) were moved and showed the greatest degree of admiration for the young artist's talent.
