The concept of "creaturely freedom" within libertarianism continues to be a topic of debate among philosophers and theologians. Molinists, who advocate for the compatibility of divine foreknowledge and human free will, concur that entities have freedom in the libertarian sense. However, they argue against the notion that counterfactuals of creaturely freedom lack truth values, as some critics suggest. Some philosophers and theologians who raise the grounding objection propose that instead of counterfactuals of freedom being definitively true, probable counterfactuals are the ones that hold true. This suggests that rather than stating, "God knows that in situation C, being X will freely choose A," a more accurate expression would be, "God knows that in situation C, being X would probably choose A." However, Edward Wierenga has pointed out that probable counterfactuals are classified as contingent truths and thus face the same issue of grounding. Molinists have offered two main responses to this argument. First, William Lane Craig argues that for a counterfactual of freedom to be true, it is not necessary for the events they refer to actually exist. Instead, it is enough that they would exist under the given conditions. This perspective suggests that if God were to create multiple universes in various dimensions, granting libertarian free will to individuals in these universes, counterfactuals of freedom could be grounded based on the events occurring in these different universes. The second reply to the grounding objection raises the question of why God would require the creation of these universes in order to understand the course of events. Some critics argue that the fundamental nature of how events could develop might serve as a foundation for making predictions about what is most probable. This line of reasoning opens up further discussions and objections within the philosophical and theological discourse on divine omniscience and human free will.

Petrofiction, also known as oil fiction, is a literary genre that centers on the significance of petroleum in society and its influence on the human experience. The phrase was initially coined by Amitav Ghosh in 1992 during his review of Abdul Rahman Munif's book "Cities of Salt." Ghosh sought to categorize literary works that examine the petroleum industry and its effects on society, with a focus on the overlooked interactions between oil-producing and oil-consuming countries regarding oil. In 2012, Imre Szeman expanded the definition of petrofiction in an editorial for a special edition of the American Book Review. Szeman suggested that the genre includes any works that analyze "the significant role oil plays in today's society." This broader scope allows for a more comprehensive understanding of how oil shapes various aspects of modern life. The 2000s and 2010s saw a surge in petrofiction works, driven by growing concerns about climate change and the concept of peak oil. Consequently, the term has gained widespread use in literary analysis to examine fiction that challenges societal dependence on a petroleum-driven economy and the cultural values it promotes. Although originally aimed at examining works connected to the oil industry before "Cities of Salt," petrofiction has come to play an increasingly important role in non-Western literature. This genre provides a distinctive viewpoint on the ways in which oil-related interactions overlap with other critical concerns in the Global South. Some scholars have drawn connections between petrofiction and the emergence of climate fiction, as both genres address the challenges and concerns arising from the Anthropocene era. By examining the impacts of human actions on the environment, these literary works prompt readers to consider the importance of sustainable development and responsible environmental management. Notable examples of petrofiction include Abdul Rahman Munif's "Cities of Salt" series, which delves into the lives of those affected by the oil industry in an imagined Arabian Peninsula setting. Other works in this genre continue to shed light on the complex relationship between society, petroleum, and the environment, fostering a deeper understanding of our world's dependence on oil and its implications for the future.

As the travelers descended from their vantage point, the view of Mary's River came into sight. With just two miles remaining on their trip, the Captain started to sing an old song from their past, his voice strong and clear, like that of a professional performer: "The moon, the moon, the jolly moon, And a jolly old queen she is!" She has wandered o' nights for a thousand years, With the finest company. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon!" Why, Garret, the wine merchant, are you taking a nap, my friend? the Captain inquired. "Why don't you join in the chorus?" "To your hand, Captain," Weasel exclaimed, shaking off his drowsiness and singing out the refrain— "Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon!" which he repeated with enthusiasm at each repetition. Dauntrees continued: "She trails a royal following, And keeps a merry mad court, With her chirping boys that walk in the shade, And wake when the bailiff's asleep. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon! "Master Owl is her chancellor, And the bat is his servant; They tell no tales of what they see, But wink when we turn up the can. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon! "Her chorister is Goodman Frog, With a glow-worm for his torch; And all who would make court to her, Must, in truth, be ready to drink. Sing, Hic and hoc sumus nocturno, Hurrah for the jolly old moon!" The song had barely ended—extended by several noisy repetitions of the chorus—when the group arrived at the Fort's gate. The sleepy sentinel opened the door at the Captain's call, and soon, the weary adventurers were enjoying the deep sleep of the truly tired. CHAPTER XII. There remains a rugged trunk, dismembered and unsightly, Waiting for the final bolt to burst And shatter it into splinters. THE DOOM OF DEVORGOIL. The shore of the Chesapeake between Cape St. Michael—known by early settlers as the northern headland at the mouth of the Potomac—and the Patuxent, is typically flat, marked by a clear, pebbly beach. This shoreline, spanning about twenty miles, is intersected by a single creek, that of St. Jerome, which flows into the bay some five or six miles north of the Potomac. The beach, occasionally interrupted by small elevations that would not be considered hills elsewhere but are notable in this area, rises just enough to offer a clear view over the expansive waters and to distinguish the inland landscape for mariners navigating up the bay. At certain points, these gentle hills end abruptly at the tide in the form of a cliff, while at others, they form a knoll that slopes down to the beach, covered in grass. This feature can be seen near St. Jerome's, where the slope descends steeply to the tide level, leaving a strip of low ground about fifty paces wide between its base and the ordinary waterline. It was on this flat area that, in ancient times, stood the dwelling of Paul Kelpy the fisherman—a long, low building made of deal boards, constructed in the shape of a warehouse or magazine. A quarter of a mile down the beach, concealed beneath the incline of the hill and almost hidden by the surrounding vegetation, there stood a simple cottage. Its modest height enabled a person of average height to reach the roof ridge while standing at the entrance. The cottage was small, with only two rooms, the largest of which was no more than ten feet square. It was built of hewn logs, and its door, reinforced with thick nails and a heavy padlock, was secure against any but the most determined intruders. A small enclosure surrounded the cottage, providing space for a few common garden plants that were well-tended. A few acres on the higher plain above the bank showed signs of cultivation, and fishing equipment scattered around, along with a skiff on the sand, indicated the livelihood of the cottage's occupant. The day before the events of our story, about an hour before sunset, a light drizzle fell with a steady wind from the northeast, casting a chilly gloom over the scene and enhancing the sense of solitude. A slender column of smoke curling from the cottage's chimney indicated that someone was living there, as evidenced by the sight of a big, cross-eyed mastiff dog peeking out from beneath the roof—guarding this lonely spot in a sour mood. The waves, driven by the flood tide, crashed almost at the cottage's door with a ceaseless, harsh roar.

Relativism, a philosophy that posits different viewpoints can be equally valid, has faced criticism from prominent thinkers like Hilary Putnam and Susan Haack, who view it as being misdirected. John Dewey, in his book "The Quest for Certainty," criticized what he called "the philosophical fallacy." He argued that philosophers often take for granted specific categories, such as the mental and the physical, without recognizing that these are nominal tools created to address specific issues. This oversight can lead to metaphysical and conceptual confusion. Examples of this fallacy encompass the "ultimate Being" within Hegelian philosophy, the idea of a "realm of value," and the conviction that logic, derived from actual thought, operates independently of the concrete thinking process. David L. Hildebrand encapsulated the issue, stating that a lack of attention to the specific functions of inquiry has led both realists and idealists to project the products of extensive abstraction back onto experience. Pragmatists, right from the start, sought to transform philosophy so that it better reflects the scientific approach. They argued that idealist and realist views generally portrayed human understanding as lying outside the realm of scientific inquiry. These philosophies, according to pragmatists, often relied on either a Kant-inspired phenomenology or correspondence theories of knowledge and truth. Pragmatists criticized the former for its a priorism and the latter for its reliance on the concept of correspondence.

The idea of "human wisdom" has long been a topic of discussion and reflection across different periods in history. In 1920, historian J. B. Bury suggested that the final aim of human progress for many is a society in which every individual experiences complete happiness. However, he also admitted that it is still unclear whether humanity's ambiguous future truly has a beneficial outcome. The idea of progress, Bury argued, is akin to concepts like Providence or personal immortality—it can be seen as either true or false, and its validity cannot be definitively proven or disproven. Belief in progress, therefore, is ultimately a matter of faith. In the 1980s, postmodernist thought began to challenge the grand claims made by modernizers. This movement questioned the very notion of social progress, scrutinizing the actions and visions of radical modernizers like Joseph Stalin and Mao Zedong, who are often viewed as totalitarian despots with a distorted view of progress. Postmodernists claim that the ideas of progress from the 19th and 20th centuries, whether in capitalism or Marxism, are inaccurate. They believe that these ideologies place too much emphasis on technological advancements and material wealth, neglecting the importance of inner happiness and mental peace. According to postmodern perspectives, the notions of dystopia and utopia are fundamentally alike, symbolizing broad narratives that lead to unreachable endpoints. In summary, the idea of progress has been a topic of ongoing discussion and debate. While some view it as a necessary and desirable aspect of human development, others question its validity and implications. The postmodernist perspective offers a critical examination of traditional notions of progress, urging a reevaluation of what truly constitutes societal advancement.

The narrative surrounding Daniel Home and his supposed supernatural abilities has been a subject of intrigue and skepticism for many years. It is claimed that Home had an amazing ability to channel this energy to others, a statement which has sparked both admiration and doubt. However, a more grounded perspective suggests that the phenomena attributed to Home can be explained through more mundane means. Take, for instance, the incident involving a live coal. While some may argue that Home's ability to handle a burning coal without injury shows his supernatural powers, a more plausible explanation lies in the inherent properties of the coal itself. It is not uncommon for certain parts of a coal to be less active, or "dead," allowing for safe handling. Furthermore, the description of Mr. Hall's white hair, described as looking "silvery" against the coal, implies that the coal was not emitting light, suggesting it may not have been as hot as one would typically expect. The involvement of Sir William Crookes, a renowned scientist, adds a layer of credibility to these events. However, it is crucial to keep in mind that even the most knowledgeable people may fall victim to deception. Crookes' account of witnessing Home placing his hands in the fire lacks the precision and detail one would expect from a scientific observer. His description of Home handling a "bright red" coal is also questionable, as it does not account for the possibility that the coal may not have been uniformly hot. The narrative then shifts to the subject of musical phenomena, with Home once again at the center of the discussion. His supposed talent for making spirits play the accordion while he held it is an intriguing assertion, yet it can be readily accounted for by means of sleight of hand and trickery. The conditions under which these performances took place—often in dim lighting and out of sight—provide ample opportunity for trickery. The use of a cage to contain the accordion during a séance led by Sir W. Crookes presents a more challenging scenario. However, the lack of any eyewitness to the keys' movement during the performance casts doubt on the genuine nature of the event. The possibility of a hidden musical box or the use of hooks and loops to manipulate the accordion cannot be discounted. The story of Mrs. Annie Eva Fay, yet another medium who asserted she could communicate with spirits through musical performance, serves as another example of how such acts can be deceptive. Her séances, which involved her sitting in a circle with a bell and a guitar, were designed to create the illusion of supernatural activity. The use of darkness and the presence of her husband, "Colonel" Fay, in the circle suggest that the couple may have been working together to create the appearance of ghostly musicians. The revelation that Mrs. Fay's performances could be replicated through the use of simple tricks, such as the manipulation of tapes and the use of hidden objects, casts doubt on the authenticity of her claims. The fact that she offered to reveal her secrets for a fee further undermines her credibility. In conclusion, while the stories of Daniel Home and other mediums may be captivating, it is essential to approach these accounts with a critical eye. The use of deception, sleight of hand, and the manipulation of the senses are common tools employed by those seeking to create the illusion of supernatural phenomena. Just like any other historical record, it is important to take into account the circumstances, the intentions behind the actions of those involved, and the existence of other possible explanations prior to concluding that these stories serve as proof of the paranormal.

As the solemn silence was broken by the declaration "Condemned to death," a collective murmur of compassion rippled through the crowd. This was followed by a hushed silence as the rest of the document was read out. Another murmur arose upon hearing the sentences: Maroncelli to hard imprisonment for twenty years, and Pellico for fifteen. The Captain signaled for us to descend, and we cast one last glance around before returning to the court-yard. We ascended the grand staircase and were led back to the room from which we had been taken. The shackles were taken off, and we were quickly taken back to San Michele. CHAPTER LIV The prisoners who had been sentenced before us had already departed for Lubiana and Spielberg, accompanied by a police commissary. He was now expected to return and guide us to our destination. However, a month passed before he arrived. To distract myself, I spent my time conversing and listening to others, including Maroncelli, who read me some of his literary works, and I reciprocated by sharing my own. One evening, I read my play "Ester d’Engaddi" from the window to Canova, Rezia, and Armari, and the following night, "Iginia d’Asti." However, during the night, I felt restless and unhappy, having difficulty falling asleep. I was filled with both excitement and anxiety, hoping to find out how my family had reacted to the news of my bad luck. Eventually, I received a letter from my father, which revealed that my last letter to him had not been sent as I had requested from the Inquisitor. This caused me great distress, as my father had been under the impression that I would be released, only to read the dreadful sentence in the Milan Gazette. I could not express the contempt and anger I felt upon learning that my letter had been withheld, and I deeply empathized with the suffering of my family. Although I now believe there was no intention to cause harm through this delay, I still view it as a cruel action, motivated by an intense, tormenting desire to cause immense suffering to my loved ones. I was further enraged to learn that my companions were planning to celebrate Easter week before their departure. As for me, I simply could not fathom the idea of forgiveness, and the thought of joining in such a celebration seemed completely beyond my comprehension. CHAPTER LV Finally, the German commissioner arrived and informed us that we would be departing within two days. He also shared some comforting news: upon his return from Spielberg, he had met with the Emperor in Vienna, who had informed him that our punishment would not last for twenty-four hours, but only twelve. This was meant to signify that the pain would be divided, or half the punishment remitted. Although this information was not officially communicated to us, there was no reason to doubt the commissioner's words, especially since he was open about it and it was known to the entire commission. However, I could not find solace in this news. To me, seven and a half years of imprisonment and seclusion seemed no different from fifteen; I believed it would be impossible to survive such a long time. My health had deteriorated, with severe chest pains and a persistent cough, leading me to fear that my lungs were affected. I ate little and struggled to digest what I consumed. Our departure occurred on the night of the 25th of March. We were allowed to bid farewell to our friend, Cesare Armari. A sbirro chained us in a transverse manner, linking the right hand to the left foot, making escape impossible. We boarded a gondola, with the guards rowing us towards Fusina. Upon arrival, we found two boats prepared for us. Rezia and Canova were placed in one, while Maroncelli and I were in the other. The commissary accompanied two of the prisoners, and an under-commissary accompanied the others. Six or seven armed police guards completed our convoy, some in the boats and others in the Vetturino's box. Being forced to leave one's country due to misfortune is always painful, but to be torn away in chains, exiled to a harsh climate, and confined to solitary dungeons for days, hours, and years, is a fate so terrible that words cannot convey its full horror. Before we crossed the Alps, I realized how much my country meant to me. The sympathy we received from people of all ranks was an irresistible appeal to my affection and gratitude. In every village, community, and even the simplest of dwellings, the story of our trial had made its way, and we were met with eager expectation. In various locations, the commissioners and guards struggled to break up the crowds that had gathered around us. It was remarkable to witness the benevolent and humane feelings expressed on our behalf. In Udine, we experienced a touching incident. Upon arriving at the inn, the commissary ordered the courtyard door to be closed to keep the people at bay.

Eschenbach's "Parzival," the Ethiopian national epic "Kebra Nagast," the legends of Prester John, and the iconography of Chartres Cathedral are among the historical and mythological sources explored in the book. The author, Graham Hancock, posits that the Knights Templar sought the lost Ark of the Covenant and other relics at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem during the 12th century. It is proposed that an Ethiopian monarch in exile, potentially Lalibela, established contact with the Knights Templar while living in Jerusalem during that period. This hypothesis is supported by the architectural legacy of Lalibela, particularly the Church of Saint George, which is intriguing in the context of Gothic architecture's development. The Ethiopian Church, worried about the possible theft of the Ark by the Knights Templar, reportedly sent envoys to Pope Clement V in 1306. The book argues that the Catholic Church's apprehension regarding the Knights Templar gaining the Ark's power was a contributing factor in Pope Clement V's decision to initiate the prosecution and arrest of the Knights Templar in 1307. The book achieved commercial success but was met with unfavorable reviews from critics. Jonathan Kirsch of the Los Angeles Times described it as a blend of travelogue, true adventure, and mystery-thriller, but primarily characterized it as amateur scholarship combined with an imaginative narrative, akin to telling ghost stories around a campfire. Desmond Ryan of the Philadelphia Inquirer playfully raised doubts about how much of the author's work was based on speculation.

Horace Townsend, known affectionately as "H. T.," emerged from a perilous ordeal with a renewed vigor, his cheeks flushed with warmth and his body imbued with a newfound strength. He rose, barefoot and dressed only in his shirt-sleeves, his hair pressed against his forehead and his garments sticking to his skin, presenting an unremarkable appearance yet one that would command the attention of any artist—a man who had just faced a formidable peril driven by selfless kindness. Margaret Hayley, observing his tall and upright form, saw not the slightest hint of anything unromantic. Perhaps in her view, his dark skin appeared to glow with a sort of holy radiance, a symbol of her reverence, standing in sharp contrast to the emotions she had recently been forced to reveal. It was only such a profound estimation that could explain her subsequent actions, which, for a woman of her considerable pride, led to a terrible internal conflict that made any calamity that might have occurred in the waters of the Pool seem like a mercy in comparison. Halstead Rowan, confident in his admiration for his new friend's actions and not in a hurry to voice it, had done what his injured hand allowed—leaping across the stream to retrieve the abandoned shoes and coat from the rock where they lay. While the rest of the group, with the exception of the distraught Mrs. Brooks Cunninghame, who was still tending to her barely revived son, gathered around the new hero to offer their thanks and congratulations, it was Margaret Hayley who took his hand. Ignoring the disapproving scowl of Captain Hector Coles, she said, "I do not know, sir, by what name to thank you—" "I believe I am right in calling you Miss Hayley," he replied, his voice still somewhat weak and tremulous. "My name is Horace Townsend, and I am a lawyer from Cincinnati." Thus, the mystery of the initials was solved, and we can now refer to him by his full name, as those who had noticed the initials but not taken the trouble to learn his full name from the arrival book at the office had done. "I was only half intentionally the cause of your dangerous situation, Mr. Townsend," Margaret continued, "and yet I cannot regret the liberty I took, for it may have saved a life that would have been lost, and allowed me to witness an act of selfless generosity that I will never forget, nor fail to honor for as long as I live." "You do me too much honor," he responded, his voice now a bit steadier. "I have done nothing more than expose my weakness. There was no danger to me in the water, as I am a capable swimmer and should be able to dive well. However, I must have stayed under too long, for I could not find the child immediately, and the cold water undoubtedly affected me after getting warm from climbing over the logs. That is all, and I sincerely hope we can all put this disagreeable matter behind us, as I will definitely do once I manage to find some dry clothing. He spoke pleasantly, yet without the carefree cheerfulness that characterized his rival of the day—the hero of the bear-stakes. As he finished speaking, he bowed and turned away, suggesting that the conversation had reached its conclusion. Margaret Hayley also moved away and rejoined her escort. Halstead Rowan approached with the coat and shoes, and as he placed them on the rock at Townsend's feet, he grasped his hand with his unwounded one, conveying a deep sense of respect and admiration. "I am nowhere!" he exclaimed. "I challenged you over that log, but you have gone where I would not like to follow, and done it for a noble cause, while mine was merely a prank. And by the way—" They had now moved a little away from the rest, and Rowan spoke in a hushed tone, "do you know where your thoughts were when you arrived?" "Hush! For heaven's sake, hush!" Townsend responded urgently, his expression prompting Rowan to immediately cease the conversation. The company quickly started climbing the stairs, transporting the revived child and following closely behind his mother. Townsend managed to put on the discarded shoes over his wet stockings, donned his coat, and joined the rear-guard with minimal assistance. Despite the discomfort of his continued dampness, he was undoubtedly consoled by the thought that he had survived a plunge into the Pool where few men had ventured and emerged alive, and perhaps even more so by other, more complex reflections. An hour later, the whole group had made their way back to the Profile House, where Horace Townsend, now identified by his full name, relished a dry set of clothing, a mild headache, and a rest that left him revitalized, as though he had immersed himself in the Pool for therapeutic purposes.

"Extending MARC for Subject Access," edited by Toni Petersen and Pat Molholt, is a publication by G.K. Hall that delves into the use of MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) for subject access in libraries. The book features multiple articles focused on visual materials, including "Access to Diverse Collections in University Settings: the Berkeley Dilemma" by Howard Besser and Maryly Snow, and "Visual Depictions and the Use of MARC: A View from the Trenches of Slide Librarianship" by Maryly Snow, both released in 1990. In 1991, Tim Berners-Lee began working on a hypertext graphical-user-interface (GUI) and coined the term "World Wide Web" for his program. That same year, "Facilities Standards for Art Libraries and Visual Resources Collections," edited by Betty Jo Irvine, was published by Libraries Unlimited for ARLIS/NA. Additionally, "World Architecture Index: a Guide to Illustrations," compiled by Edward H. Teague, was released by Greenwood Press as part of its Art Reference Collection No. 12. The Visual Resources Association (VRA) established its mailing list, VRA-L, in 1992, providing an essential channel for communication among its members, who are experts in the field of visual resources curation. In 1993, Oxford University Press published the "Users' Guide to The Art and Architecture Thesaurus" alongside the electronic edition. The VRA formed its Data Standards Committee in March 1994. Later in that same year, during September, Marc Andreessen left the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) to establish Mosaic Communications Corp, which later developed into Netscape. Mosaic's launch marked the beginning of the World Wide Web for the general public. Also in 1994, the first image database, SPIRO, made its debut on the World Wide Web. In 1995, the "Concordance of Ancient Site Names" was edited and published, further contributing to the growing body of work on visual resources and subject access in libraries.

The remarkable story of carrier pigeons, a breed with an innate ability to return home from great distances, has fascinated societies for centuries. These birds have been subjected to trials involving travel across hundreds of miles of ocean, yet they consistently navigate their way home with unerring precision. This distinctive ability has proved highly beneficial in numerous human activities, especially in times of war when they were employed to carry messages through enemy territory. A notable instance involved the German Emperor, who, curious about their reliability, sent a batch of these pigeons from England to Germany. Released from Dover, they all made their way back to Düsseldorf within six hours, an occurrence that caused both fascination and worry among the English, which later resulted in a debate within the House of Commons. In another fascinating discovery, a rock in Mexico's Magdalena district, state of Sonora, was found inscribed with characters strikingly similar to Chinese script. A well-educated Chinese individual confirmed the inscription to be authentic, dating back two thousand years and suggesting a Chinese settlement in the region. This calls into question the commonly held belief that Columbus was the first to set foot on the American continent, implying that Chinese explorers may have reached the area far earlier than previously thought. Evidence of widespread Chinese expeditions during the early stages of civilization has also been discovered in the Pacific Islands and Australia. King Menelik of Abyssinia's appointment of a Russian General as Governor-General for provinces around the equator reflects his desire to bring civilization to his people. M. de Leontieff, who had earlier traveled to Abyssinia and carried gifts from the Czar, is anticipated to have a beneficial impact on the country's progress, similar to how General Gordon contributed in Egypt. The text highlights the unity of humankind, implying that the distinctions between different countries are slight, much like the varied abilities present in one household. It shows how environmental factors, like climate and way of life, can greatly affect the physical features of a group over time, as observed in the offspring of people with lighter skin who reside in tropical areas. The author posits that the human races have evolved through detachments from the original human family, each developing unique traits under local influences over thousands of years. The quest to understand the history and origins of various nations is likened to discovering long-lost relatives, prompting curiosity about their journeys and the reasons for their separation from their forebears. The author acknowledges the limitations of written records, which span only a few hundred years, and highlights the importance of other forms of historical evidence, such as inscriptions on buildings and structures. However, the narrative also recognizes the long stretch of time prior to the development of writing systems, leaving the accounts of early humans to be reconstructed from scattered remains and interpretations.

Postmodernism is a complex and multifaceted cultural and intellectual movement that emerged in the mid-20th century. It is characterized by skepticism, relativism, and a general distrust of grand theories and ideologies. Postmodernism has exerted a major influence across multiple disciplines, such as music, art, literature, and philosophy. In the realm of music, postmodernism has manifested in diverse and innovative ways. Jonathan Kramer, an expert in this field, has noted that avant-garde works, which some might classify as modernist, frequently challenge and expand the conventional limits of what is deemed musical. These compositions can be provocative and unsettling, pushing the listener to reconsider their understanding of the art form. During the 1960s, a group of composers, including Terry Riley, Henryk Górecki, Bradley Joseph, John Adams, Steve Reich, Philip Glass, Michael Nyman, and Lou Harrison, sought to move away from the perceived elitism and dissonance of atonal academic modernism. They created music with simpler textures and more consonant harmonies, offering a fresh perspective on musical expression. Concurrently, artists like John Cage questioned the established notions of beauty and objectivity that were prevalent in modernism. Cage's work often incorporated unconventional sounds and methods, further expanding the definition of music. Alongside these advancements in classical and avant-garde music, postmodernism has also had an impact on popular music genres. Dominic Strinati, an author on postmodernism, highlights the significance of "art rock" and the blending of styles seen in the works of groups like Talking Heads and performers such as Laurie Anderson. The Pet Shop Boys' self-conscious reinvention of disco is another example of postmodern musical innovation. Hildebrand Gurlitt was a prominent German art dealer during the Nazi era. From 1939 to 1944, he obtained many artworks, aside from those intended for his private collection. Out of these acquisitions, 168 pieces were earmarked for the Führermuseum, a planned museum dedicated to Adolf Hitler's vision of German art. Gurlitt took advantage of his authorized buying missions to Paris, a city filled with artworks of uncertain origin, some of which have since been identified as stolen. These trips allowed him to expand his own art holdings and amass considerable wealth from commissions on the substantial sums paid by the Nazi regime for art acquisitions. In addition to his official responsibilities, Gurlitt also acquired paintings personally, especially from artists targeted by the Nazis. One such artist was Max Beckmann, who was living in exile in the Netherlands by 1944. Gurlitt and his associate, Erhard Göpel, who served as the regional representative for Hitler's Führermuseum, acquired five pieces from Beckmann in September 1944. Among these was the painting "Bar, Brown," which Gurlitt retained for himself. After Gurlitt's passing, his wife attempted to sell the painting, but she was unable to find a buyer. Some time later, his son Cornelius put it up for sale at an auction held by Ketterer in Stuttgart in 1972, and it was eventually sold for DM 90,000 following the auctioneer's commission. The identical artwork was subsequently put up for sale again at Sotheby's in London, fetching £1.2 million. Beckmann's family did not contest the distribution of the sale proceeds, considering Gurlitt's first purchase legitimate, despite the challenging circumstances faced by the artist at the time. After the war, Gurlitt was captured along with his wife.

In his essay on gardening, Horace Walpole presents a concept that reflects a fundamental principle: the modern method of garden design traces its origins to the invention of the "ha-ha" by Bridgeman, a prominent figure in the field of landscape gardening. The "ha-ha" allowed a garden to blend harmoniously with the surrounding countryside, separated only by an invisible barrier rather than a wall. This concept challenges the notion that a garden lover would prefer nature to art, as a garden is, in essence, an artistic creation that replaces the untamed wilderness. The love for nature, as expressed by later figures like Lord Byron, can sometimes verge on misanthropy, admiring the wild for its own sake. However, the landscape gardener believes that their art should be subordinate to nature, incorporating the wider scenery into their designs rather than excluding it. This outlook echoes that of Telford, who viewed rivers as serving the purpose of supplying canals, and Gilpin, who assessed nature through the lens of the "theory of the picturesque." Gilpin noted that while nature's compositions may be cold and singular, it never succumbs to "mannerism." In other words, nature functions as a sublime landscape artist, whose creations ought to be embraced and integrated by the human gardener. An intriguing illustration of this idea appears in a speech given by Henry Tilney during Jane Austen's "Mansfield Park." According to Walpole's theory, the development of the "ha-ha" symbolizes a growing alliance between man and nature, the landowner and the countryside. This collaboration is reflected in improved roads and inns, the gradual blending of urban and rural areas, and a rising awareness of the issues brought about by crowded cities. The affection for nature has strong origins, as poets since Chaucer have praised the beauty of scenery, the coming of spring, and the grandeur of storms and sunsets. The indifference to nature displayed by the Pope school was a temporary phenomenon, reflecting the self-assuredness of the urban population and their disdain for the rustic outside world. However, the love for field sports remained strong among the squire class, and as they began to receive intellectual influences from the city, they started to express emotions that found clear expression in works like Izaak Walton's "The Compleat Angler." The old poets often used nature as a backdrop for human action, focusing on concrete facts and the joys of sports or rustic amusements. They followed traditional forms and participated in dialogues with fictional shepherds, Robin Hood, or symbolic knights within idyllic woods. In contrast, during Pope's era, nature was regarded as an abstract or metaphysical idea that called for a separate kind of respect and admiration. Pope himself, influenced by Bolingbroke and Shaftesbury, expounded on the stars and the animal world in his "Essay on Man." Shaftesbury, in particular, highlighted the aesthetic view of nature, claiming that the Good, the True, and the Beautiful are unified, and that the universe appears to us as an artistic expression of harmony. This outlook fostered a genuine growth in appreciation for beauty, exemplified by works such as Akenside's "The Pleasures of Imagination" and Henry Brooke's "Universal Beauty." James Thomson's "The Seasons," with its fine "Hymn of Nature," represents this current of sentiment. Thomson's descriptions of nature, intended to serve as a sermon, show a growing interest in country life and a challenge to the supremacy of the urban wit. However, Thomson's philosophy and observation remain somewhat separate, and his masterpiece, the didactic poem on "Liberty," remains largely forgotten. In summary, the affection for nature has changed through the years, shifting from serving as a setting for human activities to being regarded as something worthy of admiration and reverence in itself. The landscape gardener's approach to subordinating art to nature and incorporating the wider scenery into their designs reflects a growing appreciation for the beauty and harmony of the natural world.

He was a jay, indeed, and I had just witnessed his rather cad-like behavior towards Mrs. Bevidge," one character remarked. "Then I'm at a loss as to why you were in his company," another responded. "Oh, you do understand, Alan. You mustn't apply logic here! It's like questioning how you became more serious than sober." The brother laughed, unable to argue. "It was the excitement," he explained. "But you can't indulge in such behavior, Bess," he chided, his tone heavy with the weight of his own past mistakes. "I know I shouldn't, but I do," she retorted. "I understand it's detrimental to me, if not to others. Let's make a pact to stop!" "I'm always ready to make such a promise," the young man agreed, his voice tinged with melancholy. He added, "But you have a sharp mind, Bess, and I dislike seeing you act foolishly." "Do you truly, Alan?" the girl inquired, seemingly pleased by his criticism as much as his compliment. "Do you think I have a sharp mind?" "You're the only girl who does," he affirmed. "Oh, I didn't mean to ask for that much! But why can't I utilize it effectively? Other girls draw, play music, write. I only seek the excitement that's bad for me. I wish you could explain it." Alan Lynde did not attempt to answer. The question appeared to draw his attention inward, leading him to experience a sense of discouragement. "I possess a sharp mind too, I believe," he began. "Lots of them!" his sister interjected, generously. "There's no man who can compare to you. If I could talk with you all the time, I wouldn't need the company of jays. I'm not flattering you. You're always a feast of reason; I have no interest in emotional outpourings. You always take the right view of things when you're being yourself, and even when you're not, you're not stupid. You could be anything you chose." "The problem is that I can't choose," he replied. "Yes, I suppose that is the problem," she agreed. "You shouldn't use such language, Bess," her brother admonished, sternly. "Oh, I don't with everyone," she defended herself. "Never with ladies!" He glanced at her with a smile that was both rueful and humorous. "You got me, I guess," he admitted. "'Touché,' Mr. Durgin says. He fences and speaks French. It's like an animal speaking French; you always expect them to speak English. But I don't mind your swearing in my presence; I know it helps to dissipate the tension." She laughed, and coaxed a laugh from him as well. "Is there anything to him?" He asked, once their laughter had died down. "Yes, quite a bit," Bessie replied thoughtfully, and then she went on to recount all that Jeff had told her about himself, describing his composure in dealing with the benevolent Mrs. Bevidge, as she referred to her, and sketching his character as she perceived it. Her sketch was filled with astute conjectures and she made it entertaining for her brother, who, from his own perspective of mischief, undoubtedly judged the original more intelligently. "Well, you'd better avoid him after this," he advised at the end. "Yes," she agreed pensively. "I suppose it's like developing a taste for a very common type of whiskey, isn't it? I see what you mean. If one must indulge, it should be in champagne." She turned to him with a look that showed both sharp and restrained comprehension, a demeanor that consistently renders women's speculations on vice either amusing or deeply touching to men. "Better avoid the champagne as well," her brother suggested darkly. "Yes, I know," she conceded, slumping back in her chair and staring wistfully into the flames. After a while, she asked abruptly, "Will you stop if I will?" "I'm afraid I couldn't," he replied. "You could try," she encouraged. "Oh, I'm accustomed to it," he said. "Then it's a deal," she declared, jumping from her chair and going over to him. She smoothed his hair over his forehead and kissed the spot she had smoothed, despite its unpleasant dampness to her lips. "Poor boy, poor boy! Now, remember! No more jays for me, and no more sprees for you. Goodnight." Jeff Durgin was uncertain whether Miss Bessie Lynde intended to attend Mrs. Bevidge's Thursday gatherings or not.

Social inequality refers to the existence of unequal opportunities and outcomes for different groups of people based on social factors such as race, gender, socioeconomic status, and others. The roots of social inequality are complex and multifaceted, ranging from broad problems such as wealth disparity and resource distribution choices to narrower issues like ambiguous data regarding the poorest populations and differences in school environments. One of the primary causes of social inequality is institutional discrimination, which refers to policies and practices that give preferential treatment to some groups over others based on their social identity. For instance, racial bias in employment or educational access may restrict opportunities for specific groups and maintain social inequality. Additionally, individual characteristics such as implicit biases and stereotypes can also contribute to discrimination and perpetuate social inequality. Another macro-level factor that plays a role in fostering social inequality is income segregation. Income segregation refers to the spatial separation of different income groups into distinct neighborhoods, with wealthier individuals living in prosperous areas and those with lower incomes residing in less prosperous areas. This may limit access to resources and opportunities for residents in low-income areas, perpetuating social inequality. Development prioritization is another factor that contributes to social inequality. Development initiatives such as infrastructure, housing, and economic expansion are generally given greater attention in affluent areas, while less prosperous regions are often neglected.

Cooking is the process of preparing food in a manner that makes it safe to eat and also enhances its taste and texture. However, in order to accomplish this objective, it is necessary to have knowledge of the different cooking techniques. Different cooking methods can be classified based on the use of heat and moisture. The core of grasping cooking methods and how they affect food is realizing that heat and moisture are essential in determining the way food is prepared and the outcome it produces. There are several methods of cooking that primarily differ in their use of heat and moisture. Firstly, cooking techniques that utilize dry heat are those that take place without the addition of water or any other liquid. These methods include roasting, grilling, broiling, baking, and frying. In these techniques, the food is exposed to dry heat, which causes the Maillard reaction, leading to the formation of desirable flavors and textures. Conversely, moist heat cooking techniques use a liquid medium, such as water, broth, or wine, to cook the food. These methods include poaching, simmering, boiling, steaming, and braising. Water or some other liquid helps in cooking food at lower temperatures and helps in the transfer of heat more efficiently, making the food tender and moist. Furthermore, a combination of dry and moist heat methods is used in some cases.

Trade secrets include formulas, methods, techniques, and other confidential information that give a business an edge over its competitors. Without adequate protection, trade secrets could be accessed or stolen by competitors, resulting in significant financial losses, reputational damage, and other adverse effects. Therefore, safeguarding trade secrets is crucial for the success of every business, and unlawful access or leakage of trade secrets may lead to serious legal repercussions. One of the most common forms of trade secret protection is through agreements, with non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) being the most popular. NDAs limit the ability of employees and other individuals with access to trade secrets from sharing that information with others or utilizing it for personal gain. Other types of agreements include non-compete provisions, which restrict former employees from working for a competitor within a specified period following their employment termination, and non-solicitation pacts, which prohibit employees from persuading clients or colleagues to switch to another company. Technology also plays a critical role in safeguarding trade secrets. Encryption tools help protect digital documents and messages, and access restrictions ensure that only authorized individuals can see particular information. Common security tools like passwords, firewalls, and antivirus programs are often employed to defend against cyber attacks. Trade secret holders also have legal options available to them, such as the possibility of taking legal action against involved parties.

Organizational structure describes how teams, departments, or whole organizations are organized and controlled. Different types of organizational structures include functional, divisional, matrix, and flat structures. Each structure has its own implications on decision-making and communication within a team, which can impact the effectiveness of achieving team goals. Functional structures rely on well-defined job roles and clear chains of command. In this structure, individuals with similar skills and expertise are grouped together, such as marketing or finance departments. This allows for clear communication and decision-making within teams who understand the specific tasks required of them. However, inter-departmental communication can be sluggish, and decision-making might suffer from a lack of creativity and innovative thinking as a result of isolated perspectives. For instance, if the marketing team focuses only on marketing goals, they may miss opportunities that would be obvious to other departments, such as product development. Divisional structures involve a company organizing its activities into separate areas based on geography, like various countries or states. This structure allows for customized approaches to local markets, as each region operates independently. However, communication among regions can be challenging, which can lead to inefficiency and a lack of coordination. Matrix structures combine functional and divisional structures. In a matrix setup, teams are organized according to their specific field of expertise, but they also focus on a specific project or assignment.

Democracy represents a form of governance where citizens play an active role in making decisions. There have been many forms of democracies throughout history, including ancient Athenian democracy and modern democracies. While modern democracies share several features with Athenian democracy, they differ notably in aspects like inclusiveness, representation, and who can vote. One of the most significant differences between modern democracies and Athenian democracy is inclusivity. Athenian democracy excluded certain groups, like women and slaves, from engaging in political activities. In contrast, modern democracies have evolved to be more inclusive by allowing all citizens to be involved in political participation regardless of their gender, race, or social status. Another notable difference between the two forms of democracies is representation. Athenian democracy operated as a form of direct democracy, allowing eligible citizens to directly vote on laws and policies. Conversely, contemporary democracies have moved towards representative democracy, in which citizens choose representatives to act on their behalf. This transition has enabled greater representation of more varied and extensive populations, irrespective of their social standing or place of residence. Moreover, voting eligibility is another aspect that differentiates modern democracies from Athenian democracy. In current democracies, the voting privilege is contingent upon citizenship status.

Robert Nozick's theory of entitlement is a philosophy that fundamentally supports the principles of free-market capitalism. According to Nozick, individuals have a right to the fruits of their own labor, and this right to property should be respected and protected by the state. Therefore, any attempt to redistribute wealth by force violates an individual's entitlement, and consequently, Nozick believed that taxation should be minimal or non-existent. The implications of Nozick's theory are significant for economic justice. Theoretically, if everyone starts off with equal opportunities in society where property rights are protected, then any outcome is just. This acceptance of unequal outcomes is contentious, with some believing that this is a failure to acknowledge the socio-economic inequalities that people were born with, and that some may never be able to overcome. Furthermore, there is evidence that supports the argument that entrenched economic inequalities perpetuate across generations. Additionally, Nozick's entitlement theory overlooks the possibility that property rights can originate from sources other than labor, such as inheritance, social ties, or private trusts. Therefore, wealth does not stem exclusively from personal exertion. People are born into different economic situations, and although hard work may bring some benefits, the chances for success are not the same for everyone.

A confidence interval consists of a set of values reflecting the degree of uncertainty about a population parameter, depending on the sample used in the research. The concept of confidence intervals allows researchers to attach a certain level of confidence to the estimate and determine how accurate it is likely to be. Colonialism is the term which describes the process of an imperial power establishing political and economic control over a region outside its borders, seeking to exploit the region's resources and impose its culture and governance on the people who reside there. The roots of colonialism date back to the Age of Exploration during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, as European nations such as Spain, Portugal, France, and England started exploring and engaging in trade with areas outside Europe. There were several essential characteristics that defined colonialism. Firstly, it was a project of empire-building, with imperial powers seeking to establish and maintain their dominance over foreign territories and peoples in order to expand their own influence and wealth. Secondly, colonialism entailed the imposition of European culture, values, and systems of governance upon the native populations, frequently via the administrative structures of colonial administrations. Thirdly, colonialism depended on the extraction of natural resources and the utilization of local labor to create wealth for the colonizing powers, while providing little advantage to the indigenous communities. The impact of colonial governance reached far and wide, leaving lasting effects that continue to shape international relations and social systems in the present day. On the contrary, colonialism brought new technologies, products, and ideas to regions that had previously been cut off from the wider world, enabling greater access to fresh resources and information.

Plato's allegories, including the Allegory of the Cave and the Divided Line, have been widely studied and interpreted since they were first introduced in his famous work, Republic. The allegories serve as a representation of the different levels of awareness, knowledge, and understanding that characterize human life. While these allegories were written over two thousand years ago, they still hold significance in the modern world, specifically in relation to people's attachment to social networks. The Allegory of the Cave describes a group of people who have been chained up their entire lives inside a cave, unable to see anything other than shadows on the cave wall. The only reality they know is that which is presented to them by these shadows. When they are eventually freed and led out into the daylight, they are first struck by the brightness of the light and find it difficult to grasp the reality that now confronts them. This metaphor illustrates how our view of reality is often limited by prior experiences and personal perspectives. Similarly, the Divided Line allegory emphasizes the idea of different levels of knowledge and understanding. According to the allegory, human grasp of reality is divided into four separate phases: imagination, belief, understanding, and pure reason. The allegory emphasizes the importance of moving past basic belief and imagination, striving for true understanding and pure reason.

The original oath functioned as an ethical guideline and set a benchmark for conduct among medical practitioners and their trainees. The original oath prohibited doctors from performing abortions or euthanasia, forbidden the use of poison, and emphasized the importance of confidentiality between patients and doctors. It also required doctors to provide adequate care to their patients regardless of their social status. Over the centuries, the Hippocratic Oath went through various revisions, reflecting changing attitudes, cultural values, and ethical considerations. The contemporary form of the Hippocratic Oath differs considerably from its original version. For instance, the current edition places greater emphasis on the duties of physicians toward their patients and their broader role within the healthcare system. The revised Oath now centers on addressing ethical issues such as informed consent, confidentiality, and the importance of these principles.

Slavery and racism are closely linked, as the former established the economic and social base for the latter. While slavery has existed in various forms throughout human history, the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of millions of Africans in North and South America was a unique and unprecedented system of bondage that shaped the course of world history. The origins of racism can be traced back to the economic benefits of using enslaved African Americans. At the heart of slavery was an economic system that relied on the unpaid labor of enslaved Africans to create wealth for their owners. Enslaved Africans were treated as property rather than human beings, and their labor was considered a commodity to be bought and sold on the open market. The slave trade brought millions of Africans to the Americas to work on plantations, in mines, and in domestic service. The exploitation of enslaved Africans was justified by a system of racial categorization that placed white Europeans at the top of a hierarchical social order, with Africans and other people of color considered inferior and subhuman. This ideology was reinforced by religion, science, and other cultural institutions, and it served as a justification for the brutal treatment of enslaved Africans. The dehumanization of enslaved Africans greatly shaped American society, playing a key role in shaping racism as a widespread social problem.

This process is referred to as nitrogen fixation, occurring through the activity of nitrogen-fixing bacteria. After nitrogen fixation, it becomes available for plant uptake and supports their growth and development. Tech giants Netscape and Microsoft made an unusual announcement yesterday, declaring the "browser wars" to be silly and pledging to work together to improve and standardize web technology. However, even with their stated commitment to cooperation, tensions and rivalry continued to exist between the two firms. The browser wars in question refer to the ongoing battle between Netscape's Navigator and Microsoft's Internet Explorer, which have been vying for dominance in the browser market for years. The competition has been intense, with both companies trying to outdo each other with new features, faster speeds, and better user experiences. But now, in the face of evolving market conditions and a more established web industry, the two companies have come to recognize that their competition has been unhelpful. In a joint statement, representatives from Netscape and Microsoft agreed that "the battles of the past are pointless in today's web ecosystem," and announced their intention to work together towards a common goal. The statement outlined plans to improve the interoperability of web technologies, with a focus on advances like HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript. The two firms also committed to working together on security protocols and data protection, areas that have grown more critical as cyber threats continue to rise. However, even though this appeared to be an agreement, tensions arose during the press conference where the truce was announced.

This move is expected to enhance the stability of the region, promote unity, and deter any security threats. The proposal was put forward by Italy's Prime Minister, Giuseppe Conte, at a meeting with the heads of state from Slovakia and Romania, and garnered widespread approval. In his remarks, the Prime Minister lauded the contributions made by Slovakia and Romania to NATO, particularly in peacekeeping missions, and urged members of NATO to support their integration. "We strongly support the inclusion of our eastern partners, Slovakia and Romania, into the NATO family. We believe this will not only strengthen the security of the region but also promote unity and mutual solidarity among our member countries," said Prime Minister Conte. The integration of Slovakia and Romania into NATO is crucial for regional security and stability. Both nations have encountered various security challenges, such as cyber threats, terrorist activities, and pressure exerted by Russian military presence. Joining NATO would provide them with the security they need to address these threats and promote stability in the region. In addition, bringing new members into NATO would strengthen the organization's dedication to collective defense, which is outlined in Article 5 of the NATO charter.

International Partners to Invest US$4.7 Billion to Double Production in Australia's Largest Gas Project International partners have pledged to invest US$4.7 billion to double production in Australia's largest gas project. The investment will be made in the Gorgon gas project, located off the coast of Western Australia, and will help meet the growing demand for natural gas. The Gorgon project is a joint venture between Chevron, ExxonMobil, Royal Dutch Shell, and Australian energy company Woodside Petroleum. The project began production in 2016 and currently produces 15.6 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) annually. The funds will be allocated to construct a new offshore production facility and improve current onshore infrastructure. The new offshore module will be the fourth production unit at the Gorgon project, and will enable the joint venture partners to extract gas from an additional area within the Gorgon field. The expansion project is expected to create over 1,000 jobs during construction and support an additional 350 jobs during operations. It is also expected to generate significant economic benefits for Western Australia, including increased tax revenues and royalties. The Gorgon project plays a crucial role in Australia's energy strategy, offering a dependable and stable supply of natural gas.

Boeing Co. has reported an impressive 13% increase in profit for the third quarter, citing high sales of commercial planes and rising interest income. This news comes as a welcome relief to the aviation giant, which has been grappling with the fallout from the 737 MAX grounding and the COVID-19 pandemic. The company's revenue for the quarter was $19.98 billion, beating analyst estimates and showcasing a 10% increase from the same period in 2019. The gains were largely driven by the delivery of 28 wide-body aircraft, including the 787 Dreamliner and the 777. Furthermore, Boeing's interest rate hedge portfolio contributed to $84 million in pre-tax earnings for the quarter. The strong performance was reflected in the company's share prices, which rose by 3% after the earnings report was released. Shares have climbed more than 50% since hitting a low in March, indicating growing investor confidence in the company's ability to rebound from recent difficulties. Boeing CEO Dave Calhoun said the results were a "testament to the resilience of our team and the quality of our products and services." He also acknowledged that the company's recovery would take time, given ongoing uncertainties around the pandemic and the aviation industry as a whole.

Barclays has announced that it is restructuring its Global Markets division in an effort to compete more effectively with its rivals. The investment banking arm of the British lender is hoping that the changes will help it to revive its fortunes after several years of lacklustre performance. The restructuring will involve splitting the Global Markets department into two separate units, one focused on sales and trading functions and the other dedicated to strategic advisory services. The move is intended to improve the efficiency of the bank's operations and make it more responsive to changes in market conditions. According to Barclays, the changes are part of a broader strategy aimed at "strengthening the bank's competitive position in key markets". The bank has faced difficulties in keeping up with competitors in recent years, with numerous investors pointing to the absence of a defined strategy as a significant issue. The restructured Global Markets division will be headed by Tim Throsby, who was appointed as chief executive of Barclays International in 2017. Throsby has a strong track record in the financial services industry, having previously worked at JP Morgan and Citigroup. Commenting on the restructuring, Throsby said: "We are focused on building a business that is client-centric, agile and efficient. By reorganizing our Global Markets division, we will enhance our ability to operate with greater efficiency.

CA, a leading provider of enterprise software solutions, stated that acquiring Cheyenne Software will enhance its standing in the storage management market. Cheyenne Software, based in Alpharetta, Georgia, is a major player in the storage management space. The company provides backup and recovery software for a variety of different operating systems and platforms. According to the terms of the deal, CA will acquire all of the outstanding stock of Cheyenne Software for $30 per share in cash. This signifies a price increase of over 35% above the present market value of Cheyenne Software's shares. "We are delighted to be acquiring a company of Cheyenne Software's caliber," said Ken Cron, president and CEO of CA. This acquisition will allow us to strengthen our position as market leaders in storage management, while also offering a range of complementary products and technologies that will enhance our ability to meet customer needs.
